#3421. Meet the Biggest Ralph Lauren Fan in France

Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes. When I heard about a Parisian who had amassed thousands of Ralph Lauren pieces, my curiosity got the better of me and I wanted to learn more. Séverin Naudet, a former digital adviser to François Fillon when he was France’s prime minister, lives on the fifth floor of a beautiful Haussmann-style building. The tall, dark-haired 50-year-old appears not to age. Since leaving his role with the government in 2012, he has started a digital marketing company and is now also exploring opportunities in luxury and wellness.

At his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true. He shows me dozens of pairs of sneakers, tuxedo jackets and velvet shoes, pants and shirts, more jackets, and then there are also mugs, books, and pillows. In the bedroom, the linens bear the American designer’s label, while tableware from Ralph Lauren’s Burleigh Collection, carefully wrapped up and placed in a Carrefour bag, is ready to be taken to his house in Brittany, where “more sailboat-inspired” pieces are stored. There are also sorbet-colored swimsuits piled on the plump armrests of a club chair. “About 20 years ago I donated all my other clothes to a charity. Since then, I’ve worn nothing but Ralph Lauren,” he explains, barefoot and dressed in jeans and a Polo shirt, next to a jacket from Denim & Supply, a Ralph Lauren brand that existed from 2011 to 2016 and is now coveted by collectors. Naudet’s Ralph Lauren pieces represent more than just a wardrobe; they embody a way of life that embraces every facet of the American brand founded in 1967—from preppy cool to sophisticated, Gatsby-style chic, and including many nautical pieces that connect to another of Naudet’s passions: sailing.

A selection from his collection of sneakers and dress shoes

But how does one fall in love with a brand to the point of making it part of every facet of their life? “As a teenager, I had body image issues. I had bowlegs, and I didn’t feel comfortable in my own skin,” he explains. Walking into a Double RL store changed everything: “I tried on a pair of Low Straight jeans and it was magical—they were perfectly cut, elegant, and stylish. I almost felt sexy. I had straight legs and a nice butt,” he says with a laugh.

His connection to the American brand speaks volumes about that magic formula that is the goal of retailers around the world: combining storytelling with emotional attachment. “Polo was the cure for a certain melancholy that was the result of a gloomy childhood. Ralph Lauren instilled in me a spirit of joy, where yellows, pinks, and sky blues, stripes and madras fabrics, evoke summer, the sea, and sailing,” explains the man who has amassed several thousand Ralph Lauren items.

As retail experiences increasingly take place online, there’s nothing Naudet loves more than going to a physical store. Walking into one is like stepping into “the family home I never had,” he explains. “A Ralph Lauren flagship store can feel like visiting a house in the Hamptons, a Parisian hotel for a perfect Christmas, or a New York apartment with a view of Central Park.” Ralph Lauren locations are must-visits on the entrepreneur’s itineraries. In Manhattan, he always visits the West Broadway store. He knows, of course, the ones in London and Los Angeles, as well as Manda in Brussels, where he goes in search of vintage pieces. His favorite store, however, remains the one in the mansion on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris, where every year he celebrates Christmas at its Ralph’s restaurant.

One might call him a “perfectionist,” but he prefers “meticulous.” He will go to lengths to repair clothes, even if it requires tracking down the original fabrics or finding an expert to repair braided leather straps. He’s also interested in the story behind the brand and how design choices and corporate strategies have made it what it is today. “Ralph Lauren is a marketing genius, and his advertising is never simply advertising. He works instead like a filmmaker; he tells a story. All you need is an image, even without a product. He created a family that we all dream of being a part of by, for example, choosing his wife, Ricky, as his muse. Their marriage has lasted 60 years!” the former adviser shares. And at a time when the world is wondering and worrying about the future, Ralph Lauren and his mythologies are calm and soothing: “In a daily life saturated with screens, images, and now artificial intelligence, Ralph Lauren continues to offer a world that is profoundly real, tactile, and inhabited.” The proof? In a fashion world sometimes tinged with gloom, Ralph Lauren posted a 15% increase in revenue for 2025, surpassing $8 billion for the first time. And in the first quarter of 2026, growth continued strong at 14%.

He quotes from memory Tocqueville’s description of New England in 1835 as “a region left to the dreams of the imagination, which one ought to abandon to the free trials of innovators.” Ralph Lauren is, for Naudet, the brand that stands above the fray, its founder a dreamer embodying “the finest qualities of the United States, from Tocqueville to the present day.” We ask if, as the ultimate embodiment of the American dream, Ralph Lauren, 86, would make a good president? Naudet, an expert on the inner workings of power, smiles: “He possesses at least three key qualities needed to be a good president: He understands the times, he has broad appeal, and he inspires people to dream. The rest is part of the mystery of democracy, and America is a great democracy.”

If the self-made New Yorker has ever wondered who his biggest fan in France is, Vanity Fair has found him. Before our conversation ends, Naudet tells me that recently, as he does every year around this time, he bought two pairs of Heritage Straight jeans, and also spotted a leather jacket lined with shearling that he wanted. It’s “admittedly a bit pricey,” but he’s certain it’ll be perfect once the temperatures drop.

This story was originally published in Vanity Fair France.

#3420. Catastrophic 'GTA 6' Leak Officially Kickstarts PC Port Race

Hackers are trying to get GTA 6 running on PC, Mac, and Linux

Grand Theft Auto 6's official release seemed like the end for apparent hacker Cyberleek, who raised millions of dollars in cryptocurrency by sharing unauthorized video of the open-world game ahead of launch. Rather than fading into obscurity, Cyberleek upped the ante by releasing an apparent build of GTA 6 onto the internet. And now, hackers, vibe coders, and programming enthusiasts are rushing to try and make GTA 6 playable on PC before Rockstar does.

Those following along might recall Cyberleek as the hacker who spent weeks provoking Rockstar Games. In addition to supplying the internet with leaked footage of the unfinished version of the game, Cyberleek also critiqued Rockstar and parent company Take-Two Interactive's business practices. The leaker claimed they objected to GTA 6's digital-only release as well as its pre-order bonuses. Cyberleek encouraged Rockstar and Take-Two to change course by dangling the possibility of sharing the files they were using to play the game to the public.

This suggestion was particularly shocking since Rockstar has not made the game available outside of console platforms. The game also doesn't exist on a disc, meaning that players don't have access to the game files. Without such data, players can't peek under the hood of the game — and they definitely could not tinker with it in unintended ways, like forcing the characters to appear without clothes in the overworld.

Cyberleek's motives seemed questionable, especially since the hacker gated the release of the alleged files behind monetary milestones. One of those early milestones included nude gameplay featuring the game's co-protagonist Lucia which successfully rallied fans to donate money. Once Cyberleek shared the footage, however, the hacker lost their leverage and the public moved on.

More recently, the hacker reappeared with a more appealing proposal: they would drop the apparent files free of charge. "The torch passes to the open source recomp and emulation projects," Cyberleek said on their website.

Polygon cannot confirm the veracity of these files; Rockstar Games and Xbox did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Yet even as some hoaxes related to Cyberleek seem likely, the larger claim about the game files appears to be legitimate. Since Cyberleek dropped the alleged executable, savvy GTA 6 fans gathering on Discord have shared steady progress on making the game accessible on Linux, Mac, and Windows PC. These initial attempts don't seem impressive, especially when the game barely functions, stutters, or displays rudimentary graphics without textures and lighting.

It would be a mistake to dismiss the reverse engineering projects though. The first big hurdle — getting the game to run at all — has already been overcome​​​​​​​. A few hours after entering the game for the first time, hackers managed​​​​​​​ to load some of GTA 6's shaders, which help the game get closer to its full visual fidelity.

Under normal circumstances, before artificial-intelligence coding assistance became readily available,​​​​​​​ incremental progress like this could have taken years for a game as complex as GTA 6. To be sure, it may still be weeks, if not months, before​​​​​​​ an unauthorized PC port of GTA 6 seems plausible. Given the enormous interest in the game — and the PC gaming community feeling slighted​​​​​​​ for being left out — a port may just be a matter of time. If it comes to pass, fans may also be able to access the game without paying for it.​​​​​​​

Rockstar and Take-Two, it seems, are determined to stop that from happening. At least one leading Discord server attempting to recompile the game has been banned, and the project leader has called it quits.

"I’m sorry," the former port overseer wrote on X.com. "I really want to make cool stuff but every single time shit happens that I can’t control so I’m stepping away."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is now available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. An official PC port has not been announced.

CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss has made headlines for multiple reasons since being hired for the job in October 2025, but one specific aspect of the job she continues to receive backlash for is 60 Minutes. This past summer, Weiss and executive producer Nick Bilton cut ties with several high-profile employees and, more recently, the show has seen losses in viewership. Now, some fresh numbers regarding the news magazine show’s 59th season have arrived, and they mark yet another setback for Weiss and her staff.

Going into this latest season of 60 Minutes, which premiered in September amid the 2026 TV schedule, there was much speculation as to how the show would fare ratings-wise. This latest Nielsen data update from The Wall Street Journal (via The Independent) suggests that the show has indeed been underperforming with its broadcasts. Per the report, the series averaged 8.3 million viewers for the nine episodes that aired between September 9 and November 16. That marks a 16 percent drop from the previous season.

Months ago, Season 59 premiered to 6.5 million viewers on CBS, and that sum differed from the initial report of 7.7 million (which was not finalized at the time). One of the key commonalities between both reports, however, is that the news program has seen losses within the 25-54 demographic. In that demo, 60 has apparently seen a 25 percent decline compared to last season. This demographic is critical, especially when considering on-air advertising.

These ratings mark another less-than-desired situation for CBS News during what’s been a major year of change for 60 Minutes. In May, correspondents Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi were fired along with executive producer Tanya Simon and several others. Just recently, Vega said she found it “disturbing” that she still didn’t know the exact reason she was let go. And, shortly after those moves were made, Scott Pelley was also fired from the show after allegedly accusing Weiss of “murdering” the series.

Another topic of discussion revolves around the claims of “journalistic interference” at 60. Series alums like Pelley and Vega have alleged that they were encouraged to insert what they considered to be news bias into their reporting. CBS veteran Dan Rather also chastised Weiss and co. for their reporting. The E-I-C has denied that employees’ editorial autonomy has been taken away from journalists at the company.

With the team at 60 Minutes being aware of the chatter that’s surrounded the show as of late, Bari Weiss recently addressed concerns. She recently spoke at a conference organized by The Information, where she said the show had been doing “tremendously well.” She also emphasized that her main objective for CBS News as a whole was to build a news media organization built on trust. In doing so, she’s made changes to several programs, with the aforementioned show really receiving a makeover.

Bari Weiss Apparently ‘Arrived Like A Conquering Hero’ At CBS News. Why Things Reportedly Changed

After parting ways with Pelley and co., Weiss hired several other broadcasters to fill out 60 Minutes’ new broadcasting team. Ross Douthat, Gianna Toboni, Sebastian Junger, Sir Trevor Phillips and Ariel Levy were ultimately brought on. Those newcomers are now working alongside the show’s three on-camera veterans: Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker and Jon Wertheim. Just recently, Stahl addressed the backlash she faced due to remaining with the show under Weiss’ leadership and said she did so in order for the series as they know it not to “vanish.”

There may still be some level of continuity from a talent perspective, but the ratings still stand. As of this writing, neither Bari Weiss nor anyone else from CBS News has addressed this latest viewership update on 60 Minutes. Time will tell how Weiss, Nick Bilton and more might seek to remedy the situation.

It was impossible not to get emotional during The Voice's Dolly Parton tribute night.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There was no doubt that Dolly Parton tribute night at The Voice would be special. NBC’s long-running singing competition, which is currently airing on the 2026 TV schedule, brought the Top 10 together to perform duets to the greatest hits from the late country icon. It was an hour of performances that were entertaining and emotional as each pairing came from different teams, allowing the coaches to work together in rehearsals for the first time.

All of the performances had an added weight to them because the coaches and singers clearly wanted to do the legendary Dolly Parton justice. After a group performance of “9 to 5” that included an entire troupe of backing dancers, BigCountry (Team Queen) and Dakota Cohen (Team Adam) kicked things off with a rockin’ version of “Jolene” that was big on personality and a fun blend of country and rock. It was smart to start the night with such a jolt of energy, allowing the competitors to keep riding that wave all night.

When it finally came time for the most anticipated song of the night in any Dolly Parton tribute, it was up to Connor Closs (Team Adam) and Brianna Cameron (Team Kelly) to tackle “I Will Always Love You.” A song so big it’s terrifying for any singer to take on, let alone a male vocalist and a 14-year-old, these two beautifully blended their vocals in ways that allowed them to uplift each other and soar even higher. Hands down, it was a showstopper, and it stepped Brianna up as a real contender to win it all.

While it was clear the duet of “I Will Always Love You” stole the show, it definitely wasn’t the only memorable performance of the episode. Ferryn & Brinkley (Team Riley) and Kyle Davis (Team Kelly) were paired up on “Islands in the Stream.” It was already charming that the 61-year-old dad was dueting with sisters who are the age of his own daughters and they had a very father-daughter vibe going on. But the reveal that Ferryn & Brinkley both work full-time at Dollywood, the amusement park owned by Dolly Parton herself, and that they even had footage of Ferryn on stage with the icon was really special to see.

Since first appearing at the Blind Auditions, Ferryn & Brinkley have been hugely marketable. From their talent to their personalities, they look and feel like they could easily join the ranks of country stars who've also broken big in movies and TV, whether they ultimately win The Voice or not. As we move ever closer to the unveiling of the winning coach and star, it’s getting harder and harder to watch the singers get sent home, but I get the feeling that many of them are going to have a life in entertainment beyond this season.

The only real complaint I’ve had about the Live Shows has been the lack of coach banter and shenanigans, which was absolutely delightful earlier in the season. Seeing Dolly Parton in past The Voice appearances being her sassy self really helped make up for some of that and was a fitting way to remember her.

The Voice Season 30 will continue to air on NBC on Mondays until the two-hour finale on December 14th when the winner is finally crowned. You can also watch the next day with a Peacock subscription.

#3414. An Unexpected Arcade Classic Is Getting a Live-Action Movie From Controversial Studio

Brought to you by Saudi Arabia’s government

In a film and TV landscape where it feels like every other video game is getting an adaptation, we can add another (unexpected) candidate to the pile. Variety just broke that the ‘90s shoot-‘em-up series Metal Slug is getting a live-action movie. As you might expect, given that Metal Slug publisher SNK is owned by the Saudi Arabian government's Electronic Gaming Development Company (EGDC), the film is being made by the Saudi-backed production studio The Arena.

The proposed movie will follow the characters Marco Rossi, Tarma Roving, Eri Kasamoto, and Fio Germi, who Variety describes as “four misfits and inseparable friends who become the army’s most unlikely squad — until General Morden’s tyrannical uprising forces them to become the improbable heroes standing between the world and an even greater evil lurking behind him.” The inclusion of these characters is unsurprising: Marco and Tarma are the protagonists of the original Metal Slug, while Eri and Fio first appeared in Metal Slug 2. The most recent game in the series was Metal Slug Tactics, a turn-based roguelike RPG that marked a big departure from Metal Slug’s typical run-and-gun gameplay. Another more traditional reboot is in the works.

The movie is being written by James Morosini, an actor and filmmaker who previously wrote, directed, and starred in the 2022 comedy I Love My Dad. Melissa Goodall and Sajan Algiri from The Arena are overseeing the adaptation.

Beyond Metal Slug, The Arena is currently working on several other adaptations of SNK properties. The studio is producing a Fatal Fury movie written by David S. Goyer (Man of Steel, Foundation, The Dark Knight trilogy) and a Samurai Shodown film, with Laeta Laogridis (Altered Carbon, Alita: Battle Angel, Shutter Island) handling the screenplay. The studio is also backing an Art of Fighting webtoon by digital creator Brandon Chen.

In 2022, the EGDC, owned by the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation, acquired a 96.18% stake in SNK. As for the studio producing the new Metal Slug film, The Arena is owned by MBC Group, a Saudi media conglomerate, and the Misk Foundation, also known as the Mohammed bin Salman Foundation.

The Saudi government’s purchase of Electronic Arts and backing of a film studio tie into broader efforts to invest in entertainment products, such as sports leagues, video games, movies, and more. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) recently acquired EA alongside Jared Kushner’s Affinity Partners and Silver Lake. The PIF also has stakes in companies such as Capcom, Nintendo, and Take-Two, as well as ownership in e-sports events like the fighting game tournament EVO.

As for why Saudi investments in the video game industry have proven controversial, these acquisitions have been criticized as a type of “sportswashing,” a method of sanitizing the Saudi government’s image on the world stage by associating itself with “fun” topics, like soccer and golf, instead of human rights abuses. The Saudi government has been accused of exploitation of migrant laborers, enforcement of anti-LGBTQ laws, and the killing of political opponents, such as the alleged murder of Washington Post journalist Jamal Khashoggi. Basically, the Saudi Arabian government would much rather you think about a movie adaptation of that nostalgic game series you used to love instead of these many accusations, all while you contribute to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's war chest.

#3413. Hexed Review: A Safe And Solidly Witchy Disney Original

Some of us grew up dreaming of becoming princesses and knights in fairy tales, others of becoming astronauts (or in my case, uh, the guy who gets to drive the garbage truck). Only the coolest — and weirdest — kids among us imagined themselves slapping on some eyeshadow, living it up from atop flying brooms, and casting gnarly spells. Who else but witches can transform the rigidly bland world around us into one positively teeming with magic and color and life?

The wish-fulfillment of it all probably explains why this makes for such a neat premise in a movie like "Hexed" ... even if that potential isn't fully realized. Disney's latest animated original, from directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand and co-director Josie Trinidad, is mostly content to play things safe and deliver a fairly predictable coming-of-age story. While this family-friendly, PG-rated romp doesn't linger too much on the darkness inherent in witches, there's an undeniable undercurrent of something much more provocative at work.

Because being a witch isn't all fun and games. Along with strong personalities and powers beyond compare, they also come with the baggage of being profoundly misunderstood. Their curse is to be loners, outcasts, and pariahs, forever looking for a coven to call their own. Whenever the script by co-writers Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller fully leans into this, embodied by misfit high schooler Billie Doe (voiced by the always-capable Hailee Steinfeld) in search of a deeper sense of belonging, "Hexed" takes on a life of its own. When relying on frenetic pacing and joke-a-minute thrills to sweep us along and glide past any discomfort, it struggles to come together.

There's a greater movie somewhere inside "Hexed," just waiting to break free. Instead, we're left with a safe and solid enough adventure that could've been something more.

Right from the opening exposition dump of "Hexed," we're taken through a prototypical backstory of how witches were chased out of "normal" society and forced to create a mystical refuge of their own called Hexe. Unfortunately, the founding witch died before she could complete this new utopia, dooming her followers to wait for the prophesied "Chosen One" to cast a spell known only to themselves and restore everyone's powers to their fullest. ("The foretelling was foretold," as numerous characters amusingly reference this event.)

This intersects neatly with Billie's arc, our rule-breaking teenager with latent witchy powers whose mother Alice (the rather obvious voice-casting of Rashida Jones) has hidden away from the world and from her supposed destiny. When Billie's abilities manifest as an infant and nearly spirit her away to Hexe, Alice takes great pains to hide her daughter's true origins from herself — even to the point of moving out of Salem altogether and into the blandest, most unassuming place on Earth to pass as an unremarkable normie (Ohio). All in all, it's a pretty standard setup for a parable about identity, puberty, and being yourself (alongside a hint of queer subtext), which "Hexed" pulls off with the appropriate amount of emotional, tear-jerker aplomb.

But otherwise, this is largely an excuse to show off the film's stunning world-building prowess. Yes, Hexe oftentimes tends to resemble Universal's Wizarding World of Harry Potter. But once Billie finally makes it to this living and breathing realm — marked by an expanding aspect ratio to soak in the full scope of Hexe — and assembles unlikely allies like an enchanted pot, Walton Goggins' cat-like and delightfully-named familiar Beef Roger Crummchuk, and neurotic owl Nigel (Henry Winkler), you'll never want to leave this kaleidoscopic wonderland.

Where "Hexed" struggles most, ironically, is in its attempt to carve out a niche for itself amid the vast canon of Disney's animated movies. On one hand, it's strangely fitting for a story about individualism to be so preoccupied by what's come before. On the other, it has the side effect of triggering a tangible identity crisis. At this point, Disney's house-style CG animation has been set in stone and nothing here diverges all that much from the likes of "Frozen" — down to the look of the film's main villain Queen Celeste, brought to life by a scenery-chewing Jodie Foster. Elsewhere, some of the imagery of Hexe itself feel cribbed from classics like "Cinderella" or "Fantasia," coming across less like a loving homage and more like a copy of a copy. Even Kris Bowers' distinctive score is overshadowed by a parade of on-the-nose needle drops, from Queen to Dua Lipa.

This has the cumulative effect of making "Hexed" an oddly meta experience, in a way that both livens things up and makes for a somewhat awkward addition to the Disney pantheon. Much of the humor comes from the script's winking self-awareness and its many "Can you believe this?" visual gags, which could've fell flat on their face but instead (mostly) work. But even its most inspired moments of creativity and imagination feel undercut by a script that's either unwilling or unable to push such boundaries beyond its most surface-level joys.

Still, parents could do far worse than "Hexed" when it comes to movies their children will inevitably re-watch a million times over once it comes to Disney+. While that might seem like damning with faint praise, it does speak to the basics of storytelling that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn, Jason Hand, and Josie Trinidad manage to get right — especially within a noticeably tight, 103-minute runtime. For all intents and purposes, this breezy storyline might as well be designed to function like a runaway train, constantly keeping the action at a sprinter's pace and hardly giving young viewers a chance to catch their breath. Even the "camera" stays in motion at almost all times and makes the few, much-needed moments of respite and quiet conversation stand out all the more.

This "Get in, get out" approach at least provides a jolt of energy right from the get-go and carries the emotions along with it, even if it can occasionally get exhausting. At its heart, "Hexed" lives or dies by the mother/daughter bond forged between impulsive Billie and overbearing Alice, and its best moments soar as direct result of never losing sight of these two characters.

There are plenty of narrative holes left oddly unexplained and an unfortunate bit of sequel-bait sweatiness to contend with, likely included in the off-chance this kills it at the box office. (This raises another question, of course: Was holding this Halloween-friendly movie about spooky witches closer to the extended Thanksgiving holiday weekend really worth it?) But thanks to dazzling visuals, a strong emotional undercurrent, and killer world-building, "Hexed" is a solid — if safe — family outing.

"Hexed" opens in theaters on November 25, 2026.

#3412. The Best Tech Deals From Costco's Early Black Friday Sale

Sam's Club, Walmart, Amazon, and other retailers have been churning out early Black Friday deals since last week, so if you haven't been paying attention, you've already missed out on some good deals. But all hope is not lost: Costco recently started its own early sale, so you're still in time to find something you want at a low price. Below, I've rounded up my favorite tech deals from their sale—but keep in mind you'll need a membership to take advantage of these deals.

A powerful monitor with high-end specs can make gaming more immersive and greatly reduce input lag, which is helpful for any serious gamer looking for an edge over their opponents. The Samsung Odyssey G9 is a 49-inch gaming monitor with some impressive specs, including a 240Hz refresh rate and a 1 ms response time. It's available for $699.99 (originally $899.99), $200 off and the lowest price it has reached this year.

If you're looking for a more premium (and far more massive) gaming monitor, the 57-inch Samsung Odyssey Neo G9, one of the best ultra-wide gaming monitors on the market, is currently on sale for $1,449.99 ($2,499.99 at launch). This monitor came out in 2023, earning an "excellent" review from PCMag for its impressive 7,680 x 2,160 4K resolution, its great color range and accuracy, a 240Hz refresh rate, 1,000 nits of brightness, and its overall design. To make full use of its powerful 240Hz refresh rate, you'll need to use DisplayPort 2.1, or you'll be limited to 120Hz. You'll also need a powerful graphics card. But if you have the right setup, this thing really delivers.

The 15.3-inch Lenovo Legion is a powerful gaming laptop with premium specs, and with the current $600 discount, it's down to $1999.99 (originally $2,599.99). It has a powerful AMD Ryzen AI 9 processor, 32 GB of RAM, a GeForce RTX 5070 graphics card, and 1TB of SSD. PCMag gave the more affordable 5i version an excellent review for its price and performance, so if you have the cash for it, this one is even better.

A soundbar is a great way to improve a home entertainment system without spending too much money. This 5.1 TCL Q6CH setup is currently $199.99 (originally $299.99), including a soundbar and subwoofer. This soundbar came out in 2024 and supports Dolby Atmos and DTS:X for that 3D sound, as well as AI Sonic, a tool that tunes your sound settings based on the setup of your room.

The latest AirPods Pro are a big step up from their previous generation. The third iteration of Apple's iconic earbuds deliver a number of quality-of-life and software improvements that make them worth the typical premium over the AirPods Pro 2—and right now, the AirPods Pro 3 are even cheaper than the previous generation: They're $179 at Costco (originally $249) in an early Black Friday deal.

The 15-inch MacBook Air is down to $1,249 (originally $1,499), the lowest price since Apple hiked prices this past summer. The M5 MacBook Air is the best laptop for most people looking for a new machine in 2026. In comparison to the already excellent M4 Air, the M5 base model has double the storage, and the powerful M5 chip makes the performance even smoother, according to Mashable's review. The aluminum design is as good as you'd expect from Apple's most popular portable laptop, and it includes a Liquid Retina display, Touch ID, a 12MP Center Stage Camera, and the Magic Keyboard.

The 15.6-inch Acer Aspire Go is a great value at its current $499.99 price (originally $699.99). The display is a touchscreen; it sports an AMD Ryzen 5 processor and it has 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. These aren't specs you normally find at this price, making it a great laptop for anyone looking to stretch their money as far as possible while getting a workhorse of a laptop.

I'm a fan of TCL TVs, and currently own the "non-pro" version of this TV. The 65-inch QM6K Pro is $599.99 (originally $999.99) and has the same internal hardware and Mini-LED panel as the regular QM6K, but it adds a CrystGlow anti-reflective coating that makes it more viewable in well-lit rooms and helps maintain a high picture contrast. The 144 Hz native refresh rate makes gaming smooth, and support for Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG means you're well positioned to get the best sound quality when streaming movies or shows.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3411. Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series

The other day, one line in an otherwise unremarkable marketing email caught my eye: “Discovery is exactly what fans come to Netflix for.”

Even with a dangling preposition (in a press release littered with errors), the claim felt like the more glaring mistake: Netflix is where fans go for discovery. They do? Still? Are you sure about that?

But when it comes to Netflix’s core business — streaming television — the service is largely a preferred destination by default. Being an industry pioneer helped establish Netflix as a utility among TV fans, many of whom still turn to it when they want to see “what’s on,” but it’s hard to imagine why anyone would head there first when searching for their next favorite show.

That would require the customer to trust Netflix — either as the service offering the most bang for their buck, the shows everyone is talking about, or, most likely and simplest of all, the best series on TV. Can the streamer really stake a claim to any of those distinctions?

Throughout 2026, Netflix has been plagued by problems and complaints. Viewership for returning seasons is dwindling, subscription prices are rising, hot new franchises are scarce, and high-quality programming — a subjective designation, to be sure — isn’t what it used to be. Netflix is no longer the most affordable SVOD service. It’s not the most award-winning, nor is it the buzziest.

A sustainable hit could quiet things down, but those have been hard to come by. Netflix’s most popular new shows this year were limited series (like “His & Hers” and “I Will Find You”), which only offer short-term juice. Promising first seasons (“The Boroughs”) faced quick cancellations that left fans fuming and analysts searching for answers. Even touted chart toppers (“Man on Fire”) don’t get a quick Season 2 renewal, let alone a quick turnaround between seasons.

Ignoring these very-online narratives, none of the aforementioned shows earned rave reviews, and the streamer’s awards output echoed what’s felt like a dearth in quality. Total Emmy wins were cut nearly in half this year, from 30 to 16, causing Netflix to fall to third place (behind HBO and Apple) for the first time since topping the town in 2021.

A month after Emmy night, all the criticism reached a crescendo when a plunging stock price and lack of hits forced mass layoffs, including the dismissal of chief content officer Bela Bajaria and other key executives. Peter Rice is at the helm now, and his new team is setting the table for changes in 2027 — much like Netflix did in 2022 after The Great Streaming Correction opened the door for an ad-tier and shut the door on password sharing.

While it would be foolish to believe fixing one aspect of a diverse business would make all its other problems go away, it would be equally foolish to pretend there’s not a TV problem at Netflix. A healthy TV slate only benefits engagement across the platform, and the streamer is still the big dog in SVOD — it’s just losing ground year by year. So what’s to be done?

Well, that depends on how much Netflix is willing to change. If it’s all on the table, there are a handful of reasonable shifts they could make to improve their reputation. If not, well, I’ve got an idea for that, too.

At the root of Netflix’s TV problem is that its shows feel disposable. Sometimes that’s by design: Netflix makes a lot of programs that can be watched while scrolling, which can be OK. TV has long been a medium built for background entertainment, and it’s still nice to have an easily digestible distraction while doing dishes or folding laundry.

But Netflix may have gone too far. Setting aside quality (for a moment), the streamer’s focus on “discovery” paired with its faith in the almighty algorithm to sort through its substantial monthly programming influx emphasizes new shows above all else. There’s always another new series, new special, or new live event to watch, but there isn’t always more of the show you already love. Some original series take years between releasing new seasons. Some only dole out six or eight episodes every 18 months. Some get canceled after one or two seasons, and very few run more than three or four seasons in total.

Whether or not the approach works from a financial perspective, it fails to foster audience investment, and investment is where TV thrives. Just look at this year’s most-watched shows on streaming, per Nielsen: “Stranger Things” holds down the No. 1 spot, but then it’s “Bluey,” “The Pitt,” “Grey’s Anatomy,” and “The Big Bang Theory.” Keep scrolling and it’s even easier to spot the dominant trend: Shows with huge libraries that first aired on network TV.

These are the kind of shows that people keep up with for years, decades, or more. They like the characters, they like the structure, they like the setting — they like being in the show’s world, whether it’s a hospital filled with hot doctors or a nerd’s living room. Offering access on a regular basis encourages investment, which breeds loyalty, which creates longevity. Producing more episodes, more often — like broadcast TV has done all along — creates bigger libraries that fans will happily live in for years on end because they enjoy spending time with those characters and within those stories.

Streamers have been reluctant to adopt their predecessor’s production model (for reasons both valid and ridiculous that I’ll get into in the next section), but the success of long-running (and long-gone) broadcast series on streaming, paired with the recent popularity of “The Pitt,” makes it hard to argue against making longer seasons, consisting of more episodes, that are released on a regular basis. It’s what audiences want now, and it’s what they’ve shown they’ll want later.

Which brings us to the binge model. One of the reasons Netflix hasn’t experimented with more broadcast-style streaming shows (like “The Pitt”) is because it can’t. Its release model is different. The binge model requires everything be done before anything premieres, including timely post-production work like subtitles and dubbing, which Netflix needs to serve its global base. While episodes of most network series are still being written, shot, and edited as earlier, completed episodes roll out, episodes of a Netflix series drop all at once.

Luckily, Netflix already made the change. Or started to, at least.

Nowadays, Netflix’s most popular original series are often released in batches (or “parts”), including the last two seasons of “Stranger Things” and “Bridgerton.” Both shows are among the most-watched programs on the planet, so the shift in release strategy hasn’t hurt their popularity. Other shows are already released weekly, like “The Great British Baking Show,” or close to weekly, like “Love Is Blind.”

Moreover, the addition of live events has forced Netflix to implement new tactics to raise awareness for time-sensitive content (instead of just relying on the algorithm), which should limit fears over viewer confusion. (For seasons released in parts, the Netflix platform tends to list how many episodes will be released and when. You can even set reminders for upcoming programming, even if none of it is available yet — like, say, the NFL game on Thanksgiving Eve, which is a thing, I guess.)

Netflix decided long ago to break up the binge, now they just need to keep going. After all, the binge model was created to disrupt Hollywood. No one was releasing full seasons at once, and Netflix executives recognized how DVDs had primed viewers to marathon TV shows. Instead of old favorites (like “The Office”), why not give them new ones to devour?

But Netflix isn’t a disruptor anymore. It’s the industry leader. It doesn’t need a gimmick to draw attention. It needs a strategy to help keep it.

A weekly release model could help. Netflix doesn’t need to enforce it on every series — let people binge “Ginny & Georgia” — but for shows that could benefit from the regular cycle of anticipation, fulfillment, dissection (repeat), the tried-and-true strategy could do wonders for audience investment. In the short-term, it could help prevent dips in engagement and help foster engagement with newly beloved series. In the long-term, it could help build franchises, libraries, and loyalty.

You can’t just make the next “Pitt.” You have to create the system to support it.

Speaking of support, it’s time to talk about quality. What constitutes a good show and a bad show will always, in the end, remain in the eye of the beholder, but a company aiming to “replace all television” can’t rely on subjective interpretations to define its brand. Nor can it rely primarily on an algorithm to elevate the best options instead of the easiest ones. Otherwise, you risk a narrative like this year’s, where objective measurements like ratings (where the three most-watched new shows average a 56 rating on Metacritic) and awards (where Netflix landed one more win than NBC and Peacock combined) create the impression of less-than-“gourmet” service.

Some such schemes are already underway with pre-show ads running before episodes and prominent brand campaigns helping connect viewers with their new favorite programs. Hopefully, that signals more old-school advocacy efforts are coming. Eventize episodes, not just new seasons. Build channels for episodic programs to elevate their best moments. Add permanent subsections to Netflix’s genre listings.

This is not a new idea. At various times for various reasons, various experts have suggested Netflix launch a free subscription tier in order to promote its growing library to a wider audience. FAST (free, ad-supported streaming) platforms like Pluto, Tubi, and The Roku Channel are growing quickly mainly by replicating the broadcast model for the streaming age, and Netflix could take a page out of their playbook to expand their business in any number of ways. But in terms of solving their TV problem, they should use it to distinguish their premium original programming from their recent obsession: YouTube slop.

I’ll be honest: I don’t think of Netflix and YouTube as competitors, mainly because Netflix isn’t free. Sure, there’s YouTube Premium, but YouTube is instantly accessible, sans subscription, and that’s how most users get hooked. I don’t care how many more hours people spend watching YouTube than Netflix because the hours I spend watching movie trailers, how-to-videos, and late-night clips are not the same as the hours I spend watching “Little House on the Prairie,” “Long Story Short,” and “East of Eden.” One I’m willing to pay for, one I’m not. So the idea that Netflix, as a business, should be trying to surpass YouTube never made sense to me.

It still doesn’t, but I understand the market demands constant growth, and I understand why Netflix would want YouTube’s viewers, especially in the younger demographic. So Netflix has been busy signing content creators, adding podcasts, and filling the service with easy-listening videos (aka videos you don’t need to watch, but can play in the background without much disturbance). If that helps bring the next generation to Netflix so they can discover the glory of “BoJack Horseman,” great! But right now, BoJack is sitting side by side with random content like “Conspiracy Theories,” “Small Town Murder,” and “Bill Simmons.”

That’s a problem. We shouldn’t equate those very distinct experiences, and Netflix shouldn’t suggest we do. At best, it builds a false equivalency that steadily lowers our artistic standards for visual entertainment. At worst, it leads to more fans of this “Bill Simmons.”

So let’s create some tiers. Launch a free version of Netflix where all the podcasts, creator videos, and short-form content can live. Make money the old-fashioned way — from ads — while offering select TV shows to sample in the hopes viewers will get hooked and pay for an upgraded subscription. Keep original series, movies, and other top library offerings on the paid tiers, and structure those however you like. (Currently, there’s Standard with Ads, Standard, and Premium, each with their distinct perks.)

Is creating a FAST version of Netflix a whole lot of work to dispel the notion that Netflix makes too much disposable TV? Yup, and I won’t pretend to know how feasible it is, financially or otherwise. But Netflix needs to take a big swing or two if it hopes to fix its reputation, which brings us to my last option.

Netflix is still the dominant streamer in Hollywood. Plentiful stats support its case, but why look any further than how many other streamers license content to their biggest competitor? Disney+, Hulu, Paramount+, and more each lend their once-exclusive series to their rival in the hope of getting the Netflix bump (or a quick influx of cash). Never did I think I’d see the day where HBO would be available on another streamer, and yet everything from “Sex and the City” to “Ballers” has graced Netflix in 2026.

With that in mind, Netflix may choose to stay the course. The once-and-future tech company is notorious for sticking to certain brand tenets, like trusting the algorithm over traditional marketing and its binge model over traditional release strategies. Even when Hollywood pushes back, Netflix’s broader goals continue to evolve. Originally, it wanted to be the HBO of streaming. Then it wanted to replace cable. Then it wanted to replace all television.

What it wants to be now isn’t so clear. Wall Street keeps forcing comparisons to YouTube, some of which are invited by Netflix’s pursuit of its content and podcast creators. Maybe Netflix executives believe they can raise their market cap with vertical videos and video game previews, with new decision-makers and added theatrical grosses, with a few small tweaks here and a few surprise wins there. It has the leverage to wait out complaints and keep making TV exactly as it has been, if it so chooses.

But because of its relative health, I hope Netflix sees its TV problem as more of a TV opportunity. Yes, it needs more hits. Yes, it needs to build back trust. But it also wants to grow, and the suggestions above are all about sustainable growth through better TV. Longer seasons, more episodes, weekly releases, stronger support, clearer delineations, a FAST service — none of these ideas are revolutionary. They’re not meant to be. They’re meant to give the people what they want.

If Netflix is going to be where fans go for discovery, it first needs to be a place they can trust to get what what they need.

#3409. If You're Tired Of Colleen Hoover Movies, Watch This Overlooked 2026 Rom-Com

Colleen Hoover is the reigning queen of BookTok-phenomenon-turned-movie entertainment. The woman just has a knack for writing the kinds of books that might not get a lot of critical love but which social media crowds cannot resist. Thus far, that has resulted in four Colleen Hoover movie adaptations. Unfortunately, none of them are very good. At least, the critics didn't like them. Audiences, on the other hand, keep showing up. Following the less than enthusiastic response to the latest Hoover movie, "Verity," however, even fans might be in need of a break. In which case, might I suggest "You, Me & Tuscany," directed by Kat Coiro.

Corio previously helmed the 2022 glossy rom-com relic "Marry Me" starring Jennifer Lopez and Owen Wilson. Like your standard Hoover affair, it movie earned an okay 61% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes, but managed to push the "popcornmeter" to 92%, meaning audiences absolutely loved Coiro's movie — which was based on a webcomic.

In 2026, Coiro — who also directed several episodes of "She-Hulk: Attorney at Law" — returned with another romantic comedy: "You, Me & Tuscany," an original story written by Ryan Engle, who, oddly enough, has mostly written actioners such as the Idris-Elba-vs.-a-lion survival horror "Beast" and the Liam Neeson outing that was 2014's "Non-Stop." With "You, Me & Tuscany" he embraced his more tender side with a story of a young cook who finds love in the titular Italian region.

"You, Me & Tuscany" stars Halle Bailey ("The Little Mermaid") as Anna, a young woman who after losing her house-sitting job, meets a strapping Italian named Matteo Costa (Lorenzo de Moor). Following their brief encounter, Anna decides to fly to Italy and manages to find a spare key to Matteo's empty Tuscan villa. There, Matteo's mother, Gabriella (Isabella Ferrari) arrives and Anna decides to lie and tell her that she's Matteo's fiancé.

It might seem as though "You, Me & Tuscany" is yet another fake dating rom-com, whereby a feigned romance becomes real. But the movie diverges from that well-worn path when Matteo's cousin, Michael (Regé-Jean Page) arrives and there's an instant attraction between he and Anna.

Page is, of course, best known for playing Simon Basset, the Duke of Hastings, in Season 1 of Netflix's hugely-popular series "Bridgerton." But he's since enjoyed a successful film career and is quickly making a name for himself in Hollywood. Page's Simon Basset left "Bridgerton" after the first season, after which the actor appeared in "Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves," and in Steven Soderbergh's sleek spy thriller "Black Bag." With "You, Me & Tuscany" he further proved he has leading man chops. Otherwise, however, the movie doesn't do much to separate it from the glut of sort-of-okay romance movies with which we've been inundated in recent years. But it has at least outdone every Colleen Hoover movie on Rotten Tomatoes.

The latest Colleen Hoover movie was the dead-on-arrival "Verity," which no doubt left many viewers disappointed in the lack of straightforward romance. Much of the movie features Anne Hathaway glaring silently at Dakota Johnson from a medical bed or wheelchair. "You, Me and Tuscany" on the other hand should delight those hoping for more schmaltzy romance in the vein of Lili Reinhart's Prime Video smash hit "The Love Hypothesis" or Sofia Carson's similarly popular Netflix romance "My Oxford Year."

Over on Rotten Tomatoes, it's a familiar state of affairs. "You, Me & Tuscany" earned a somewhat respectable 65% critic score while managing to push the "popcornmeter" all the way to 91%. This is the rom-com pattern of late. Audiences clearly got what they came for here, even if Nikki Gemmell of The Australian called the movie "the filmic equivalent of paint by numbers, lift muzak, Fruit Loops, Contiki Tours and The Voice," essentially "anything that feels bland, inauthentic and deeply commercial." Sadly, this is just where we are in 2026. We used to make rom-coms like "Sleepless in Seattle" and "When Harry Met Sally." Not anymore.

"You, Me & Tuscany," however, isn't the worst example of the modern day rom-com (Netflix's "The Wrong Paris" might have claimed that title in 2025). If you happen to be looking for a Hoover palette cleanser that also isn't too far removed from the author's BookTok-friendly brand of romance, then this one's worth a go. "You, Me & Tuscany" is currently available to rent from the usual platforms, and can be streamed via Peacock with a premium subscription.

This year, we’ve talked a lot about Taylor Swift’s wedding and her song in Toy Story 5. However, amid chatter about her CMA performance and her supporting Travis Kelce at his games, the conversation about the pop star has shifted to a Vanity Fair story about her image and rise to fame. Many have called it a “hit piece” about the singer (who is never explicitly named in it). So, now, as people continue to discuss the claims made, one of the pop star’s former classmates, who is quoted in the piece, is clearing the air about her Ugg boot comments.

In a piece published by Vanity Fair, it goes over a comment Swift made early in her career about not having friends when she was younger. That is followed by claims from a classmate, Chanice Skinner, about how she was “always part of the popular crowd.” She also claimed that Swift was “one of the bullies.” After that, she said she thinks Swift’s parents funded her dream.

Then came the part about the Ugg boots. Arielle Peppers, who also went to school with the pop star, shared that tale, and it was told in the VF piece as follows:

Arielle Peppers was a year behind The Star and sat on the other side of Skinner in Luyben’s class for multiple quarters. She remembers The Star coming to class in Ugg boots. Peppers had transferred from the nearby city of ReAding after her neighbor was stabbed in the neck. She asked her mother for a pair of the same boots. ‘Do you know how much they cost?’ her mother said. A pair of Uggs amounted to half her single mother’s paycheck working variously at a bakery, at a dairy mill, and as a caretaker. Peppers recalls The Star owning multiples of Uggs: ‘She had the brown one, the black one, the blue one.’

Along with this story about the Uggs, Peppers explained that she saw Swift get teased at a school talent show after she sang a song about a crush.

In the wake of this story going live, the comments about the Uggs have gone viral. One tweet in particular said their “favorite part” of the piece was when it covered someone “harboring a legitimate grudge over Taylor owning Uggs.” Many others commented on this quote, too. However, Peppers wants to clear the air.

Arielle Peppers wants to make it clear she was not trying to throw shade at Taylor Swift. During an interview with TMZ, she explained that, too, saying:

I shared a straightforward childhood memory with a reporter about school and what was affordable for different families at the time. It wasn't intended as an attack on anyone.

This former classmate was one of the very few sources named in the Vanity Fair piece. While May Jeong interviewed more than 100 sources, many stayed anonymous. In the wake of the story being published, Peppers said she’s gotten threats and had to deal with online chaos and hate. Overall, she just wants to focus on her own life, as she told TMZ:

I'm focused on my own life, raising my twin daughters, working, and pursuing my own musical goals as A. Star. I wish Taylor Swift continued success.

She ended by saying she wants to “move forward with positivity and love.” Meanwhile, a source alleged to Page Six that Swift, who is no stranger to online hate and speculation, “isn’t going to lose sleep over any of this.”

Between her ongoing Oscar campaign for her Toy Story 5 song, the anticipation and theories surrounding the potential re-release of her first album and more, she’s clearly got a lot going on at the moment. And when it comes to the Uggs, her former classmate made it clear that she meant no harm by these comments that went viral.

#3406. Leighton Meester's Christmas Movie Is Officially Netflix's Biggest Streaming Hit

Former "Gossip Girl" star Leighton Meester is currently dominating the Netflix streaming charts with her latest movie. A now-famous actress whose career started on "Law & Order," she's come a long way over the years. To that end, Meester's "Guarding Stars" is now the biggest streaming hit on the biggest streaming service in the world.

Described as "a cozy, snowy Christmas rom-com," director Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum's "Guarding Stars" is currently sitting in the number one spot on Netflix's most-watched movie charts, per FlixPatrol. The movie co-stars former "Supernatural" star Jared Padalecki. Since The CW canceled Padelecki's "Walker," he's had more time to focus on other stuff, such as this holiday flavored romantic comedy.

The movie centers on a no-nonsense bodyguard (Meester) who is assigned to protect a charming action star over the holidays. Sparks fly, secrets unravel, and Christmas gets a whole lot more complicated. The movie is inspired by the 2022 novel "The Bodyguard" by Katherine Center. The ensemble cast also includes Andie MacDowell ("Magic Mike XXL"), Noah LaLonde ("Deer Camp '86"), Toby Sandeman ("Running Point"), Rachael Ancheril ("Star Trek: Discovery"), Shaun Johnston ("Heartland"), pop star Ava Max, and country singer Walker Hayes in his acting debut.

Netflix wisely decided to drop this movie just before Thanksgiving. The holidays are kicking off and this is very much on point with the theme of the holiday. It's precisely the kind of thing people are looking to throw on while scrolling for something to watch. This sort of stuff thrives this time of year. As further evidence of that, the Colleen Hoover movie "Reminders of Him" was also recently Netflix's biggest streaming hit.

Rom-coms can still find success at the box office these days, with Glen Powell and Sydney Sweeney's "Anyone But You" serving as a fine example from recent history. But Netflix has really managed to dominate this space in recent years. They've made genuinely charming gems like "Always Be My Maybe," one of the best rom-coms on Netflix, and launched full-on franchises such as "The Kissing Booth."

But the king of the streamers has really thrived when it comes to romantic holiday fare. One of the most prominent examples was when 2024's strange Christmas movie "Hot Frosty" took over Netflix, becoming a genuine cultural sensation at the time. Admittedly, "Guarding Stars" is much more traditional than a movie in which a snowman comes to life. All the same, that almost makes its success more noteworthy, as it didn't have to rely on some goofy hook to get it across the finish line.

There's probably an element of this premise that seems cozy and fitting the spirit of the season, but pairing two former CW stars like Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki, especially with one in an against-type role as a bodyguard, appears to have intrigued viewers quite a bit.

The movie was written by Erin Cardillo and Richard Keith ("Isn't It Romantic," "Virgin River") alongside Gina Matthews and Grant Scharbo. Robin Fisichella served as the executive producer, with Matthews, Scharbo, Jared and Genevieve Padalecki on board as producers.

"Guarding Stars" is streaming now on Netflix.

Per MUBI, “Surrounded by brutality but bound by tenderness, two World War I soldiers find a fragile sanctuary of love and art amid the shadows of the Belgian trenches. ‘Coward’ asks a profound question for a generation sent to war: when the world demands violence, is walking away the truest act of bravery?”

More from IndieWire’s review: “Belgian filmmaker wrestles the tenderness and softness between soldiers from the brutality of the battlefield in his visually arresting if thematically by-the-book third feature, ‘Coward.’ Starring newcomers Valentin Campagne and Emmanuel Macchia as achingly beautiful soldiers of the Belgian front in World War I who fall in love and learn to discover that, in one of the most fascinatingly contradictory ideas of Dhont’s highly contradictory career, the violence of war is what both enables and protects their attraction, and allows them to be together at all.”

There’s more, as “in 1916, on the western front of World War I, the flamboyant Francis (Valentin Campagne) leads a not-so-merry band of rejects among his infantry, of soldiers whose job it is to entertain and raise the morale of their comrades. In this case, it’s forming a theater troupe of the soldiers in drag as they move from battle to battle, a role that’s become almost as instrumental in keeping spirits high as actual combat is to wearing them down. The withdrawn, ethereally beautiful Pierre (Emmanuel Macchia) becomes drawn into the world of the troupe, and he’s intrigued by the outré Francis’ ostentatious theatricality, and how comfortable he is in dresses and makeup. … Through an attraction that’s only allowed to flower because of and in context of their closeness to each other on Francis’ performances, he and Pierre become secret lovers.”

Watch the new trailer, an IndieWire exclusive, below. MUBI opens the film in theaters throughout the United States and Canada on December 25 (that’s Christmas Day).

#3402. Stranger Things Star Noah Schnapp Reveals Photo From Failed Hunger Games Audition For Haymitch

Now that he's free of "Stranger Things," we're going to find out if Noah Schnapp can fulfill the promise he flashed over five seasons of the Netflix sci-fi/horror series. His character, Will Byers, had arguably the most emotional arc of the show, with viewers watching him go from missing boy to psychically tortured returnee from the Upside Down to out and proud young adult. Byers' journey mirrored Schnapp's personal voyage to coming out of the closet in 2025. It was a lovely moment for Schnapp, both as an individual and also for his character, who presented a positive gay role model for kids who too often struggle with prejudice and outright hatred in their everyday lives.

I've no idea if Schnapp will return to the "Stranger Things" universe (he's only just portrayed a disaffected rich kid and, when the plot jumps forward 20 years, the kid's son in Andy Sandberg's controversial stage play "Affluenza"), but he had a shot at joining the "Hunger Games" franchise as a young Haymitch Abernathy in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." The "Hunger Games" prequel is currently tearing up the box office, so it would've been a sweet gig for the 22-year-old actor. But he congratulated Joseph Zada like a gentleman for landing the role, and, as an egoless bonus, the brunette Schnapp posted a still picture of himself in blonde hair from his screen test to Instagram. (See below.)

After a couple of ... emojis, Schnapp tagged Zada and added, "Think they picked right for this one."

I have no true measure of Noah Schnapp as an actor. He's handsome, he's got some mystery to him and, in the right role (e.g. Will Byers), he connects. Do I think he would've been an effective Haymitch Abernathy, given all the horrible things that happen to the character on his way to growing up and becoming Woody Harrelson? Maybe not.

"Affluenza" ended its London run on November 21, and, boy, did the critics lay into this sucker. In a one-star review for The Guardian, Arifa Akbar called it an "epic wreckage," adding, "You want to look away, for shame, but simply can't stop gawping." Most critics concurred, but that actually worked out for Schnapp, as they were too busy lambasting Sandberg to pay much attention to his performance. Writing for The Times, Clive Davis simply noted that Schnapp "doesn't disgrace himself." If you get cast in a disaster, you can live with that.

It's unclear where Schnapp will go from here, but thanks to "Stranger Things" he has a pretty sizable fan base. I can't see him being a part of the forthcoming series "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure," which is a prequel set in the 1950s, but we'll certainly see more of him in the future.

#3401. GTA 6 Data Reveals Only 40% of Players Have Cleared Chapter 2

Many are taking in the Keys at their own pace

If your feed is full of clips and streams from people who’ve already gone deep into Grand Theft Auto 6, here’s some reassurance: most players aren’t as far along as you probably think.

According to PSNProfiles, only 66.22% of Grand Theft Auto 6 players on PlayStation 5 have earned the trophy for completing Chapter 1, which takes place in the Leonida Keys. The numbers on Xbox are similar, with 56% of players having beaten that part of the game, according to TrueAchievements. This completion percentage feels particularly significant because the first chapter of the game is a big departure from classic GTA, with Jason living out a relatively low-key existence interrupted by the occasional shootout with backwoods drug dealers. Still, it seems a solid chunk of players are more than happy fishing with Cal for now.

Meanwhile, only 40.55% of players have cleared Chapter 2 on PS5, and 31% on Xbox. Again, considering that Chapter 3 is arguably where the game becomes more of a traditional Grand Theft Auto entry, as you officially enter Vice City, it’s a bit of a surprise that the numbers are so low, even if it takes close to 20 hours to get there.

As for the rest of the game, few have gotten past Chapter 3: 6.45% have cleared that chapter on PS5, compared to 4% on Xbox; 1.26% have cleared Chapter 4 on PS5 against 1% on Xbox; and a tiny 0.88% have cleared the final mission on PlayStation against fewer than 1% on Xbox.

Although it’s tempting to assume these low completion numbers are simply because the game came out so recently, Sony released player engagement numbers that made it clear most have already put a ton of time into GTA 6. Mat Piscatella, senior director at market research firm Circana, revealed that players spent an average of more than 8 hours playing the game on launch day. As of Nov. 23, PS5 players had already spent an average of 17.4 hours playing. While users are playing a lot and sticking with the game, most are taking their time. Rockstar previously said the main story takes around 50 hours to finish.

Shortly after GTA 6 was released, publisher Take-Two Interactive announced that the game had set a “new record for entertainment across any medium,” making it the biggest launch in entertainment history. It sold 32.5 million copies during its pre-release period, generating $3.79 billion in revenue. In the previously mentioned post that announced PlayStation engagement numbers, Sony also said GTA 6 was the biggest launch in PlayStation history and that 39 million people had played it on the PS5 as of Monday.

As for its critical reception, the game has a staggering Metacritic score of 99, tying it with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time — the Nintendo 64 version — for the highest-rated game of all time. By every metric, GTA 6 has been a cultural event.

#3400. Oobah Butler Wants to Expose the World’s Stupidest Industries, but They Get Worse Faster Than He Can Plan His Stunts

It’s a spectacular time to be a grifter. Basic truths keep getting harder for people to agree on, marketing is more dependent on hackable algorithms than traditional gatekeepers, and it seems like everyone is willing to uncritically listen to anyone offering them a shortcut. As Oobah Butler puts it in the first episode of his new HBO series “Scams for a Better Tomorrow,” we’re living through a “gold rush of bullshit.”

If that’s the case, Butler is a prospector who hits a paystreak everywhere he looks. After beginning his career as a musician, the British performance artist has devoted much of his past decade to the art of the scam. In 2017, he made headlines for creating a TripAdvisor profile for a nonexistent restaurant that briefly became the highest-rated eatery in London. His penchant for scams has only grown since then, culminating in “Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow.” The five-episode, “Nathan for You”-esque series sees him grift his way to the top of some of the slimiest industries on the planet including wellness supplements, wine, and dating apps with an approach that blurs the line between satire and how-to guides. Related Stories Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

When we spoke over Zoom, it was the first time I had ever interviewed a scammer. I naturally had to ask Butler if that was his preferred term (he had no problem with it), and how he would characterize his own unorthodox line of work.

“I think it sits somewhere between gonzo journalism and comedy. And I think we’re in a moment, in a culture, that’s just so rife with inauthenticity and scamming,” Butler said, explaining that just watching run-of-the-mill advertisements on a streaming service are enough to convince you that we live in an insane world. “One in three [ads] are AI now. And I don’t know why, that stuck in my mind recently where I was like, ‘Wow, these aren’t real people trying to sell me a product. They’re like prompts in a machine.’ So it’s an interesting line of work, but I think it feels very now, to be honest.”

The series should be essential viewing for anyone who either wants to laugh at the state of our seemingly elite spaces or just wants to make a quick buck in a dirty industry. Episodes illustrate how ecosystems of influencers and online ratings can be easily manipulated in pursuit of accomplishing ludicrous goals, like turning an undrinkable bottle of smoke tainted cabernet into one of Napa’s highest-rated wines of the year or marketing a skincare product as “endorsed by Cameron Diaz” because a random Hispanic guy was willing to slap his name on it for $50.

It’s a funny enough premise, but Oobah and his small team (which included frequent Safdie collaborator Ronald Bronstein) found that their best laid plans left them insufficiently prepared for the greed and stupidity that they’d encounter in the real world. The first episode begins with a scheme to market a new skin serum that’s allegedly made from the tears of small children. They thought that ridiculous idea could serve as the climax of an episode, but they soon found that the grifters they encountered had little issue with the idea — some of them even thought they could make money on it with the right tear-shaped bottle. The joke remained in the show, but it had to be reduced to a starting point before the episode devolved into crazier plans.

“We had a tip from a journalist that dermatologists can be full of shit and that they often can take money in exchange for recommendations. So we set up a lab where I had these kid actors with goggles on with tubes coming off them, and it was like we were milking the kids for the tears or whatever. We were like, ‘Right, we’re going to invite this dermatologist down here,’ a high-end Manhattan dermatologist, and we expected the dermatologist to laugh us out of the room,” he said. “What we couldn’t plan for doing that stunt is that the dermatologist would be like, ‘Awesome. Yeah, this is cool. Yeah, all right, interesting product. Maybe we could keep on working together, but I expect an endorsement fee.’ And I’m like, ‘Oh, you don’t give a fucking shit. You don’t care.'”

The incident cuts to the central problem of a show like this: it’s hard for satire to keep up with a world that only seems to get crazier every day. But Butler is not shying away from the challenge. He works quickly (the show began shooting this spring and wrapped in October before premiering on November 22), and is willing to change his plans whenever it turns out that a sincere actor has beaten him to one of his comedic scams. He already has plenty of ideas for a hypothetical Season 2, including taking on the recent trend of hotels and vacation rentals using AI-generated images that look nothing like their actual rooms. But the one thing he can count on is that the bullshit gold rush is not going to end any time soon.

“It’s hard to satirize something that’s so insane and fucked up,” he said. “That’s why in the first episode, we go and make a new product because it felt like the children’s tears thing wasn’t crazy enough. You know what I mean? So I literally go and make a human meat supplement, a lab-grown human meat supplement, and we go to this lab in Austin, we take stem cells from my stomach, we grow it over months and we create this thing. Because the actual reason we did that was like, ‘Oh, I don’t think children’s tears is scary because influencers would promote that.’ So I suppose that the crazier things get, the crazier the satire has to be able for it to be effective.”

“Oobah: Scams for a Better Tomorrow” airs Sunday nights on HBO at 11 p.m. ET/PT before streaming on HBO Max.

The Hunger Games star should obviously play a Gold... but which one?

Now that we know that a Red Rising movie is in the works, it's completely understandable that we'd be on the edges of our seats waiting for any word on who might be cast in the book-to-screen adaptation. Eagle-eyed Red Rising fans -- yes, that's an intentional nod to the Bellona sigil right there -- have picked up on the fact that author Pierce Brown has followed Joseph Zada on Instagram, which has led to a lot of enthusiastic speculation that the Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping star might be in talks to play a role in Red Rising movie. I've seen one specific character name coming up a lot as the perfect role for Zada to take on, but wait a second, because there are options here.

To be clear up front, there is no official word that Zada is in talks to star in the Red Rising movie. However, it's not a stretch that his name would be circulating. As mentioned, fans noticed Pierce Brown followed Zada on Instagram. Then there's the fact that Zada is currently starring in Francis Lawrence's most recent movie adaptation. Given the news that Lawrence will be directing the Red Rising movie, it stands to reason that he might be considering people he's worked with already for the cast.

On the other hand, the fact that Pierce Brown and Francis Lawrence have known each other for years (per Lawrence) also needs to be acknowledged, as Brown could've met Zada through the director and followed him just to follow him... as people do. In short, the follow could mean nothing or it could mean something.

However, since we're speculating, I want to talk about the role(s) he'd be right to take, starting with the one that seems to be a crowd favorite.

The handsome Bellona's name came up quite a bit in the comments discussing who Zada should play, and I get it. Even as Golds go, Cassius is known to be extremely handsome, and well, Zada fits that description. Zada's also got the blond curls, which is one of the most distinctive things about Cassius' looks. Also, as a Gold, Cassius is tall, and so is Zada.

When it comes to casting the Gold characters (and Obsidians) in the movie, it seems unlikely that they're going to find the perfect actors to play the roles, who also just so happen to be around or above seven feet tall. How they make the size differences among the colors stand out on screen is going to be a challenge by itself, whether they use forced perspective, special effects or other techniques. Still, if they want to cast actors on the taller side for the Golds, IMDB has Zada listed as 6'2".

Relative to men of average height, Zada's reported height (or anywhere in the ballpark of six feet, really) seems like a good fit for a Gold on screen. That brings me to the alternate speculation, because I don't think Cassius is the only option, or possibly even the best one.

Darrow's the other name I've seen circulating, and honestly, he's the first person I thought of when I saw the topic of Joseph Zada possibly starring in the Red Rising movie. Maybe it's seeing him play a District 12 kid in Sunrise on the Reaping that makes it easier for me to envision him as a lowRed with a score to settle. There are a lot of sides to Darrow, especially when we factor in the teen that he is at the start of Red Rising, and the transition (and drama) he goes through in the first book. I can see Zada tackling that arc really well.

Nah. I can't even picture it... but it'd be fun to see his take on the role.

I'm going to cross Pax off the list right away. Even if Zada bulked up a lot for the part, I picture a guy with the size and personality of a jovial (or ferocious, when necessary) bear for the youngest Telemanus son. However, Roque would be an interesting option. I don't think Zada fits how I imagine Roque to look, but I do think he'd have an interesting take on the thoughtful character.

The last person I considered was The Jackal. While his role in the first book is fairly limited -- he's present more by reputation than he actually is on page -- he does get one of the most memorable scenes, and after playing the hero in the Hunger Games movie, I really wouldn't mind seeing what Zada does with a dark and twisty character like The Jackal.

Whether or not Zada gets cast in the Red Rising movie remains to be seen, but he does seem like a great candidate for a role, and from what he told Xtra, it sounds like he's interested in being involved.
