#3397. This X-Men Character Is The One Marvel Hero Doctor Doom Respects The Most

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Doctor Victor von Doom's ego and conviction in his own superiority are as enormous as the universe, but in his cold heart, he does respect some of the "foolish" heroes who oppose him. Doom unconditionally loves his goddaughter, Valeria Richards of the Fantastic Four. He is frenemies with Namor the Sub-Mariner, and also maintains a friendly rivalry with his fellow sorcerer Doctor Stephen Strange; their dynamic lacks the bitterness that defines Doom's feud with Reed Richards. Doom also acknowledges Captain America as a paragon of his chosen ideals, and sees even Spider-Man's puerility as if he's a court jester, the one willing to tell a king what no one else will.

But there's one hero that Doom most consistently views and addresses as an equal, and that's Ororo Monroe, Storm, of the X-Men. Storm is easily one of the strongest X-Men; she can control the weather itself and is a self-styled "goddess." Even Doom concedes her that description. Unusually for Doom, he rarely tries to downplay Storm's power next to his own. Ororo's strength intrigues him — as does her beauty.

Now, Doom isn't the kind of man to act on romantic whimsy. "Doom needs no one" is one of his self-affirming catchphrases, and he once drove away his childhood sweetheart Valeria to prioritize his quest for knowledge and power. Part of Doom's self-inflicted misery is choosing to believe that no woman could ever love a man with a scarred face like his, yet another reason Doom hides behind a mask: "How could she... when even I am driven to madness by the sight!" But even so, one feels Doom would revel in the fantasy of Storm sitting by his side. It all goes back to their first meeting in "Uncanny X-Men" #145 by Chris Claremont and Dave Cockrum.

"Uncanny X-Men" issues #145-147 comprise a short arc where the twisted gamesman Arcade teams up with Doom to destroy the X-Men. In #145, Storm shows up at Doom's castle... and he welcomes her as an honored guest, treating her to a feast while the other X-Men are attacked by mecha-armored guards. Storm herself is charmed by Doom, thinking he is "a fascinating man," and he reciprocates.

"Storm seems drawn to me, as I am to her. Lioness to lion. Queen to king. She does not fear me. She should. She will."

Indeed, Doom soon defeats the X-Men, Storm included, as he dismisses them all as simple "children" next to him. While the others are thrown into deathtraps, Doom — charmed as he was by Storm — transmutes the still conscious Ororo into a chrome statue, while creating a robot in Storm's image to serve him. For Ororo, who is claustrophobic, being trapped inside her own body is a living hell. Once freed, she lives up to her name and unfurls a terrifying storm. Echoing Doom's own words, Storm declares: "Am I not beautiful, Lord Doom? And terrible? Do you not fear me? You should. You shall."

Normally, this would be a bungled first impression. But after surrendering Arcade, Doom apologizes to Storm for his behavior, suggesting his infatuation with her was real: "I would hope that we might begin anew. You are a fascinating woman. I should like to know you better." Ororo grants him the grace of a clean slate.

The events of this arc are referenced almost any time Doom and Storm meet, such as in issue #4 of Storm's 2024 solo series, where Doom hosts her in Latveria. He's not alone among villains in his view of Storm, either.

Read any of Chris Claremont's writing, including the hundreds of "X-Men" stories to his name, and it's easy to tell that he's got a thing for powerful women. No "X-Men" character more consistently shows that than Storm, the strongest of the team and their frequent leader. It often feels like Claremont wrote his own infatuation with the character into the text; "powerful villain tries to take Storm as theirs" is a stock Claremont "X-Men" plot, and not just with Doom.

Claremont and Bill Sienkiewicz's "Uncanny X-Men" #159 sees Dracula himself try to turn Storm into his bride. (New comic series "Midnight X-Men" takes place in a timeline where he succeeded, and Storm reigns as a vampire queen.)

An attraction to Storm binds Doom and Dracula... or does it? Shortly after Doom's guest appearance in "X-Men," writer-artist John Byrne took over "Fantastic Four." Byrne had made his name drawing "X-Men," but ultimately left due to creative differences with Claremont. A lingering mark of those differences shows up in "Fantastic Four" #258. Byrne, apparently dissatisfied with how Claremont wrote Doom, suggests the Doom who teamed up with Arcade was one of Doom's robotic duplicates, or Doombots.

Now, in the "X-Men" issues themselves, there's no hint this isn't the real Doom. Years later, in Al Ewing and Stefano Caselli's "S.W.O.R.D." #7, Storm hosts Doom for dinner, and their conversation is loaded with references to "X-Men" #145. Doom blames his unbecoming behavior of attacking Storm, his guest, as a Doombot's faulty programming (but he would, wouldn't he?). Across the conversation, Doom demonstrates his interest in Storm is all too real, to the point Ororo tells him: "Don't flirt, Victor. It's unbecoming." Except, Doom would likely argue, with an exceptional woman like her.

#3396. The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’

Rita Coburn‘s “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is an extraordinary documentary about an extraordinary man, a film that spans nearly 100 years in two hours, yet never feels rushed or superficial. In her storytelling, Coburn shares with her subject a talent for distilling complex ideas and expressing them with force and clarity; the result is a movie that fully honors the breadth and depth of Du Bois’ achievements as a groundbreaking Black writer, historian, and activist.

One of Coburn’s most potent tools in this regard is the music by composer Kathryn Bostic, who previously collaborated with the director on “Marian Anderson: The Whole World in Her Hands.” Bostic incorporates a wide array of styles and influences in her score, which references the various types of music Du Bois encountered and appreciated as a Black intellectual but isn’t beholden to them; as evocative of Bach and American folk music as it is of 19th-century spirituals and Asian motifs, it’s the sonic equivalent of Du Bois’ literary works. Related Stories ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner 26 Years After He Wrote ‘Meet the Parents,’ John Hamburg Brings Comedy Back to Theaters with ‘Focker In-Law’

The scope of the project required Bostic to come at the material from multiple angles and perspectives. “Rita and I talked about what types of touchstones we needed to define the narrative musically,” Bostic told IndieWire. “There was the regional touchstone, the era-specific touchstone, the interior emotional aspects that we wanted to heighten with music. Then there’s always the discovery process as you begin to create.”

For Bostic, that discovery process is one of the most exciting aspects of film composing. While she had a number of reference points as she began work on the score, she soon found herself following intuition to take them in different directions than initially intended. “There’s always what I call the hands-on-the-clay moment,” Bostic said. “You have your list, and you have your frame of reference, but the process is fluid.”

According to Coburn, Bostic’s ability to bring a historical perspective to her scores made her an ideal collaborator for the film. “Kathryn pulled from the region of Great Barrington [where Du Bois was born] as well as New York in that time period, and then what was happening with the African-American community that Du Bois was entering,” Coburn said. “There wasn’t gospel then, so you were looking at a small group of Black people going to the churches there in New England. What were they listening to, and therefore what was he listening to?”

Bostic drew on the music of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, a Black a capella ensemble that inspired Du Bois, but then moved in a completely different direction to explore his time in Berlin, when he encountered and fell in love with classical music. She also incorporated Wolof music from Senegal and the Gambia in collaboration with Coburn’s daughter, who studied classical music and worked in the music department on “Rebel with a Cause.”

“She found a Senegalese professor online who worked with her so she could sing the Wolof,” Coburn said. “Kathryn and I agreed that we had to put the Wolof in the film because it connects Du Bois to his Ghanaian roots. But we had to find it, and we wanted it to be as authentic as possible.”

For Bostic, the challenge was taking an audience from 2026 and presenting the music in a way that would recreate the way in which Du Bois experienced it over a hundred years earlier. “There’s the historic arc of the times, as well as what he’s experiencing emotionally,” Bostic said. In the places where her score was informed by spirituals and the work of the Fisk Jubilee Singers, the composer tried to tie the emotional subtext to the context in which she knew Du Bois was consuming the music.

“When he went to Fisk University, his mother had recently died,” Bostic said. “So that music was a wellspring for his grieving, and I think that depth of sorrow and the catharsis that resulted from that sorrow inspired the sort of deep self-reflection that became such a deep part of who he was. That self-reflection led to a basic decency and humanity, and even now I think of him as being light years ahead of people in the way he embodied justice. I want to shine a light on that.”

Coburn felt a similar sense of purpose, especially since the more she dug into Du Bois’ life the more she realized how relevant his insights were to America in 2026. “He speaks to this current time,” Coburn said, adding that the importance of Du Bois’ work gave her own work a sense of urgency and responsibility. “I knew that it might be 20 or 30 years before we get another Du Bois documentary. I hope not, but I looked at his life and knew that I had to do the best job that I could. We did everything we could for Du Bois because we felt he had done everything he could for us.”

The greatness of “W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause” is that it brings the viewer into Du Bois’ perspective as his world view continues to expand over a 95-year life, and the music is a major part of that subjectivity.

“Kathryn understands that music is a character in any documentary, and her music embodies the character of W.E.B. Du Bois,” Coburn said. “ In the music, we had to grow with him. We had to expand with him. We had to see that his love of Rembrandt and his understanding of classical music, of music that came from an Asian culture, that all of that was important to him. We were catching up with him, and he was driving us.”

“W.E.B. DuBois: Rebel with a Cause” is currently streaming on the PBS app and website.

#3395. Six Things You Should Do Now to Optimize Your Setup for GTA 6

You’re almost ready for Grand Theft Auto VI. You’ve preloaded the game on your console, you’ve taken the next month off work, and you’ve locked your phone in a Faraday cage and set it adrift at sea. You’re prepared to lock in, and you haven’t forgotten a thing…right? Well, just to make sure, here are the most important tips to optimize your setup before you fire up the most anticipated game of the decade.

GTA 6 is absurdly large. According to Rockstar, you’ll need up to 212GB of storage space. For high-end consoles like the PS5 Pro, that’s more than 10% of the available storage space, and close to half the space on the more budget-conscious Xbox Series S. There’s a good chance you’ll have to delete something to make room.

Alternatively, it’s pretty easy to add more storage (if you can afford it). External SSDs are probably the cheapest route, though you’ll want to make sure to use a high-speed USB cable to connect it. It’s even worth shopping around for alternate models of SSD. For example, at the time of writing, the popular 2TB WD_BLACK external drive was close to $200, but the exact same drive in pink was $132.

You can also directly upgrade the storage of your console with expansion drives. The Xbox Series X|S supports proprietary expansion cards, while the PS5 and PS5 Pro can accept most M.2 internal SSDs. These will generally be faster, since they plug directly into the console via higher-speed connections than a drive hooked up via USB.

Let’s face it: Half the fun of any sandbox game is the weird, unique stuff that happens to only you. So you’re probably going to be hitting that “record recent gameplay” button more often than usual. While you’re cleaning up your storage space (or adding more), make sure to account for all the video clips you might want to save.

File size of video clips depends on a lot of factors, but 4K recordings can generally take up to 0.5GB per minute of footage. You can cut that down by saving footage in 1080p instead, but either way you’ll want to leave a little extra space.

Game footage is also a pretty good place to look if you need to make room on your console and don’t want to delete any games. Be honest with yourself: You don’t need all those clips from Horizon Forbidden West you saved four years ago. Dive into the settings on your console and find the biggest media files you forgot you even had on there.

According to Rockstar, GTA 6 will be targeting 30fps across consoles at launch, which is pretty low as modern AAA games go. Part of the reason for that is all the processing power going to rendering a complex environment, but it also means you won’t need a fancy high frame rate TV or monitor any time soon to get the most out of it. Still, it couldn’t hurt to check a few settings on your display.

First, make sure you’re using a higher refresh rate than 30Hz. While the game is targeting 30fps, it is technically capable of more, so if your console can keep up, you don’t want to accidentally bottleneck your frames. This setting will vary by device, so check the manual that came with your screen.

Also, make sure you have HDR enabled on your hardware. There’s a good chance this is already turned on for your TV, but sometimes other devices can switch display modes if they only support SDR. The game will help you calibrate your HDR settings for GTA 6 specifically when you launch it, but only if it detects HDR compatibility in the first place.

If you’re planning to buy a console specifically for GTA 6, this might be one of those rare instances where a PS5 Pro really is worth the upgrade. According to Rockstar, certain features like ray-traced shadows will only be available on the Pro version of Sony’s console.

More importantly, the PS5 Pro version supports PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (or PSSR), which upscales lower-resolution images to get better detail and higher frame rates out of the same hardware. Given that GTA 6 is already starting at a meager target of 30fps on most consoles, anything that can give your frame rate a boost is probably going to feel like a welcome improvement over the baseline.

I’ll tell you a secret as someone who’s spent a lot of time testing different game controllers: Most of the time, you really don’t need an expensive “elite” controller. Most of the time. I don’t buy into the idea that a taller control stick is going to make you an esports athlete. It can be nice to have, but it’s not a game changer. What does matter is customizing your controls, especially for long gaming sessions.

The DualSense Edge wireless controller is a favorite of mine, mainly because of the rear paddles and adjustable triggers. The former lets you map any button to a rear lever that you can access with your fingers underneath the controller, which can often ease some of the wrist strain of awkward button combos. And the adjustable triggers let you activate the buttons with less motion, again reducing repetitive stress.

The Xbox Elite Series 2 controller has similar features for the Xbox, as well as custom caps for the D-pad. Both consoles’ versions of pro controllers are more expensive than the standard ones, but if you’re planning to game for many hours, it can be worth it to get a controller that’s more comfortable for you.

If you have an Xbox One, you don’t necessarily have to upgrade your console to play GTA 6, but you might want to take a look at your network. GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on day one, and you’ll be able to stream the game to an Xbox One console (as long as you purchase Cloud playtime as well or get some with your Game Pass subscription). This is the only way to play on a console older than the current generation, so if you don’t want to shell out for new hardware, this might be your best bet.

Xbox recommends a minimum of a 20Mbps connection to run cloud gaming, but more is obviously better. If you can connect your console to a wired Ethernet connection, that would be better and provide more stability. If you can’t connect a cable, then at least make sure you’re well within range of your wifi router, and try to limit any other bandwidth-hogging applications on the network while you’re playing.

#3394. The One Thing to Know About Jason and Lucia Before You Play Too Much GTA 6

GTA 6 is at its best when Jason and Lucia are together

Even after clearing Grand Theft Auto 6’s long story, I keep finding myself drawn back to Leonida. That’s thanks in large part to Jason and Lucia, a pair of charismatic protagonists that I genuinely enjoy spending time with. While you can treat them as independent characters and take them out on solo adventures, GTA 6 shines brightest when you travel around Leonida as a pair. In fact, you’re bound to miss a whole lot if you aren’t letting Jason and Lucia enjoy a date from time to time.

While playing as one character in GTA 6, you have the option to invite your partner to hang out with you. (This feature unlocks partway through Chapter 2 of the story.) If you’re playing as Jason, for instance, you could text Lucia and ask if she wants to hang out, prompting her to drive to your location. You can coordinate crimes this way too; if you find a bank you want to rob, you can ping Jason and tell him to meet Lucia at the spot to pull off the job together. There are a lot of benefits to working together, as heists will become easier and you’ll be able to ask your partner to run off and fence any goods you grab.

But keeping Jason and Lucia together has some less obvious benefits, too. When the two explore together, they’ll occasionally break out into natural conversations. One time while driving through Lummox County listening to a country radio station, Lucia talked about how she thought the genre was a joke growing up. A little odd couple exchange ensued, where Jason talked about how much he loves country music. Later, upon finding a stray bicycle, Lucia told Jason about the time she tried to ride a bike as a kid and crashed into an ice cream truck.

There are even entire running gags that you’ll only hear while playing together. One recurring bit involves Lucia constantly answering spam robocalls and gradually losing her cool over them. That culminates in her giving the AI voice a firm thrashing, while Jason chuckles from the sidelines. Those bits of contextual chatter help make Jason and Lucia feel like an authentic couple rather than voiceless pawns to be moved around.

More importantly, crucial story details can come out of those moments. One time while exploring a swamp in search of Skunk Ape effigies (weird game!), Jason and Lucia broke out into a conversation about their family dynamics. It started when Jason mentioned Lucia’s mother doesn’t like him very much. After a bit of unconvincing denial, Lucia admitted that there’s truth to Jason’s anxiety: Lucia lied to her mother, saying that Jason essentially walked out on her and their child. That revelation triggered a conversation where Lucia recalled a moment where Jason once told her he didn’t want children, which is why she initially didn’t tell Jason about their son. It’s an important moment that gives depth to Jason and Lucia’s history and fills in some questions about why Tommy was kept secret for so long.

So, if you’ve been exploring Leonida solo for most of your GTA 6 playthrough, make sure to invite your partner to hang out regularly. You’ll miss some of the best human moments in the game if you do, and you’ll understand each character so much more by listening to their chatter. And, of course, you’ll also be able to send Jason off with a bag full of cocaine if you don’t want to trek back to Vice City to sell it.

#3393. Guy Pearce's Gory '90s Horror Western Movie Deserved Better At The Box Office

One of the enduring American monster myths is the Wendigo or the forest spirit that possesses and compels men to become cannibals. Originally a myth of the Algonquian peoples, the Wendigo has become a monster of comic books, horror films, and more, like Stephen King's chilling novel "Pet Sematary."

Possibly the strangest Wendigo movie is the 1999 horror western comedy "Ravenous," inspired by real tales of 19th century cannibalism on the frontier like the Donner Party. During the Mexican–American War, Lieutenant John Boyd (Guy Pearce) plays dead during battle. Hidden among a cart of deceased soldiers, Boyd takes an enemy fort. A hero but also a coward, Boyd is then reassigned to a remote outpost in the Sierra Nevada mountains.

Curiously, during Boyd's seizure of the fort, he seemed to gain strength when the blood of the dead dripped down onto his tongue. In that moment, Boyd became an unknowing Wendigo, acquiring the strength of the men whose blood he drank — and he's not the only one on the mountain. A traveler named F.W. Colqhoun (Robert Carlyle) shows up at the fort, claiming to be the survivor of a band of wagon travelers killed and cannibalized by their guide, one Colonel Ives. But "Colqhoun" is Ives and, seizing control of the camp, plots to turn it into a cannibal colony. He recognizes Boyd as a seeming kindred spirit, and the movie becomes a test of whether Boyd will succumb to Ives' pressure and his own Wendigo hunger.

"Ravenous" was a box office bomb in its day, grossing $2 million against a $12 million budget, and it received largely underwhelmed or confounded reviews. But don't take that as a mark against the movie, which has a following to this day. (Any "Yellowjackets" fan should make watching "Ravenous" a priority.)

For "Ravenous" to work, Boyd's temptation needs to feel real. When you've got someone as charismatic as Robert Carlyle playing Ives, it sure does. That performance isn't the only way that Carlyle saved the movie.

"Ravenous" had a tumultuous production, and Guy Pearce has called "Ravenous" his worst experience shooting a movie. The film's original director Milcho Manchevski was fired mid-filming with 20th Century Fox moving to replace him with "Home Alone 3" director Raja Gosnell. The cast rejected that, and so Carlyle brought in director Antonia Bird, who he'd worked with on the 1997 crime film "Face." Bird is the credited director of "Ravenous," but was she able to wrangle the mess she'd inherited?

Even a "Ravenous" fan will admit the movie is, tonally, all over the place. After a scene of Ives revealing his true murderous self, the movie breaks out into a chase scene with comical banjo music. If you'll pardon the pun, "Ravenous" bites off a lot and tests how much it's capable of chewing. But that strangeness is a strength, as there's no other movie quite like "Ravenous."

In a 2015 retrospective review for Rolling Stone, critic David Ehrlich showed the kind of praise that has earned "Ravenous" a fanbase. Ehrlich complimented its unique tonal recipe and how, through its setting, it equates manifest destiny colonialism with literal cannibalism... while conceding those qualities are likely what turned off audiences in 1999.

Considering the 1990s saw Anthony Hopkins make Hannibal Lecter into a cinematic icon on the heels "The Silence of the Lambs," I can see why studio execs would invest in cannibal horror. But "Ravenous" was just too weird a movie to ever be a massive hit, even though it's found its supporters with time.

#3392. Watch the ‘Project Hail Mary’ VFX Supervisor Explain Why Having Puppeteers on Set Was Worth All the Extra Work

The making of “Project Hail Mary” was a miracle on par with the outer space rescue mission that Ryan Gosling is tasked with pulling off. Phil Lord and Chris Miller’s adaptation of Andy Weir’s bestselling novel manages to be epic without ever losing its intimacy, as Gosling traverses the galaxy and saves the world with only a very lovable rock acting alongside him. The final product was a complicated blend of practical effects, on-set puppetry, and a healthy dose of VFX magic.

Incorporating so many production elements creates more work for all involved. The puppetry team lead by James Ortiz had to fit into very small spaces, which frequently meant they showed up in the frames. Visual Effects Production Supervisor Mag Sarnowska and her team were tasked with removing all of the puppeteers. But as she explained during the VFX panel at IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables, it was a small price to pay for the way it enhanced Gosling’s acting performance. Related Stories The Extraordinary Music Worthy of an Extraordinary Life in ‘W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel with a Cause’ ‘Coward’ Trailer: Lukas Dhont’s Belgian Oscar Entry Is a Queer Stunner

“It was so good to have James and his puppeteers, which we called Rocketeers,” Sarnowska said. “It was great to have them there, but it did not work out sometimes. Our sets were really, really tiny. Having five people there to puppet Rocky was hard sometimes. But to everyone’s point, having something there in the frame was so helpful, especially for Ryan to act to. The eyeline? That’s a real thing. Even though our Rocky didn’t have eyes, a person’s brain makes it easier to figure out where the eyes would be just by having that constant relation between Rocky and Ryan.”

Sarnowska — who will share the Innovation Award at the IndieWire Honors with Ortiz, Neal Scanlan, and Paul Lambert — explained that having a real reference point for VFX sequences is what ultimately makes the most effects-heavy sequences feel real.

“In Ryan’s space, he has to be in the xenonite glass, so having reflections, adding the glass, it was a lot of work,” she said. “But having that real thing, having that reference, even if we had to replace it, that was so important. Because we knew what Rocky would look like.”

#3391. You Can Get One of These Pocket E-Readers for As Little As $55 Before Black Friday

Black Friday is usually a great time to grab a new e-reader, but the ongoing RAM crisis has made that a question mark this year: Amazon recently raised the prices of all its Kindles by around $50 and refreshed the entire lineup, which means your odds of grabbing one at a big discount are low. But you aren't totally out of luck: If you haven't noticed, micro-e-readers—I'm talking credit card-sized, with screens that measure around four inches—are all the rage in 2026, and right now, you can pick up one of them for around $55.

If you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is currently 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink quickly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 launched at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also important to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing new firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. #3390. Chris Evans Reveals Whether Avengers: Doomsday Shows Doctor Doom's Face Under The Mask

Marvel Studios certainly made an impression, for good or ill, when it announced at San Diego Comic-Con 2024 that Robert Downey Jr. would be returning to the Marvel Cinematic Universe... but as Doctor Doom, not Iron Man. Marvel fans instantly assumed, with good reason, that Doom was being reimagined as having some connection to Iron Man (i.e. that Victor von Doom would be a Tony Stark variant turned evil).

But surprisingly, the marketing for "Avengers: Doomsday" has not been leaning on any connection between Doom and Iron Man. The second "Doomsday" trailer confirms that he comes from the Fantastic Four's universe, Earth-828, and shares a history with them. The closest thing has been a new post-credits scene from "Avengers Endgame: Encore" that shows Doom forging his mask in a way mirroring Tony doing so back in 2008's "Iron Man." Speaking to Empire, Marvel Studios President Kevin Feige also stressed that, despite the double casting, RDJ's Doom is indeed Victor von Doom and not a Tony Stark variant.

Now, there is an easy out here. Doom is famous for wearing a metal mask to hide his supposedly scarred face. In the comics, he almost never takes that mask off. If it wanted, Marvel Studios could keep Doom in the mask and make it so him sharing an actor with Tony Stark becomes a non-issue. In fact, Chris Evans told Empire that's exactly what happens in "Doomsday," explaining:

"[Doom is] wearing a mask the whole time. That's not an easy challenge, to try and get your message across and be emotionally available to connect with. It just reinforces what I've always felt: Downey can do anything."

It feels pretty implausible Marvel would hire RDJ like this and not take full advantage of him, but I want to believe it.

When "Doomsday" directors Joe and Anthony Russo announced Robert Downey Jr. as Doom on the SDCC stage, they said they felt they needed the "greatest actor in the world" to play the villain. Chris Evans' words to Empire echo that narrative: Downey is Doom only because he's the best actor for the part.

And in a vacuum, sure, yes, there's little doubt he can pull it off. During his MCU hiatus, RDJ won an Oscar for his turn in Christopher Nolan's "Oppenheimer" as Lewis Strauss, who destroys J. Robert Oppenheimer's (Cillian Murphy) life out of a petty, misplaced grudge. Strauss is to "Oppie" as Doom is to Reed Richards!

But when you bring back your franchise's biggest star in a different role? And as part of a story that's all about different versions of characters from different universes colliding? Yeah, you can't blame people for assuming there's going to be an in-universe reason for Stark and Doom sharing a face.

This is pure speculation, but one going theory in Marvel fan communities is that Downey's casting as Doom is a smokescreen to hide that he'll also be returning as Iron Man in "Avengers: Secret Wars" (i.e. there's no need to hide him on the "Secret Wars" set because everyone will already know he's there playing Doom). You could pull that off if Doom indeed wears his mask the entire time, so the films don't present him and Stark as twins, and that bypasses the issue of RDJ getting no facetime if Doom keeps his mask on. I'll admit this appeals to me because it keeps Doom and Stark separate, which has always been my preference. But again, no clue if that's even remotely true.

It's worth noting that Chris Evans is also only talking about "Avengers: Doomsday." Perhaps that film will have Doom keep his mask on the whole time, and then only in "Secret Wars" will Doom be unmasked. There's some narrative sense to that: Part one of this story builds up Doom's threat, and then once he's won, you can explore the man underneath. In the original 1984 "Secret Wars" comics, after Doom steals the power of the godlike Beyonder, he uses it to heal his scarred face.

An adaptation of that scene practically writes itself. Doom, revealing his new power, unlatches his mask and shows himself free of any scarring. But this time, some of the heroes recognize Doom's face as Tony Stark's, and that opens up a mystery of why they look identical.

For what it's worth, Doom's co-creator Jack Kirby always maintained Doom's face being "horribly scarred" was an exaggeration. No, Doom actually only has a small scar on his chin, but he's such an insecure egotist that he can't stand to let anyone — even himself — see that reminder of his imperfections, no matter how small they are. That's my preferred interpretation of comics Doom, but I'm not convinced crowded, multiverse-shattering blockbuster movies like "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars" will have room for that sort of psychological nuance.

"Avengers: Doomsday" is scheduled for theatrical release on December 18, 2026.

#3389. The Witcher 4 Will Be a GTA 6-Sized Leap Forward, CD Projekt Red Says

CDPR addresses comparisons between its games and Grand Theft Auto 6

We're living in a post-Grand Theft Auto 6 world now, meaning that almost every other game in development will inevitably be compared to Rockstar Games' new open-world crime drama. The developer behind two other big open-world brands, The Witcher and Cyberpunk, is now fielding questions about how its future games will stack up against GTA 6.

During an earnings call on Tuesday, CD Projekt Red joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski addressed the Leonida-sized elephant in the room: how GTA 6 will influence his company's upcoming games, The Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2. Nowakowski said that he believes The Witcher 4 will deliver a GTA 6-like leap forward for players.

"Of course, we did look at the game," Nowakowski said of GTA 6, adding, "We did see the differences" between it and 2013's Grand Theft Auto 5. "We believe there's going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4. It's been 11 years. We are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game. So, yes, you should expect us to make a much, much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4."

"We have certain ambitions when it comes to [The Witcher 4] and Cyberpunk 2," he said. "They have not changed when it comes to GTA 6. If anything happened as a result of GTA 6, it's [that it's] always great to see games like that because they show you how much cool stuff can be done, and that's for sure an inspiration in many ways for our developers."

Nowakowski also addressed The Witcher 4's through the lens of GTA 6's budget. Rockstar's latest release is rumored to have a development budget of more than $1 billion, and Nowakowski categorized CD Projekt Red's upcoming games as not having "budget-driven developments."

"I'm not saying we don't care about the budgets. We do," he said. "I'm pretty sure [Rockstar] did as well. But you cannot make games like that having in mind This is the fixed number of money I want to spend and that's it, otherwise we’re gone. They're ambition-driven developments and money's important. The budgets are not indefinite, that's not what we're saying. And honestly that philosophy has not changed for us because of GTA 6's release; it has just always been like that."

As for other lessons learned from GTA 6's massive launch, Nowakowski noted that "If you want to reach a certain critical mass, you do have to get out of the core main gaming bubble, [which is] something we did achieve in the past as well. Our games are different and they require a certain different approach. But in terms of the ultimate effect in terms of breaking out to the mass market, awareness, this is something we consider critical."

In other words, while CD Projekt Red may take some cues from Rockstar Games, it's not trying to copy the Grand Theft Auto developer's homework.

The Witcher 4 is slated for release in 2028. Cyberpunk 2 does not have an announced release window.

Sylvester Stallone shares an idea for a new Taylor Sheridan series starring his former box office rival turned friend, Arnold Schwarzenegger.

Best known as Rocky and Rambo, Stallone's first leading role in a television series came in 2022, starring in Taylor Sheridan's Tulsa King as Dwight "The General" Manfredi, a New York mafia capo who, after serving a 25-year prison sentence, is exiled to Oklahoma to set up his own criminal organization. The series has been a hit, with Tulsa King season 4 currently airing new episodes on Paramount+.

Now, in Cigar Aficionado's new cover story, Sylvester Stallone says he wants Arnold Schwarzenegger to star in a Tulsa King spinoff, with their characters eventually crossing paths, much like they did in The Expendables franchise. Read his full comments below:

I would love in a perfect world to do an extension of Tulsa King starring [Schwarzenegger] in his own show. Since we’re comrades in the fantasy world, our characters meet and discuss things, like we did in The Expendables. I hope he agrees.

No such spinoff has officially been announced or entered development, so Stallone may simply be testing the idea publicly. When The Hollywood Reporter reached out, Paramount+ and producer 101 Studios had no immediate comment.

Stallone and Schwarzenegger have shared the silver screen four times, including in three Expendables movies (2010–2014) and the prison-set action thriller Escape Plan (2013). From the late 1970s to the 1990s, the two action stars engaged in a bitter rivalry, frequently competing with each other at the box office. By the late 1990s, they built bridges, leading to a lasting friendship.

Tulsa King already has one upcoming spinoff, Frisco King, starring Samuel L. Jackson as Russell Lee Washington Jr., who made his debut in Tulsa King season 3. Premiering on December 18, the spinoff follows Russell Washington as he relocates to Texas to build his own criminal enterprise. If Stallone gets his wish, the question will become where Schwarzenegger's character would establish his own criminal empire. While Las Vegas, Atlantic City, or Detroit are intriguing possibilities, both Tulsa King and Frisco King are set in what are seen as untapped criminal markets in the Southwest.

Of course, all of this remains wishful thinking for now, as it's unclear whether Schwarzenegger is even interested in taking on a Tulsa King spinoff. #3385. Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday Might Have The Biggest Box Office Opening Weekend Ever

There has been much discussion as to whether or not the Marvel Cinematic Universe has lost its lustre in recent years. Indeed, Marvel's 2025 box office proved the MCU has fallen from grace, at least in terms of launching newer or less surefire franchises. However, "The Avengers" remains a gold standard for audiences around the world, and "Avengers: Doomsday" is going to prove that in a big way In December. So much so that we could be looking at, quite literally, the biggest opening weekend of all time.

Directed by Joe and Anthony Russo, aka the Russo Brothers, "Doomsday" is currently expected to open with a whopping $375 to $424 million domestically on the weekend of December 18, per Box Office Theory. Mind you, that's just in North America, not worldwide. If this pans out, even on the low end, it would set a new high bar for cinema, financially speaking. "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" ruled the box office back in July with a record $360 million domestic debut, yet "Doomsday" looks like it might clear that with ease.

Even more surprising? The latest "Avengers" film is opening directly against the much-anticipated "Dune: Part Three," which is eyeing a blockbuster debut in the $91 to $115 million range. As a result, the so-called cinematic double bill known as Dunesday will blow Barbenheimer out of the water at the box office.

The latest "Avengers" cinematic event follows beloved heroes from three distinct universes as they're set on a deadly collision course and face an existential threat unlike anything they've ever encountered. Namely, Doctor Doom, played by former "Iron Man" star Robert Downey Jr. The Russos previously helmed both "Avengers: Infinity War" and "Avengers: Endgame," which also bodes well.

"Avengers: Doomsday" trailers are selling the film as the MCU's biggest event yet, and, much like "Infinity War" did in 2018, it's teeing up something even bigger. Specifically, "Avengers: Secret Wars," which will close out the MCU's Multiverse Saga by adapting one of the most beloved Marvel Comics storylines of all time.

It can't be emphasized just how staggering these numbers are. "Avengers: Endgame" smashed box office records with a $1.2 billion global opening in 2019, with its $357.1 million domestic figure serving as the opening weekend record until "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" came along. "Avengers: Endgame" also passed "Avatar" to reclaim the highest-grossing movie title earlier this year thanks to the "Encore" re-release. Its lifetime total sits at $2.94 billion worldwide.

In light of how up and down things have been for the MCU in recent years, there was doubt as to whether or not "Doomsday" could live up to sky high expectations. Evidently, audiences are still very interested in seeing Earth's Mightiest Heroes, despite anything else that's happened in the 2020s. It doesn't matter that "The Marvels" finished its box office run as the lowest-grossing MCU movie ever or that films like "Thunderbolts*" fell way short of commercial expectations. This is the Avengers.

Even more amazing is the fact that Disney and Marvel Studios are doing this without the benefit of IMAX screens. "Dune: Part Three" has those locked up, which is significant since IMAX has proved it's more important to the box office than ever before. But the Avengers don't need IMAX. Would it be nice? Sure, but they're going to shatter records either way.

"Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

You can connect the iPad to an external display, up to 4K resolution at 60Hz. It also supports two Apple Pencil models: The USB-C Apple Pencil and the first-gen Apple Pencil.

The only real consideration here is storage: This model comes with 128GB of storage, which can run out fast. It's particularly usable for users who rely on cloud storage or mostly stream their entertainment. But if your giftee plans to store photos, videos, or music on their iPad, it's worth considering upgrading. The $50 discount applies to most storage models, as well as the cellular iPad options, except for the 512GB models: The wifi-only model has a smaller discount, while the cellular option has a $100 discount.

Sure, the iPad A16 doesn't have the fastest processor, an OLED display, support for newer accessories, or Apple's sharpest cameras. But all of the specs it does have are enough to run the things you need on iPadOS. If someone on your list is looking for an iPad for web browsing, streaming, messaging, and light gaming—and they don't need something for professional work—this device is likely more than enough iPad for them.

#3383. GTA 6's Staggering Sales Still Might Never Catch GTA 5

The new game's day-one sales defy belief, but so does its big brother's long-term record

On Friday, Rockstar Games' parent company Take-Two Interactive announced sales figures for Grand Theft Auto 6 that are so dizzying, I'm still processing them. They have clearly shattered preorder records for video games and launch sales — in fact, total sales – for just about any form of entertainment.

Take-Two said that GTA 6 sold 32.5 million copies during its pre-release period, and that through the end of launch day on Nov. 19, it had racked up $3.79 billion in revenue.

Comparisons are fun to make, but apt ones don't really exist. On its day of launch, GTA 6 had made twice as much money as Taylor Swift's entire Eras tour, and more than any film has ever made across a full theatrical run. Alinea Analytics reckons that by the end of the weekend the numbers were up to 44.9 million copies sold and a round $4 billion in revenue. It took GTA 6 one day to eclipse the lifetime sales figures of The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild.

Here's a more meaningful comparison: Grand Theft Auto 5 took three days to hit $1 billion in sales. GTA 6's launch is four times bigger than its predecessor's. It will definitely crush GTA 5's lifetime record, right? Well… not necessarily.

As amazing as GTA 6's sales are, it has a long, long way to go to catch up with its big brother. GTA 5 is the second-best selling game of all time behind Minecraft (or third-best, depending on how you account for sales of Tetris). It has sold a staggering 235 million copies to date, more than two and a half times as many as the next game in the all-time ranking, Rockstar's own Red Dead Redemption 2.

When it comes to long-tail, long-term sales, GTA 5 is in a different class entirely — a class of two, alongside Minecraft. It's not a given that GTA 6 will necessarily be able to join this class. A few things have to fall into place.

Rockstar has yet to confirm a PC version of the game, for starters, though one is expected in 2027. That will unlock a whole new audience for GTA 6, especially globally, and supercharge its sales again.

Rockstar has also yet to confirm that it will create a GTA 6 version of GTA Online. GTA 5's scrappy multiplayer mode became a live-service behemoth that has driven a huge proportion of those 235 million sales, and that financially sustained Rockstar through the extremely long and expensive developments of Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 6. Analysts also seem confident in predicting GTA 6's online mode will arrive in 2027, although I think a degree of skepticism is warranted on that part.

Rockstar hasn't said one word publicly about GTA 6 Online for good reason. Migrating online gaming audiences, who’ve invested massive amounts of time and money in their accounts, from one game to a sequel is notoriously difficult. It's why there was never a World of Warcraft 2, for example, and there are vanishingly few examples of it being done successfully (Destiny 2 being, perhaps, the exception that proves the rule).

This is not to say that Rockstar won't do it, but the studio will need to be extremely careful and consider its strategy. Will it lock the new online mode behind a full purchase of GTA 6, as it initially did with its predecessor? Sell it separately and/or bundle it in a GTA Plus subscription, as it now does for GTA Online? Or maybe even go free-to-play? These approaches all have their advantages and drawbacks when it comes to tempting GTA Online players to upgrade and maximizing the new online game's revenue, but only one of them is going to help GTA 6 sell as many copies as GTA 5.

There's a final but important asterisk to consider with respect to GTA 5's astonishing sales. It has been released across three console generations, and a lot of those purchases will be duplicates or even triplicates (which is especially true for GTA Online players).

In other words, the sales figures are likely flattering to the maximum size of the GTA audience; I don't think there are 235 million GTA players out there. It's going to be challenging for GTA 6 to meet that number unless it, too, spans three generations. I hope we won't be waiting until late in the PlayStation 7's life for GTA 7, but you never know with Rockstar.

One thing's for sure: Rockstar's only real competition is itself. GTA 6 has had the biggest launch imaginable. Can it also go the distance?

#3382. John Turturro, Carrie Coon, Guitarricadelafuente, and Peter Gamble to Receive SFFILM Honors

Awards season will be making a stop in San Francisco on December 7 for the annual SFFILM Awards Night, honoring four artists who’ve made an impact this year.

John Turturro, acclaimed this year for his performance in “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” will receive the Maria Manetti Shrem Award for Acting, named for the Italian-American philanthropist. (Turturro will also receive IndieWire Honors recognition on December 3.) Carrie Coon, who made a big-screen splash this year in “The Liberation,” will receive the Katie & Todd Traina Award for Acting. The SFFILM Award for Virtuosity will go to “La Bola Negra” breakout star and beloved Spanish pop singer Guitarricadelafuente. Finally, the Nion McEvoy & Leslie Berriman Award for Storytelling goes to “I Play Rocky” screenwriter Peter Gamble. Presenters include “La Bola Negra” directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, and “I Play Rocky” star Anthony Ippolito (all of whom are also being feted by IndieWire Honors in December).

SFFILM Awards Night will take place on Monday, December 7, 2026, at San Francisco’s Gateway Pavilion at Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture.

Anne Lai, SFFILM’s executive director, said, “Film has a rare power to change how we see the world. SFFILM exists to celebrate it and to build its future. At Awards Night we do both. We honor artists whose bold, generous storytelling defined this year in cinema, and we raise the resources that power our work all year long, from students in Bay Area classrooms to the filmmakers we fund and mentor. I’m thrilled to welcome our honorees to San Francisco, where the future is always being created, and film is the gateway.”

“Carrie, Guitarricadelafuente, Peter, and John each bring a distinct sensibility and an uncommon command of their craft to the screen this season,” said Jessie Fairbanks, SFFILM’s director of programming. “We selected this group because they represent the range of talent and creative perspectives that make cinema so compelling, and their work speaks to the thoughtful, nuanced, and often unexpected films that make a season memorable. They bring a fearlessness, determination, and depth of perspective that we are proud to celebrate at SFFILM.”

Last year, Benicio Del Toro, Kristen Stewart, Wunmi Mosaku, and Scott Cooper all received SFFILM prizes. The event serves as a fundraising opportunity for the Bay Area nonprofit film organization that also hosts the San Francisco International Film Festival.

#3380. Why There Are No New NCIS, New York, & Origins Tonight (Nov 24) & When They Return For Fresh Episodes

Tuesday nights are one of the best nights for TV. It means the NCIS trio takes pride of place on the small screen, and there's certainly a lot of excitement as the shows get ready for their winter breaks. It was just last year when CBS finally put NCIS back in its rightful place, kicking off Tuesdays in style, and it was joined by two other shows.

While there has been a small change with NCIS: Sydney not returning in the fall, the new spinoff NCIS: New York has more than made up for it. LL Cool J and Scott Caan's refreshing change has brought an energy to the screen that hasn't been seen in a few years, and the rest of the team brings mystery, intrigue, and humor. Sure, there is some disappointment in that NCIS: Origins season 3 will only have 10 episodes, but each of those installments features Mark Harmon as Gibbs once more, bringing much-needed answers about Lala and a new mystery to unravel.

As for the flagship series, NCIS season 24 has gained one thing that was missing: Tony DiNozzo. Michael Weatherly's return has proven DiNozzo was the missing piece on NCIS for the longest time, while delivering a mature man worthy of the director's chair. With all this, there is the understandable question about why there are no new episodes of the NCIS universe on CBS tonight.

After just taking a week off due to the midterm elections, the NCIS franchise barely gives anyone time to recover as it takes another break. This time it's linked to Thanksgiving, as CBS has opted to give almost all shows on the schedule a break. Usually, Thursday and Friday shows are preempted because of Thanksgiving itself, and it's become expected since people want to gather with family or friends, and they're more likely to put the football on.

Taking a break earlier in the week hasn't been as common in the past. While the NCIS shows took time off in 2025, they didn't in 2024. However, as viewership has declined over the years, it makes sense to preempt most shows as people get ready to spend time with family, with some traveling during Thanksgiving Eve or earlier to beat the holiday rush.

Instead of airing new episodes, CBS will still have a night of NCIS, packing the November 24 schedule with reruns. It all starts with a rerun of the NCIS season 23 episode titled "Her," which saw the return of Ellie Bishop, finally offering closure for viewers and Torres. After that, the pilot episode of NCIS: New York will air, offering those who may have missed it a chance to see LL Cool J's newest series introduction.

While NCIS: Origins usually airs in the final slot of the night, that's not happening tonight. Unfortunately, CBS has opted for another NCIS rerun instead, airing another NCIS season 23 episode, titled "Fleeting." This brought far more trouble to Fleet Week than normal, with a sailor turning up dead in the trunk of a car.

While the break is disappointing, there is some good news. The break is not a long one, with all three NCIS shows set to return on December 1, 2026, with all-new episodes on CBS. Don't forget there's also a chance to watch whichever NCIS episode you want on Paramount+.

In even better news, these episodes won't be the fall finales. While NBC and ABC have opted to bring many of their shows to a close before Thanksgiving, CBS will continue to air new episodes later into December. NCIS, New York, and Origins will all air their fall finales on December 8, 2026, and even the winter hiatus isn't going to be that long.

When NCIS season 24 returns, it will be with an episode titled "Lucky Shot." MCRT is pulled into a case that involves a freelance nightcrawler videographer who turns up dead. It's soon clear that he was murdered, and the motive is linked to evidence he secretly recorded connected to a cover-up. Not only will the team need to figure out who the murderer is, but they'll also need to uncover a conspiracy that brings danger at every turn.

NCIS: New York will deliver its seventh hour of the season, titled "The River." Like other episodes in the new LL Cool J series, this one won't necessarily involve a murder. It could turn out that way, but the team is called in when a Marine sergeant's car is discovered after he fled Quantico. This Marine sergeant was supposed to be going on a high-stakes mission, and now the question is whether he left on his own accord or if something more serious is going on.

Although it was a gamble, the NCIS franchise taking a risk with its future is already paying off for CBS as its newest series continues to roll out.

In the final hour of the night, NCIS: Origins returns with en episode titled "Don't Let the Day Go By." This is a huge hour in the present day, as Gibbs turns to another former colleague and friend, Vera. Roma Maffia returns to the universe once more, reprising her role as Vera Strickland, to help Gibbs get to the bottom of those who are after him. Of course, he now needs to figure out what really happened to Lala, and why she wasn't on that plane.

In the past, the team would need to deal with the murder of a Marine. This is far more than a traditional murder, though, as the Marine is missing a tongue, and that usually means some sort of mob or cartel is involved. In this case, the team will come face to face with a Russian serial killer.

The fall finales of all three NCIS universe shows will air on December 8, 2026. It will then be time for the winter hiatus, but get ready for all three shows to be back before January comes to an end. CBS has set the date as January 12, 2027.

#3379. ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

A very successful “values-based entertainment” company that was begat — in the parlance of its biblical heritage — from a film-filtering service that illegally edited “objectionable content” out of major Hollywood movies, Angel Studios has since become the world’s foremost purveyor of megachurch-approved multiplex content. The bigger they got (on the strength of projects like “The Chosen” and the QAnon cause célèbre “Sound of Freedom,” the latter of which pioneered a questionable ticketing model that continues today), the more that Angel removed from the films they released. Not just sex and swear words, but also anything that even vaguely resembled a soul. Related Stories Billy Ray Joins Oscar Short Contender ‘Magan’s Fare,’ Starring Barkhad Abdi, as Executive Producer Why Is the ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Trailer So… Gloomy? Internet Erupts Over Latest Look at Marvel Movie

With “Hershey,” a decidedly vanilla biopic about the most famous chocolatier who’s ever lived, the studio has taken its socio-religious project to its logical conclusion: They’ve made a movie that’s been stripped of any flavor whatsoever. It’s the cinematic equivalent of carob powder. It’s what Ned Flanders will force his kids to watch next Halloween.

Somehow unimaginatively bland and Splenda-sweet all at once, this godforsaken affront to good storytelling may not have benefited from any of the material that its distributor has deemed amoral, but “Hershey” is so mind-numbingly absent the most basic friction of the human experience that I wanted to fall to my knees and thank the lord that a few errant Kisses made it past The Angel Promise on a technicality. It’s too bad Milton S. Hershey never used his platform to baselessly sow doubt in a foreign election, because at least one of Angel Studios’ co-founders would clearly have been cool with including that (ecocidal fascism is fine, just don’t say “fuck” while you’re razing the Amazon, as that would offend Jesus).

As you may have gathered by now, I am probably not the target audience for this unrepentant godslop.

Not because I’m agnostic (“Hershey” is as secular as Angel Studios’ output gets, its overt religiosity limited to a brief scene in which the movie’s namesake pleads for help from an unspecified higher power), but rather because I stubbornly, blasphemously insist that a womb-to-tomb biopic should bear at least some faint resemblance to the stuff of real life. I couldn’t possibly care less about the facts (though I struggle to believe that Hershey and his wife literally danced with joy after learning that a twist of fate had spared them from being aboard the Titanic), but there isn’t a single moment in this film that feels like it was written by a real person, let alone lived by one.

Let’s back up a beat. To be clear, Angel Studios didn’t technically make this movie — that distinction belongs to the spiritually aligned production company Dandelion Media, who partnered with Hershey Entities for a fully authorized feature-length commercial meant to “bring [the chocolate brand’s] story into culture in a more immersive way.” The success of that marketing spend remains to be seen, but it can’t hurt to highlight Mr. Hershey’s ostensible purity at a time when the company that bears his name has been under fire for diluting its products with compound coatings in order to save money. And so we have a punishingly straightforward film that paints the Pennsylvania icon as a square-jawed, sweet-toothed wife guy who loved candy, orphans, and sitting way too close to the edge of the massive water tower that overlooks the town he remade in his own image.

Directed by Mark Waters, but absent any trace of the poppy confidence he once brought to the likes of “Mean Girls” and “Freaky Friday,” “Hershey” opens with its first and only stylistic flourish as a match cut transforms an immaculate chocolate Kiss into a small lump of coal — Milton Hershey’s life would turn out to be sweet, but it sure didn’t start that way. The film that follows sadly feels less like “Lawrence of Arabia” than it does an AI-generated adaptation of Hershey’s Wikipedia page, its algorithmic sense of human interaction rendered all the more uncanny by its ecclesiastical approach to conflict (and also by its blown out cinematography, which suggests a very literal interpretation of Angel Studios’ promise to produce “movies and shows that amplify light.”)

Adhering to the prosaic structure and candied morality that the Erwin brothers have made endemic to the world of faith-based biopics and their immediate kin, the film sees Hershey’s life as a blessed march towards his eternal reward — one that’s only slowed down by the litany of speed bumps that pop up along his path to heaven.

Young Milton’s very serious Mennonite mom is a major bummer, but she lets him out of the house to work for a local printer. The JRPG-like town where he grows up in the 1860s seems inhospitable to dreams, but its muddy roads make it appear as though the streets are paved with chocolate. His dad (Alan Ruck, a long way from “Succession”) abandons him pretty fast, but not before bending down to the kid like Zooey Deschanel in “Almost Famous” and telling him: “You’re a Hershey, and that means when you follow your dream, you don’t let anyone get in your way.” Apparently his dad’s dream was to not live with his family anymore, but so be it. A good example is a good example.

Every stumbling block is immediately followed by a burst of divine providence, as Sharon Paul and Timothy Michael Hayes’ script adheres to the grindset mindset of the prosperity gospel while Rolfe Kent’s saccharine score blends everything together into a tasteless slurry of unrefined sugar. The film insists that a little sweetness goes a long way, as an orgasmic taste of rock candy is all that Milton needs to make it through the day, but it doesn’t heed its own advice. Milton’s passion leads him to a job working for a saintly confectioner named Joseph Royer (a beneficent Richard Kind, as close to a live-action Bing Bong as he’s ever been), who just smiles it off when the kid forgets to turn off the peanut roaster and nearly burns down the whole shop.

Later, after sprouting into Finn Wittrock and starting his own caramel company, Milton is miraculously spared from ruin several times over by virtue of his non-denominational faith in himself and the universe. One low moment is redeemed by a massive order from overseas. Another resolves with a traveling salesman busting into the Lancaster Caramel Company with an offer to invest in chocolate — the future of snacking! “This chocolate,” Milton sniffs, “it could be good if it wasn’t so bad.” I know the feeling. The next time disaster strikes, he inadvertently stumbles upon the Hershey Kiss in the very next scene. The plotting is schematic enough to make “Bohemian Rhapsody” seem like “Last Days” by comparison.

Somewhere in there Milton enjoys a meet-cute with a woman named Kitty Sweeney (Alexandria Daddario), a grinning beauty who credits caramels with curing her shyness. Her job as Milton’s wife is to be his biggest cheerleader, and then — as the years melt away — to collapse in undiagnosed pain whenever he leaves the room. At one point it is implied that she and Milton have sexual intercourse, but only so the movie can leverage the couple’s inability to conceive a child into a robust philanthropic regime that allowed them to house and educate any number of white male orphans.

Of course, expecting this movie to acknowledge the Milton Hershey School’s history of racial and social discrimination would be as delusional as thinking its third act might address the labor disputes that unsettled Hershey’s chocolate factory in the late 1930s. Such things are simply not sweet enough to befit a story about how some vague belief and a little stick-it-to-em are all a man needs to prosper in this great land — even if a warts-and-all version of that same story would still be a model of American success.

Considerably less textured than the chocolate bars that have become synonymous with its title character, Waters’ film is so determined to launder one man’s dreams into reality that it comes to assume its own kind of dream logic in return — one divorced from the basic relationship between cause-and-effect or an event and its meaning.

In what might be the single most deranged movie scene of the year, Milton and his ailing wife Kitty literally dance for joy on the bow of a ship after learning that a twist of fate has spared them from being aboard the Titanic, even though upwards of 1,400 other people went to a watery grave that night. I’m not sure that qualifies as bringing the brand’s “story into the culture in a more immersive way,” but it’s definitely what I’m going to be thinking about the next time I bite into a milky and delicious Hershey Bar. After watching this perversely chalky film about the company’s founder, it’s a wonder that I can still remember what their signature product even tastes like.

Angel Studios will release “Hershey” in theaters on Wednesday, November 25.

#3377. ‘Aquamarine’ Reboot Series Officially Set With Original Cast Returning

After twenty years, the teen mermaid comedy Aquamarine is resurfacing. The 2006 film is getting a sequel series on Hulu, set two decades after the original. Plus, two cast members from the movie are back in action.

Directed by Elizabeth Allen Rosenbaum (Sneakerella), from a script by John Quaintance (Will and Grace) and Jessica Bendinger (Stick It) and loosely adapted from the 2001 novel of the same name by Alice Hoffman (Practical Magic), Aquamarine centers around two teenage friends, Claire (Emma Roberts, American Horror Story) and Hailey (Joanna "JoJo" Levesque, R.V.). The longtime Floridian friends are about to be separated when Hailey's family moves to Australia, but fate intervenes when a storm deposits a mermaid, the titular Aquamarine (Sara Paxton, Darcy's Wild Life), in a local swimming pool. She has three days to prove that true love exists before she's married off to a merman, so her new friends try to set her up with hunky local lifeguard Raymond (Jake McDornan, American Sniper). The movie was a moderate commercial success in theaters, but has become a cult hit on home video and streaming.

Thus, it's now returning as a TV series on Hulu and Disney+. Teenager Coral (Kenzi Richardson, Vampirina: Teenage Vampire) moves to a small town in Florida, where she begins to unravel the truth behind her mother's disappearance...only to learn that her mother was a mermaid, and that she's inherited strange aquatic superpowers. The series will also star Briella Guiza (Atlas), Theodore Dalton (A Wonderful Way With Dragons) and Annika Reese (Quads and the Kicker), plus Roberts and McDornan, who will reprise their roles from the original film. The series has been greenlit and is in development, but no release date has yet been announced.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

Rosenbaum, who directed the original film, and Susan Cartsonis, who produced it, will executive produce the series alongside Melissa Carter (The Cleaning Lady), Roberts, and McDornan. Rosenbaum will direct the series' pilot, which will be written by Sarah Watson (The Bold Type).

Aquamarine is in development; no release date has yet been announced. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#3376. If You Loved 'Phony,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar shows) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

The boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

The Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a new employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.
