#3375. Guitarricadelafuente Was Terrified to Make His Acting Debut in ‘La Bola Negra’: ‘I Wasn’t Sure at All’

[Editor’s note: The following interview contains spoilers for “La Bola Negra.”]

With a head of hair, lithe frame, and the soft eyes Caravaggio would’ve loved if the Italian painter were Spanish, pop star Guitarricadelafuente is having a monumental year on- and off-screen. The gay 29-year-old songwriter finished touring his sensational, sensually charged second album “Spanish Leather” earlier this fall, and only just a few short months after his screen debut, “La Bola Negra,” won a Cannes top prize, got scooped up by Netflix, and entered the awards season fray.

Oscar talk is in the wind, not just for his performance as queer closeted trumpeter Sebastián, who joins the Nationalist forces during the Spanish Civil War to survive, but for writing the original song “La Nieve.” The sweeping ballad ties together the film’s three story threads that convene around queer Spanish playwright Federico García Lorca’s incomplete text: 1932, 1937 (Sebastián’s storyline), and 2017. Born Álvaro Lafuente Calvo, he’s now a meme thanks to his stage and screen sobriquet, which means “little guitar of the fountain.” Related Stories ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier John Turturro, Carrie Coon, Guitarricadelafuente, and Peter Gamble to Receive SFFILM Honors

Guitarricadelafuente’s performance balances both hushed repression and eventually unleashed emotions throughout “La Bola Negra,” as Sebastián nurses wounded (and handsome) Republican soldier Rafael (Miguel Bernardeau, a more established actor in Spain). They fall for each other in the process, in a furtive romance mostly framed in stolen glances and tacit looks — in other words, the sort of good old-fashioned gay yearning that’s made movies like “Brokeback Mountain,” “Call Me by Your Name,” and “God’s Own Country” so popular. “La Bola Negra” is, by now, one of the highest-grossing Spanish movies ever to play in Spain, and it’s a major Oscar contender in select theaters as it gears up for its early December Netflix streaming premiere.

IndieWire spoke to Guitarricadelafuente over Zoom where, behind him, an oversized window frame flanked the waves gently rushing up to Miami Beach. Below, we discuss his songwriting process for “La Nieve,” witnessing the breakup of directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo (which happened during filming), and how he overcame his fears to make his auspicious screen debut. That’s all while balancing a proudly out music career where his sexuality is front and center. Plus, watch an exclusive video about his role in the film at the bottom of this story.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: You’ve been all over the world with “La Bola Negra,” from Cannes in May to Toronto and, now, Miami Beach for this virtual junket interview. You’re used to being all over the place. You also toured your album this year. Did that help you prepare for promoting the film?

Guitarricadelafuente: I would say that kind of, in a way, because there’s something that I see as very similar to going and talking about the movie and talking about your character, which is something very similar to when you’re going around touring with your album. I think it’s more difficult because you need to talk about yourself and not just about playing a character because the music you make comes from a very profound place, and you need to talk about many things that go inside of you.

This is your acting debut, and there’s Oscar chatter for both your performance and the song you wrote for the film, “La Nieve.” Do you watch the Academy Awards in Spain?

Not that much recently, but I remember when I was studying architecture in college, I used to stay up late at night doing projects. I remember staying up until 3:00 a.m. and with my friends, we were doing our little houses, and we would put the television on, and see the awards. But that was one of the only times that I stayed up late, or that I used to stay up late to see the awards, because you always receive that in Spain in the morning after.

You signed up for the movie without a script. What was the pitch that the Javis gave you? You knew you’d have to learn the trumpet.

They didn’t tell me that I had to learn an instrument because it was going to be originally something that I already knew how to play, but they wanted to make it more difficult. So they said, “OK, why don’t you try a trumpet?” But yeah, the first pitch, there was not much about it. They told me about “La piedra oscura” by Alberto Conejero, which was the original play where the characters of Rafael and Sebastián appear.

I just knew that it was going to be set against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, with Lorca being so present. … They didn’t convince me, but I was so moved by how they were so confident that I could do it because I was so frightened and I wasn’t sure at all, but it was their vision. I admired them so much from before. I knew that they’ve worked with many nonprofessional actors, and people acting for the first time. So it was something that I just threw myself into.

You were frightened about whether or not you could deliver as an actor, or was it the material?

I was spending all of my time making music and touring, and it was very time-consuming and exhausting. … I didn’t know if I could put myself into that experience because I thought the proper way to dig into that role was to put your soul into it.

They were looking for someone who was openly gay for this role, right? There’s a spectrum of sexualities among the cast. Miguel Bernardeau, your scene partner, is straight.

Well, I don’t even know if we talked about that at any point because it was just assumed that I was. [Laughs] I don’t know if that was a condition. I think it was something that, to be more faithful to the story, had to happen. At the time that they approached me with the role, I was finishing my last album, “Spanish Leather.” It represented an imaginary — but not that imaginary — journey of a young gay man who comes out from his village and puts himself out to the world, discovering who he is and where he belongs.

Many people would know my music, but I would realize that not many people knew that I was gay even. There’s a big, not sexual, but I would say sensual component to [“Spanish Letter”] and this process of growing up and sexual [awakening]. So it was very special in a way to play this role … it’s something that you don’t get that much, maybe in Spain, just to see things where you can get referenced with or reflected with.

Los Javis broke up during production. Did they communicate that to the cast? How did you find out?

It was so weird because I don’t know if I’m stupid or what, I didn’t even notice. I would hear obviously so many rumors, but … you couldn’t tell that they were apart because they were acting as one. And I couldn’t believe that they were breaking up with the intensity of that shoot. It was like, “How on earth are they going to split up in the middle of this craziness and this madness?”

But I don’t even remember when they told us. I think it was at the end of the shoot. We would eventually know that something was going on. I couldn’t believe it. How have you managed to carry this shoot? But that also represented how moving this story was to them.

Of course. Even when they reached out to me with the role, I would hear rumors, and I was like, “How is this going to be possible if they’re so tight together?” It was inevitable because they are so well known in Spain, that rumors would arrive.

Miguel has probably 10 years of acting experience that you don’t have. Was he helpful as a mentor, as well as an onscreen romance?

The first time that we met, it was actually when he was doing his audition because the only character that was clear in the movie was Sebastián. We had to test how this approach was going to be with the real Rafael, because this very tight and intimate connection had to happen. He didn’t know that I was going to play Sebastián, and he just appeared in the rehearsal room. And I thought there was a very special instant connection there, that I think we’re obviously very different, or we come from very different backgrounds or different ways of seeing the world.

But there was a beauty in that because obviously I saw him as this wonderful, beautiful, talented, and professional actor that I could anchor myself in. He’s all the time lying on a bed [on screen]. And so he has to say so many things without being able to move. We were both left a lot of freedom on set and to try and to make errors. The room would get empty, and it was just Los Javis, Miguel, and I.

Were you writing the movie’s theme song, “La Nieve,” during production?

It was a very long process from the beginning, when I was told to write the song. I don’t think of me doing a song as in I get into a room and say, “OK, what I’m going to talk about right now?” And then I get a lyric, and I go back home. This Film has so many stories in it, and to try to be faithful to all of them and try to unify them in a thread, in a song, was very difficult. I was listening at the time, before they reached out to me, to Spanish Civil War songs.

It was actually a queer singer of the time who was called Rolando Alarcón. There were songs played with parlor guitars that were [made] to be sung on the waterfront. We started preparing the role with Los Javis. Lorca had to be very present also in this because he’s all over the place. He’s pretty omnipresent all of the time, surveilling what’s going on. And you had to pay a homage to him because, in the end, “La bola negra” was this unfinished script that he was writing.

I had to live my character in my own skin and properly carry that emotional baggage that he was holding. And it wasn’t until the end of the shoot, when we were in Cantabria living for two months … I obviously had this melody in my head, but when this scene with the firing squad happens, and [SPOILER ALERT] Rafael dies, it was a combination of all of that emotional journey that the character was living.

I would arrive home that day and start playing a melody on a piano and mumbling some lyrics, and I would send this to Los Javis, and I didn’t know that they were going to use this to unify the three stories that go on in the movie. And it was a way for me to let all of that emotion go.

This song will now have to be part of every setlist you perform. It’s your “My Heart Will Go On.”

I hope it turns into that. I wish to be 50 years old and be in Madrid and be singing that. That would be so beautiful. Because I feel that I was just playing in Madrid my last concert one month ago, it was kind of the closing chapter of this “Spanish Leather” tour, and the film was just released one week before that. And so I got the chance to play “La Nieve” there for the first time. After that, it was very emotional because you would hear 18,000 people singing to that. It was like goosebumps. After that, people would be commenting on TikTok, “So Sebastián had the chance to finally be a musician and get to Madrid and perform.” That’s kind of like a closing of the thread, a very beautiful thing.

“La Bola Negra” is also one of the highest-grossing Spanish movies to play in Spain ever. Have you been able to go home and experience that?

We were in Spain those first two weeks until we had the last concert in Madrid, and then we went to Toronto and all over the place. And that was a very special week because I was at my sister’s wedding. You could feel something in the air. There was a communal excitement, and people of all ages, all different ages, going to the cinema, or even people, like aunts of mine, who haven’t been to the cinema in 10 years, to see how that’s happening is something that makes us very proud.

For me, the Spanish premiere was more important because that’s all Spanish people’s lives. Everybody has been linked to that moment of time, it’s like their ancestors. So the Spanish were going to be the most critical of it. But to see how young people, old people, people from different backgrounds go and you suddenly have this sense of communion was something spectacular that you could see in the streets. Like older ladies and young queer guys coming up to you, it’s just incredible.

What are you doing next? Do you want to keep acting?

Yeah. It’s been a crazy time. I’m having the time to even make new music and to, I don’t know, to see what I’m able to, because even three years ago… I would oblige myself to be quiet and rest to be able to feel inspired. But now it’s all these hectic times that are making me feel so inspired, and to share that time and put it into making art.

“La Bola Negra” is now in select theaters will start streaming on Netflix on Wednesday, December 2.

#3374. Star Trek Officially Returns To The Deep Space Nine Era Today

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

The Star Trek franchise has spent the better part of the past six decades exploring different corners of the galaxy, expanding with each release, but in today's newest release, the franchise is revisiting the Star Trek: Deep Space Nine era among others. Although the original series established the foundation for what would become a sci-fi phenomenon, the TV and film productions that have come after Star Trek: The Original Series have all been able to explore further reaches of the universe, creating an undeniably thorough franchise. Some eras have become important to building the legacy, while others have helped bridge the gaps in the larger story.

Regardless of how popular an era has been, Star Trek has been able to introduce some of the most recognizable characters in modern fiction throughout the franchise, changing the face of sci-fi in TV, film, and on the page. Star Trek's TV presence, specifically, has fundamentally changed what a sci-fi drama on the small screen could accomplish, and continues to push the boundaries. Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, specifically, was a strong era for the franchise. Beginning in 1993, the series abandoned the typical format viewers were used to and explored long-running conflicts using a familiar crew and a stationary space station.

Now, as Star Trek celebrates its 60th anniversary as a franchise, revisiting some of its strongest eras has never been easier than with Star Trek Timelines, a brand-new release that comes out today, Tuesday, November 24. The official visual history of the franchise, Star Trek Timelines brings each of the show's eras into focus for a deep exploration.

Today's release of Star Trek Timelines: A Visual Voyage Through Generations of History marks a whole new exploration of the franchise and celebrates its milestone 60th anniversary. One of the most important eras of the franchise's history began with the debut of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine in 1993. The series, which saw a major departure from the traditional way Star Trek stories were told, was able to reinvigorate the franchise for a whole new generation of viewers. With the series having gone against the established formula that worked for the Star Trek franchise, Deep Space Nine opened new doors.

The show's stationary setting allowed Deep Space Nine to develop its plots with more depth, reaching for larger thematic elements and baking them into each story with a different type of precision than other franchise series had allowed for. A highly regarded era of the franchise, the new book breaks down the era visually, expanding on how the show's rich style and different elements allowed for an entirely different experience than what Star Trek enthusiasts had experienced before. Challenging the franchise on nearly every front, Deep Space Nine is one of the most important pieces of the Star Trek journey, and is honored in Star Trek Timelines.

Star Trek Timelines: A Visual Voyage Through Generations of History is available for purchase through this link.

With Star Trek Timelines, written by Derek Tyler Attico, Michael Dismuke, Kelli Fitzpatrick, and Jim Johnson, readers will be able to explore the franchise from its early beginnings through its latest series, all with the expert knowledge that comes from its authors. Examining the timelines of each series thoroughly, the book looks at alternate timelines as well, including the Mirror universe, the Kelvin timeline, and the Year of Hell storyline from Star Trek: Voyager. With character-focused spreads that trace each major figure's development through the franchise and a ton of information that Star Trek fans will enjoy, the book is a wonderful resource.

While Star Trek Timelines isn't exclusively dedicated to an exploration of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine, the comprehensive approach of the book gives its readers the opportunity to explore major parts of the series and works through some of its most unique pieces. With over 300 pages of exploration and a foreword from Star Trek legend Kate Mulgrew, who played Captain Kathryn Janeway in Star Trek: Voyager, Star Trek Timelines provides its dedicated readers a chance to dig further into the franchise, looking at the Star Trek journey from a whole new vantage point.

#3373. How to get your car out of the impound in GTA 6

There's the easy way and the expensive way

There's the easy way and the expensive way

It doesn't take long for one of your cars to end up at the police impound in Grand Theft Auto 6. You might have abandoned it near a crime scene, or they arrested you while you were driving it. While the circumstances may vary, you have only two ways to proceed if a car is impounded: you forget about it or you retrieve it.

If you are not ready to abandon your favorite car and want it back, we've got you covered. Here's how to get your car out of the impound in GTA 6.

There are two methods to retrieve a car from the police impound: you can either steal it back or pay for it. Both are valid, but the second one becomes available only in Chapter 2.

Stealing the car is the most plausible and cheapest option to execute. You just need to head to the impound lot, enter, and drive your car away from there. Some impounds, like the one in Port Gellhorn, have openings that you can use to enter unnoticed. Regardless of how you get inside, the challenge is escaping from the police once you leave. You must be prepared to run away, so try to come up with an escape route by setting a destination far from the city.

Now, the second option requires the Scooter Bros app, which you unlock in Chapter 2 after completing Moses' mission. If you have it already, open the app and select the impounded car (the one with a police badge icon). You will see that the first option in the menu is to pay a fee to retrieve the car.

The price varies depending on how far you are from the police impound. For example, I would have to pay $699 to get my car back from the Port Gellhorn impound while in Vice City. However, if you have upgraded your Scooter Bros account to Premium, you can use your remaining daily credits to request an impounded vehicle. Since this will essentially consume all your credits for the day, you should wait until you have only one left before using this option.

#3372. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. #3371. ‘Parks and Rec’ Showrunner Teases a Very Different Turn for Amy Poehler’s New Peacock Series

When Amy Poehler and Mike Schur get together, sitcom magic happens. We saw it with Parks and Recreation, as Poehler's Leslie Knope inspired and entertained us for seven seasons. And over a decade later, that magic is still alive with their newest series, Dig. Adapted from Kate Myers' book Excavations, Poehler stars as Elise DeBellnick, a career archaeologist who runs the annual summer dig in Greece for Dr. Neville Wycombe (Hugh Laurie). While he's charming and pompous, she’s hardworking, straightforward, and has never had her own excavation. When she uncovers an artifact from an overlooked pit, she decides to make her own mark on herstory. The series also stars Geraldine Viswanathan, Max Greenfield, and Kayvan Novak.

Ahead of DIG's release, Collider sat down with Mike Schur and J.J. Philbin to discuss their new Peacock series. The showrunners unpack their collaboration with Poehler and why they were drawn to the Kate Myers novel. Plus, Schur teases what A Man on the Inside fans can expect in its final season. You can watch the full interview in the video above, or you can read the transcript below.

COLLIDER: You both have been behind some excellent series in the past. Talk to me about why DIG was the next story that you wanted to do.

MIKE SCHUR: Because Amy Poehler called me on the phone and said she wanted to adapt the book into a show. That's why. She's the one who found it. She read it. She really locked into the main character of the book. She's been doing so much producing, directing, and developing for the last 12 years since Parks ended. She just really found it. She knew it. She saw it. She knew what it was. Then asked me if I wanted to develop it with her, and the answer was a very quick "yes."

When I read it, and I think when J.J. read it too, we both saw immediately what she had seen, which was an interesting setting, great character for her to play, very different from other characters she's played in her life. But also, putting her in a workplace comedy with women of different ages that we started to think of all four women as the same woman just at four different points in their life. What you would do if you were surrounded by previous versions of yourself, and the ways that you would love them and feel for them, but also the ways that those versions of you would drive you crazy, and you'd be embarrassed by them. And then the central metaphor of digging: digging through the past to get to the truth is a great central metaphor. If Amy had called and said, "I'd like to adapt the 'Los Angeles Yellow Pages,'" I would've been like, "Great, let's get to it." But in this case, she found a book that really had a lot of juicy stuff in it that made a good show.

J.J. PHILBIN: Mike had told me early on, I think you guys had breakfast. He said, "I had breakfast with Amy, and she pitched me this idea," and I was like, "Oh my gosh, I'm so excited." Just for myself as a viewer to be able to watch it on TV and hear about it as you guys make this TV show. Like every woman who works in comedy, it's just a dream to work with Amy Poehler. When Mike suggested that I come on board, I was just thrilled, really delighted. We'd never worked together before, so that was also just an interesting experiment. We've been married for 21 years. Let's see what that's like.

SCHUR: Well, we immediately got divorced. [Laughs]

PHILBIN: We moved to separate parts of the house. [Laughs] You know, it's funny, I don't know if this was right or not, but we didn't go into it with a lot of ground rules. We sort of said, "Let's see what it feels like," and it was immediately so easy and fun that I'm glad that we didn't torture it by going in saying, like, "You're going to pitch this. No, I'm going to pitch that."

SCHUR: As soon as Amy and I realized that J.J. was the right person to do this with us, my immediate thought was, "Is that going to be weird?" And then my second immediate thought was, "It's going to be fine." We never sat down and had a big discussion about who was going to do what. I had this gut instinct that after both working in TV comedy for 25 or 30 years, it was going to be fine. And then it was fine. It was super fun. We had a great time. We had a very easy time with it. The labor divided up very effortlessly. We were like, "Why don't you do this, and I'll do this." It was about as easy and fun as I think it could have possibly been.

PHILBIN: It's really convenient to live with your co-showrunner so that you can go home from work and keep talking about things as you do the dishes and walk the dog. So a lot of the show got broken while we were driving our kids to places. So that part made it feel very effortless and nice.

That's such a great way to take it. I know some people like to separate work from their home life. But to bring it in and figure this out together, that's so cool.

SCHUR: Yeah, it was really fun. Again, we just did it separately. So our time at home was usually spent with her telling me what problems they were encountering whatever show she was on, and me doing the same for my shows. We just kept doing that except it was the same show. That's the only difference.

You brought up Amy, and you've worked with her for many years. How has your relationship with Amy evolved over time, and what was it like working with her specifically on this?

SCHUR: The only difference between this and Parks and Rec is that, technically speaking, she didn't create the show with me. I created it with Greg Daniels, and then she was the other collaborator. By the time that show ended, it felt like a thing that she and I had been doing together. It really felt like I was in charge of half of it, and she was in charge of half of it. Our decisions were creatively made together. We had a rule on that show, with the whole cast really, with her as the captain, that when something would come up, it's like, if everyone wants to do this, we do it. And if one person vetoes it, then we say no.

That's always been the way. It's very democratic. So the only difference with this is that we were in it from the very beginning. And I'm not kidding, it felt like when we started talking about this show, it felt like yesterday Parks and Rec ended, and then today we started something new. It felt like we picked up right where we left off, and it's been a dream.

PHILBIN: I would say it's really fun to watch Amy and Mike work together. They have such a respectful and easy collaboration, and they really make each other laugh. I think that kind of spreads throughout the set and into the writers' room, and everybody just gets that teamwork is the way that we make this show. It's so nice to have that dynamic at the top of the call sheet, just defining for everybody what the vibe is going to be on set and in the room.

You are both booked and busy. You both have two mystery shows that you have about to come out. What can you preview about the new season of Only Murders in the Building and A Man on the Inside?

PHILBIN: I was not a part of Season 6. The last season that I worked on Only Murders was Season 5, and then I went straight from that show to DIG. I'm excited to watch Only Murders...

SCHUR: A Man on the Inside was really fun to make this year. We shot almost the entire thing in San Francisco. It's a celebration of that city, which is a city I truly love, and it's very much an homage to other movies and TV shows that were shot in San Francisco, so there are a lot of fun Easter eggs and stuff that people will enjoy if they're familiar with those other movies.

#3370. Will Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting Help Land Him His First Oscar Nomination?

How will Robert Pattinson‘s casting as James Bond affect his Oscar chances? The hard-working star, who was established by the “Twilight” franchise, has ricocheted from Christopher Nolan projects (“Tenet” and “The Odyssey”) and the DC franchise’s “The Batman” (“Part Two” is shooting in London) to riskier indies like the Safdies’ “Good Time” and Robert Eggers’ “The Lighthouse.”

This award season, Pattinson was juggling three long-shot potential Oscar nods: Best Actor for A24’s marital deconstruction “The Drama,” and Supporting Actor for two Snidely Whiplash villains, lead suitor Antinous in Universal’s blockbuster “The Odyssey” and shape-shifter Scytale in Warner Bros.’ “Dune: Part Three,” respectively. His best chance at an Oscar nomination, though, was always for his creepy lead turn as TV journalist Chris Hansen in “Primetime,” another A24 release. Related Stories Guitarricadelafuente Was Terrified to Make His Acting Debut in ‘La Bola Negra’: ‘I Wasn’t Sure at All’ ‘Hershey’ Review: An Unbelievably Flavorless Biopic About America’s Most Famous Chocolatier

When Daniel Craig was cast as James Bond during the awards tour for Steven Spielberg’s “Munich” (2005), the immediate result was a marked increase in attendance at all screenings, recalls one veteran publicist. “There was a different before-and-after energy,” he said. That did not land Craig a nomination, however. The only Bond to score an Oscar nod and win after a long and storied career was Sean Connery (“The Untouchables”). Playing Bond does not lend an actor cred with the Academy. But it does extend a career.

The impact for Pattinson, who is ubiquitous in online media, is the same. At this point, most awards voters will have seen “The Odyssey,” but those seeing the Christopher Nolan blockbuster for the first time will view the actor differently. “He will have heightened scrutiny,” said one studio Oscar expert. “Clearly he is being tapped to anchor a franchise. For the actors [branch], he will be someone to reckon with.”

Clearly, fewer people have screened “Primetime.” Pattinson’s Bond ascension will push the movie up in the must-see rankings. “Bond probably gets more people to watch the movie,” said one Oscar strategist. “That’s half the battle. The goal is to get people to watch the movie. But the movie has to do the work.”

At the box office, “Primetime” has fared better domestically ($47 million) than abroad ($12 million), which is significant given an Oscar voting pool of more than 10,000 voters, one-quarter of whom are international. How will “Primetime” do with the upcoming critic votes? Or BAFTAs, which will reveal the international tale? And SAG’s Actor Awards, where, at this stage, Gold Derby has “Digger” star Tom Cruise edging out Pattinson? The race between those two actors is “squishy,” said Debra Birnbaum, Gold Derby editor-in-chief, who distinguishes between early season “hopedictions” and “real predictions.”

It helps to remember that the Academy is just starting to catch up with the contenders. The experts on Gold Derby (I’m one), at this stage, have seen way more movies than the site’s users or the Academy. Later in the season, Gold Derby users and experts are more in sync. That’s why we should take with a grain of salt the recent ascension among the Gold Derby users to number five for Best Actor contender Pattinson. They’re responding to publicity. The experts have him at seven. The same is true for the betting site Kalshi’s odds. Their accuracy improves the closer you get to the Oscars. At this stage, their bettors haven’t seen everything. And the key Oscar season markers, from critics’ groups to Guild awards, haven’t played out.

The American Cinematheque came out way ahead by honoring Pattinson with its annual award fete, set to take place on February 9, 2027. Tables are selling out and Bond studio Amazon/MGM — and Hollywood — will be there in force.

While Pattinson has never been an actors’ actor, he’s a hugely bankable global movie star. He’s going to keep us interested for a long time.

#3369. Why Black Friday and Cyber Monday Are Bad Days to Impulse Buy Electronics

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a big "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

If you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

#3368. Cliff Booth Stars Explain How David Fincher & Quentin Tarantino Shaped Their Performances

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the first time in nearly a decade that audiences can see acclaimed filmmaker Quentin Tarantino's work in theaters. While the sequel to 2019's love letter to American cinema, Once Upon a Time in... Hollywood, was directed by David Fincher, Tarantino still penned the screenplay. The combination of both powerhouses has made the movie one of the year's most anticipated, and the cast even felt the magic while working on set.

Brad Pitt once again plays Cliff Booth, who now finds himself in 1977 without the trusty Rick Dalton by his side. While he is no longer at the center of Hollywood, he still hangs out with famous folk within the industry, doing their dirty work in the seedy underbelly of Los Angeles. He runs into various fascinating characters, including actor Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), whose tension with his wife Toni (Carla Gugino) becomes central to the plot. Charlie's agent, Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), finds herself entangled with Cliff romantically, while Blaxploitation movie star Roderick "Hot Rod" Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) adds plenty of charm to the proceedings.

ScreenRant's Kim Horcher interviewed Caan, Debicki, Gugino, and Abdul-Mateen about the exciting challenge of stepping into Tarantino's world through the lens of Fincher's camera in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. The actors shared their reactions to joining the project, how they got into character, and which they found to be the best parts of fictional 1970s Hollywood.

ScreenRant: How was it working with Fincher on a Tarantino project? How did it feel to get that call?

Carla Gugino: It's pretty much the best call you could ever get, honestly. I think it's almost as simple as that. You have the foundation of this incredible script, and then you have one of the greatest visionary directors interpreting it through his lens. And that combination is so unique. I don't know that we'll ever get that kind of combination. It's such an unusual opportunity. It's like falling into a pot of honey.

Yahya Abdul-Mateen II: It makes the job easy. We both have a theater background. When I go to do theater, I get a chance to say the best words, and that helps a lot. We had everything that we needed in order to succeed, and so the stage was set for us to just bring the best of ourselves without having to figure out how to make things work so much, which sometimes is what we have to do.

The job is to figure out how to make things work. But sometimes when you have to do that less, then you can just get in there, and it's just about what you get to do. "Ooh, I get to do this." That's what work felt like on most days for me. I felt like a star.

This project was a gift, a throwback to a really, really fun time. And to make a present-day movie that is a '70s movie with the flair of Quentin Tarantino's words, and under the direction of David Fincher's eye with Brad and the entire cast? It was just really, really fun.

Carla Gugino: I think the thing about Quentin's writing that's so noticeable is that nothing is ever generic. You really believe these people are real people. It's a lot like Elmore Leonard, where they act in unexpected ways. When most people are nervous, they're flirty. He brings the period to life in a really exceptional way.

And then David is so known for how impeccable he is with period stuff, so I [love] the fact that we got to embody this world of the '70s and what it represents. There's this star, and we have a stunt guy who is kind of in awe of that star. We have a lifelong actress who's made a living that way, but hasn't been as successful as she wants to be, but also is kind of okay with that. Then we have a TV star who gets a taste of all the different elements of Hollywood at that time. Everybody is sort of compromised, and that's kind of what the '70s was like in a lot of ways. So, all those things are very noticeable.

ScreenRant: Elizabeth, your character really surprised me with her somewhat contradictory nature and her multidimensionality. I feel like I've met people like her in LA. What was she to you?

Elizabeth Debicki: She was an amazing role that I found in that script. I think Quentin created a character that is quite unlike anything else he's written for a female character. She is really contradictory, and I think that is the core of human nature. We just roam around and contradict ourselves.

She obviously has real agency in this world, but she's really smart and funny and completely not ready for someone to walk into her life to kind of force her to look at herself. It's a really interesting relationship between her and Cliff, and I loved playing her.

When David and I first spoke about it, I remember us both saying our goal really was that we really wanted her to feel real, like someone you knew. I wanted her to feel like, "I know that woman. I wonder what she ate for breakfast. I bet she lives in an apartment that looks like that." She feels grounded.

ScreenRant: Scott, on the other hand, I feel like I've only met maybe one or two Charlies. What went into making him your own?

Scott Caan: Listen, Quentin writes really great characters, and when I read the script, I was like, "Wow, this one is fantastic." For me, I like to bring as much of myself into the character as I can. For this one, initially, it was like, "God, how do I justify all this stuff?" That was really my approach. "How can I justify all my behavior and all these decisions?" And it was very fun.

There's one [actor he reminded me of], which I'm not even going to mention who it is, but there was one idea. We were talking about it before, but it kind of went away. We do a lot of homework, and then when you show up, you kind of forget it all and just go try to play. I mean, the guy's got to be a version of me. So, I read something, and I go, "Alright, how can I put the version of me into this?"

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth begins playing in select IMAX theaters on November 25 before streaming December 23 on Netflix.

#3367. Mike Plante, Sundance Film Festival Shorts Programmer, Dies at 56

Mike Plante, a filmmaker and 25-year veteran of the Sundance Institute, died Tuesday after a brief illness. He was 56.

At Sundance, Plante worked as a Shorts Programmer and was a familiar, warm-hearted presence at festival screenings and events.

“Mike was a treasure to the Institute, the Festival, and our independent film community,” Sundance Festival Director Eugene Hernandez and Director of Programming Kim Yutani said in a joint statement. “His sense of wonder and humor were matched by boundless enthusiasm and curatorial excellence. Our Festival’s Short Film Program and the Sundance Film Festival Short Film Tour were shaped by Mike’s energy and superb taste in movies. Mike’s roots at Sundance Institute, and his relationships within our organization and festival, run deep. He will be remembered and deeply missed as a true cinephile, a filmmaker, a champion of short films, movie theaters, and film culture.” Related Stories Will Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting Help Land Him His First Oscar Nomination? Guitarricadelafuente Was Terrified to Make His Acting Debut in ‘La Bola Negra’: ‘I Wasn’t Sure at All’

In addition to his work at the festival, Plante directed the 2011 feature documentary “Be Like an Ant,” which followed a Vietnam War veteran who builds a house around a mobile home to handle winter living. He also directed numerous shorts including “The Polaroid Job” (2016), which looked at his parents’ work running a paid event-photography studio in the 1980s. It is available to watch on the New York Times’ Op-Doc website.

Amy Redford, the daughter of Sundance founder Robert Redford and a board member of the festival, called Plante, “a visionary.” “Through his extraordinary curatorial talent, he launched countless storytellers through the vital medium of short film, many of whom have gone on to become some of the world’s most enduring artists,” she said. “Mike embodied the Sundance ethos and played a critical role in preserving the continuity of its values. He was unfailingly generous with his time and mentorship, and a talented creator in his own right. But Mike’s most enduring legacy is his kindness. It was, and remains, the first thing people say about him. His passing is a profound loss not only to the Sundance community, but to all those fortunate enough to have known and loved him. He will be deeply missed.”

Along with directing, Plante produced feature documentaries by other directors, including “Scrap Vessel” (2009) and “Giuseppe Makes A Movie” (2014). Plante started working for film festivals as a programmer in 1993, eventually joining Sundance in 2001.

In 1998, he started the film zine Cinemad, which he wrote and produced. He also wrote “Sensation Cinema: The Audacious, Defiant History of Louis Sher and the Art Theatre Guild,” which looked at an influential arthouse theater owner and distributor.

One of Amazon’s biggest sales of the year, Black Friday and Cyber Monday, is set to start Nov. 27, but many early deals are already rolling in. To take advantage of everything the sale has to offer, you’re going to need to be a Prime Member. If you sign up for an Amazon Prime account to take advantage of the sale but decide you don’t want to pay for an ongoing membership, you’ll need to cancel your subscription before the end of your free trial.

You can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

#3365. CBS Officially Confirms Major Schedule Change for ‘FBI’ and ‘CIA’

While not as long-running on CBS as NCIS or as storied as other Dick Wolf franchises, FBI is nearing a decade of patrolling the streets of the Big Apple and has built a following all its own. In that time, the elite agents of the New York field office have teamed up with other spin-offs, changed nights, and generally experienced a lot of shuffling as the Eye sets its schedule each season. This fall, both the flagship and its spin-off, CIA, saw another change, moving up an hour with no comedy block to account for, while Harlan Coben's Final Twist Season 2 took up the later 10 p.m. slot. Those used to the old lineup won't have to wait long for things to shift back, though.

CBS set midseason premiere dates for its entire primetime slate last week, beginning on Wednesday, January 6. For FBI fans, however, the date to watch is Monday, January 25, when the original series and CIA return to continue their ninth and second seasons, respectively. The procedurals will move back into a schedule more akin to last winter, taking up the 9 p.m. and 10 p.m. time slots once more to make room for a new hour of comedy. For the first time, Ghosts will be haunting two nights a week, taking up the 8 p.m. spot on Monday, in addition to its typical Thursday slot, during Season 6, while Joe Port and Joe Wiseman's new supernatural sitcom, Eternally Yours, takes up residence at 8:30 p.m. on Mondays.

The FBI franchise shuffling is on the lighter end of CBS' changes to the schedule this winter. Starting Sunday, January 17, Cupertino, the new legal thriller from The Good Wife creators Robert and Michelle King, will air at the very end of the weekend in the 10 p.m. time slot, making way for Matlock to return for Season 3 at 10 p.m. on Thursdays alongside Elsbeth. The all-NCIS block is also getting a shake-up, with Origins returning for two episodes to close out its shortened third season before NCIS: Sydney returns for its ten-episode Season 4 run on January 26. One new scripted series is also penciled in to premiere during the midseason — Einstein. Starring Criminal Minds alum Matthew Gray Gubler, the new mystery series will slot in on Sunday at 8 p.m. starting on February 12 following the Season 5 finale of Fire Country.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

Three episodes of FBI Season 9 and CIA Season 2 remain before the holidays begin, and CBS' lineup takes off until midseason. Neither series will be taking it easy heading into the break, though. For the flagship, next week's episode, "22 minutes," will see the New York agents racing to stop a drug lord who murdered a DEA informant and now plans to take out the 16-year-old girl who saw everything. While that unfolds, Isobel (Alana de la Garza) pressures Maggie (Missy Peregrym) to rein in her relationship with OA (Zeeko Zaki) after his return from going undercover with Anna Vorpe left him in a troubled state. CIA, meanwhile, will air "Burned Rubber," following Colin (Tom Ellis) and Bill (Nick Gehlfuss) on a mission to save Colin's asset from an international crime group by uncovering a high-profile car theft ring that could lead to his whereabouts.

After next week, the two branches will once again link up in the CIA episode "Past Lives" on December 7. Nikki (Necar Zadegan) calls in some backup in the form of Jubal Valentine (Jeremy Sisto) after one of her former assets and their family suddenly vanish from their suburban block. However, as the team investigates further, the question becomes whether their allegiances have flipped or if their lives are all in danger. It'll be a welcome return for Jubal, who first introduced strait-laced FBI agent Bill Goodman to the joint operation and the more complicated world of spycraft in the series premiere.

FBI Season 9 and CIA Season 2 will make their midseason premieres on CBS on January 25 at 9 p.m. ET/PT and 10 p.m. ET/PT. Stay tuned here at Collider for further updates on both series as their winter break nears.
