#3363. Movie Theaters in 2026: Filmmakers and Exhibitors on What’s Good, What’s Bad, and What’s Changing

In 1948, movie studios held a monopoly in entertainment, owning the means of producing and distributing films, and the theaters themselves. The 1948 Paramount Decrees (named after the studio that pioneered the vertical integration) required studios to give up one of the three options. They decided to give up exhibition. The choice was easy: With low margins on ticket sales and the need to constantly bring audiences in, who wanted to run a movie theater?

70 years later, movie studios again faced the possibility of giving up on exhibition. The rise of streaming was said to bring about the end of theaters as we know them. But the COVID-19 pandemic brought exhibition to its closest brink of extinction yet. Related Stories Mike Plante, Sundance Film Festival Shorts Programmer, Dies at 56 Will Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting Help Land Him His First Oscar Nomination?

“COVID allowed people to acknowledge their inner recluse,” Tim League, the co-founder and former CEO of Alamo Drafthouse, told IndieWire.

After the global pandemic, lockdown protocols forced movie theaters to close for months. The luxury theater chain Arclight shuttered all its locations within weeks. Locations closed at a variety of companies, including Alamo Drafthouse. Some theaters survived off of private rentals. Even as theaters slowly reopened, COVID protocols required leaving some seats empty, meaning not all tickets could be sold.

“I think there was no right move,” League added. “We laid most of our people off. We spent a lot of energy trying to build up a TVOD streaming platform which didn’t entirely work for a lot of reasons… And so we went through bankruptcy, and it was rough. We just ran out of money.”

“There really was no strategy,” said Greg Laemmle, owner of the California-based independent theater chain Laemmle Theatres. Since Los Angeles did not allow private rentals, the company stayed afloat via concessions, pop-up events, and some virtual cinema opportunities. “It was all just trying to understand how we can maintain contact.”

Exhibition became such an unappetizing business that many of those who jumped on board the irony-fueled GameStop stock inflation of 2021 also bought shares of AMC Theatres, bringing the company to an all-time high in valuation.

But years later, the theater market is experiencing a rebirth. Driven by new theater operators and new kinds of theatrical experiences, the contemporary exhibition landscape looks very different from 10 years ago.

Theater operators paint a picture of an industry that is no longer weathering a storm. Instead, they reveal the trends driving theaters to thrive and the issues with the model that won’t seem to die.

The first high-profile artist-led theater acquisition was Quentin Tarantino’s purchase of the New Beverly Cinema in Los Angeles. The director had previously helped fund his childhood theater to keep it afloat before buying the cinema outright and taking over as programmer in 2014. The purchase of the 300-seat New Beverly was partly fueled by Tarantino’s desire to preserve what the digital era sought to make extinct: celluloid projection. Since the director’s acquisition, the theater proudly boasts that it screens only on film, usually 35mm.

Tarantino declined to comment on this story.

A few years later, COVID-19 brought a new threat to movie theaters. A similar mission-driven attitude took hold in a new crop of directors and artists: to protect not just how movies are screened, but to ensure audiences can still see them in communal spaces.

Independent film director Kevin Smith bought his hometown theater in Atlantic Highlands, New Jersey, in 2024. The Atlantic Twin Cinema was a five-screen multiplex Smith grew up going to, housed in a building over 100 years old. But over time, nearby multiplexes threatened to drive the theater out of business. When Smith’s friend Ernie O’Donnell told him the theater would be torn down to build condos, he resolved to help save it.

“Anything I ever learned about myself I never learned in a classroom, and I certainly didn’t learn it sitting in a church,” Smith told IndieWire. “But mostly everything I know about myself I learned sitting in the darkness of that theater, looking up at the great white mirror and seeing life reflected back at me.”

Smith invested $450,000 and partnered with several friends to buy the theater, rebranding it as Smodcastle Cinemas. While he mostly lives in Los Angeles, Smith travels to Jersey every month to work on the theater.

Smith described how the finances of owning a theater in a small town may not always reflect larger box office trends. “Avatar: The Way of Water” opened in 2024 and eventually grossed over $2 billion, making it one of the most successful films in history. But at Smodcastle Cinemas, they only sold 12 tickets opening weekend.

At Smodcastle, the theater has leaned into what Smith calls “The business of Kevin Smith.” This includes Q&As of his films featuring Smith and his collaborators like Justin Long for a “Tusk” screening, and Tracy Morgan for the 15th anniversary of “Cop Out.” The theater started a film festival to help showcase local New Jersey cinema. Smith was working on selling a reality show about the theater’s day-to-day operations, similar to the seven-season run of “Comic Book Men” filmed inside the comic shop he owns, but said progress has stalled.

“I love calling up Ernie and being like, ‘How many seats [have we sold] so far?’ And he’ll be like ‘120 out of 230,’ and I’m like, ‘All right man, I gotta put 90 more asses in seats. Let me see if I can jump on a radio show… go over to Manhattan and jump on “Good Day New York” and try to get the word out,’” Smith explained. “It’s fun, but it is definitely fucking work. I have a feeling Quentin don’t work nearly as fucking hard at his theater.”

Smith elaborated on the work it takes to keep the theater running, “We all got together and saved the theater, man. But it was the worst financial fucking decision I ever made,” Smith said. “Owning a movie theater in the 21st-century post-COVID [world], it’s a dicey proposition at best… We became a nonprofit theater because the movie theater’s never going into fucking profit.”

The nonprofit model has become an increasingly popular option for keeping theaters alive. In 2012, Los Angeles video rental store Vidiots transitioned to a nonprofit to stay afloat, recasting its mission around film preservation, protection, and education. The organization later received heavy support from Megan Ellison’s Annapurna Pictures, which kept the company running for two years after it shuttered its store in 2017.

“If you go across the country, you’re seeing a real boom in nonprofit or community-supported movie theaters,” said Laemmle. He highlighted the Tasveer Film Center in Seattle, which reopened the former Ark Lodge Cinemas in 2025 due to support from a local nonprofit that had run a South Asian film festival.

“Why not form a community organization that augments ticket sales with other sources of revenue, or that can take advantage of their not-for-profit status and do the enhanced kind of programming that you can’t do at a for-profit business?” said Laemmle.

The high costs of running a movie theater are also evident in one of the latest major theater purchases by an artist. Director Jason Reitman led a group of 30 filmmakers — including Christopher Nolan, Guillermo del Toro, Steven Spielberg, and Chloé Zhao — to purchase the historic Village Theater in Westwood, Los Angeles, in 2024. Since rebranding as Directors Village, the theater has partnered with the film nonprofit American Cinematheque, which will handle its programming.

The $12 million acquisition in 2024 rescued the historic theater after its lease with its former owner expired. The filmmakers will pour an additional $25 million into renovating the theater, which was open for programming in summer 2026 but closed in October and will reopen in 2027. The project required an alleged six-figure minimum buy-in from the artists involved.

Jason Reitman declined to comment through a representative, citing that it is too early to discuss plans for the theater’s renovation. American Cinematheque did not respond to requests for comment.

Jason Reitman and Co. also looked into purchasing the adjacent Bruin Theater but were ultimately deterred by the extensive cost of renovations, as previously reported by IndieWire.

The list of artists owning theaters is only growing. Kristen Stewart purchased the historic Highland Theatre in Los Angeles in February 2026 and plans to restore the space into a hub for the L.A. film community. Tarantino bought a second LA theater, the Vista, in 2021. Martin Scorsese, Ethan Hawke, and Frances McDormand joined the advisory board of the Upper West Side Cinema Center to turn the former Metro Theater on Broadway in New York City into a five-screen arthouse theater, funded by New York City grants and donors like the Kate Capshaw and Steven Spielberg Hearthland Foundation.

The trend highlights a new form of altruism by creatives seeking to keep theaters alive. But even if the business isn’t financially valuable, there is an argument for artists to be seen as patrons of their craft. “As more and more movie theaters start closing down, every filmmaker is from somewhere, and every filmmaker has their hometown theater,” said Smith. “And if you have a degree of success where you’ve got some side hustle loot and whatnot, what a great way to spend your money.”

In 2019, the Department of Justice marked the Paramount Decrees for termination, citing changes in the studio system structure and film market that rendered the law obsolete. In August 2020, while most theaters in the United States were shuttered, the Department of Justice ended the decree.

In November 2019, Netflix announced it would lease New York City’s historic Paris Theater, three months after a notice of closure was posted. In May 2020, the streamer bought the closed Egyptian Theatre in Hollywood to be co-programmed between the studio and its previous operator, American Cinematheque. In October 2021, Netflix also announced it would take over the lease of the Bay Theater in the Pacific Palisades.

These acquisitions had a touch of irony considering Netflix made a name for itself by rejecting theatrical exhibition. The streamer did not abide by the then-standard 90-day exhibition window before making its films available on the service. The Academy Awards require week-long theatrical runs to make films eligible for awards. Major chains like AMC Theatres and Regal Cinemas refused to show Netflix films (and still do on occasion; Regal and Cinemark recently announced they will not screen “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” due to the shortened theatrical window). But just as it became legal for Netflix to enter the theater market, it did. By becoming an exhibitor, it no longer needed major theaters to show its films.

“Netflix needs screens in the L.A. and New York market,” said James Huntsman, the co-founder of distribution company Blue Fox Entertainment Group, which purchased two former iPic theaters in June 2026. “I don’t care if you are Netflix, it’s really hard to get a screen in both of those two markets… So if you’re Netflix and you have six movies that are coming out between October and December and they all need qualifying runs of seven days, full runs in both markets, now you start seeing why they’re interested in screens.”

Amazon Studios opened The Culver Theater — the former Culver City Arclight location, which shuttered in March 2020 after the company went bankrupt due to closures from the COVID-19 pandemic — in December 2022. The theater screens a mix of new releases, repertory screenings, and hosts premieres for Amazon MGM Studios’ television shows and movies.

In October 2026, Paramount Pictures announced it took over the lease for the Bay Theater, which has been closed since the 2025 Palisades fires. The new theater, opened in November 2026 and operated by The Lot, similarly offers first-run theatrical releases from all studios, along with dine-in food.

“We’ll see if it really develops into anything more than just a novelty for them,” said Laemmle about studios purchasing individual theaters. “[They’re] one-offs and just being able to want to say that they’ve got something. But I don’t sense there’s going to be a more prolonged investment, but if it happens, it’d be great.”

The most high-profile studio entrance into the movie theater market was Sony Pictures Entertainment’s acquisition of theater chain Alamo Drafthouse in 2024. Founded by Karrie and Tim League in 1997, the company made its name as an offbeat theater option with dine-in service and strict rules against talking and phone use in its theaters.

“I think we came to it from people who loved movies but didn’t really love our options with chain theaters that we had around,” said Tim League. “We were always looking at how we can build this and build a community around sharing movies we love.”

Alamo Drafthouse began talks with Sony Pictures Entertainment in late 2023 before completing the sale in 2024.

“It was kind of essential to find a new partner as soon as we ran out of money,” said League, who has since stepped back from daily operations at the company and remains involved as Strategic Advisor.

“Why it was appealing for us as a company with our board prior to deciding that Sony was the right acquirer for us is partly because of what that also meant in terms of resources that Sony could offer… Not only in terms of Sony [being] a very big, well-capitalized company but reputationally, very financially stable, [and] very well respected in the space,” said Michael Kustermann, CEO of Alamo Drafthouse and head of Sony Pictures Experiences.

Sony is not involved with day-to-day operations of Alamo Drafthouse. But the parent company’s ownership is evident in occasional special programming, such as airing the Season 4 finale of “Breaking Bad,” which Sony’s TV division produced, in Alamo theaters in September 2026 to celebrate protagonist Walter White’s birthday.

But the largest initiative made possible by Sony’s ownership was the July 2026 announcement that Alamo Drafthouse would purchase the historic Cinerama Dome theater in Hollywood and the attached 14-screen multiplex.

“This has been the white whale for Alamo for a long time,” said Kustermann. He explained Alamo was interested in the location before the Sony deal but didn’t have the financial means to acquire a new flagship location. But after a couple of years of interest and conversations that did not progress, Alamo reached back out after the Sony deal and began serious talks in 2025.

The company plans to operate the Cinerama Dome screen unlike traditional Alamo theaters. Dine-in service will not be offered. Kustermann said that the renovations will be minimal, aiming to keep a similar seat count. The iconic curved screen that defined Cinerama projection will remain, and reprints of films screened in Cinerama such as “It’s a Mad, Mad, Mad, Mad World” will be part of the programming slate.

Renovations to the multiplex will include adding one or two 70mm projectors, karaoke rooms, an updated bar, and an aesthetic redesign inspired by the theater’s 1960s decor.

Blue Fox Entertainment was founded in 2015. The North American distribution and film sales company distributes over a dozen films a year across a variety of genres.“Exhibition is where all the glamour is, right?” said Huntsman. “Distribution is very labor-intensive; you’re supplying content to a theater, to a platform, to DVD. It’s very back office, administrative.”

“I only got into distribution as a way to get into exhibition,” Huntsman explained, adding that Blue Fox Entertainment bought its two theaters to combine the company’s passion for film and enter a new market. “I make no qualms. I’m in the money business, but I’m using movie theaters and film distribution and film sales to do that.”

When the dine-in theater chain iPic went bankrupt in 2026, Blue Fox bid on six of the 12 available locations and ultimately purchased the Westwood, Los Angeles, and New York City theaters. The dine-in service was removed, but each location has a full-service restaurant attached that does not require a cinema ticket.

By rebranding as The Cinemas, Huntsman aims to turn the theaters into viable assets that can make money beyond box office revenue. “I have private events, I have two restaurants at these locations, I do advertisements around the exterior. So if you put all that together, it’s not a bad business. If it was just a standalone straight movie theater, it’s a tough market.”

The economics of why so many new independent theaters are popping up can be traced to a basic reality of the business, according to Laemmle: the simplicity in bringing a theater back to life. “You don’t need to pay anything to acquire inventory. It’s not like opening a bodega where you’ve got to fill it with stuff. You get a film, you promise to pay a percentage of the box office to the studio, and suddenly you’re in business.”

Ticket split rates can vary per title. The rate can be anywhere from 30% for repertory screenings to over 60% for a blockbuster Disney release. Some studios send a range of split rates that can be negotiated; others (like Disney) set a non-negotiable rate.

A film’s success can also affect how much a theater owner makes per ticket sale. Speaking to this summer’s releases, Huntsman said that the underperformance of films like “Supergirl” and “Moana” meant he received a larger portion of the box office. But for big hits like “Toy Story 5,” theaters get a smaller piece of the action.

Studios can also control exhibition through clean policies: the practice that if a theater licenses a certain film, it must be on screen when the theater is open. These policies can be especially detrimental to single-screen theaters in rural areas, effectively limiting the variety of films a community can show.

At Smodcastle, Smith planned special programming with Vulgathon, a marathon of all the films in his View Askew universe from “Clerks” to “Clerks III” in order. But while ticket sales were tracking to sell out all 900 seats across five screens, Disney said that if the theater did not leave a screen open for the second weekend of “Deadpool and Wolverine,” the studio would not send them the film to screen for its opening weekend.

“So we had to leave one screen open, for fucking ‘Deadpool’ and shit, that did not sell out,” Smith said.

Advertising revenue also dropped dramatically post-COVID, according to Laemmle. He estimates that the company currently makes 25% of its pre-pandemic revenue through theater advertising. “Ad agencies had a budget that they allocated for in-theater advertising in the pre-pandemic world. All of a sudden, movie theaters were closed so they just took those same ad dollars and moved them somewhere else…That was a significant source of contribution to the bottom line that’s really gone.”

Loss of advertising revenue forces theaters to find new revenue streams. For some major chains like AMC and Regal, that includes pay-for-play trailer programming: where studios can pay to put trailers for their upcoming releases in front of new titles. This also incentivizes longer trailer blocks that can run up to 30 minutes.

Other major sources of revenue for theaters are concessions, which can offer high margins for cheap snacks like popcorn and pre-packaged candy. Beer and wine sales have also been a major boost of revenue for Laemmle Theatres.

The other option: Lean into alternative programming that may not incur as high ticket splits. The Cinemas has been experimenting with testing various repertory titles across different genres to figure out what titles will draw people back into theaters. Their upcoming lineup for November and December 2026 includes “Boyz in the Hood,” “When Harry Met Sally,” and “The Lord of the Rings” trilogy.

For Huntsman, the need for theaters to diversify revenue reflects the current model for how studios release films. “When I grew up seeing movies in theaters primarily in the ‘80s, there were like three studio releases every week…There was always the rom-com, the horror film, the action film, the indie film…Now it’s ‘Fast and the Furious’ comes out, and nobody releases anything for three weeks.” Huntsman added, “So in terms of profitability, [that’s] part of why we’re making the theater a destination.”

Rising labor, rent, and electric bills over the last few years have made it harder for theaters to improve their margins. In a search for more profits, theater operators have taken on new initiatives to upgrade the technologies and amenities associated with theater-going to bring in crowds looking for a more premium experience, with varying degrees of success.

For Alamo Drafthouse, the Sony-owned company received complaints from longtime fans in 2026 after introducing mobile ordering to its theaters, replacing the original pen-and-paper method that involved more engagement with servers. Instead, guests scan QR codes to place orders that are sent directly to the kitchen.

This move drew ire from the Alamo community, who saw it as hypocritical to the company’s prominent No Phones policy. The company’s subreddit became flooded with users saying they wouldn’t be returning to the theater amid the changes. Actor Elijah Wood, an Austin local who frequently appeared at events put on by the chain, criticized the new system, calling it “truly awful” in a post on X.

The company described the QR code ordering system as part of a larger plan to ensure long-term stability and keep innovating the experience, citing past changes like introducing reserved seating and ending its adults-only policy.

An Alamo spokesperson said that the company has not laid off any staff due to introducing QR codes and that it allows servers to handle more tabs. They added the core of the decision was to protect wages and jobs for the company’s staff working 12 months a year, but that QR codes will allow them to hire fewer seasonal staffers.

Tim League declined to comment on the QR code system.

While Alamo Drafthouse pioneered the dine-in model for theaters, League’s newest business venture is to bring exhibition into the luxury space. He launched Metro Private Cinema in 2025, a 20-screen theater in New York City’s Chelsea neighborhood that specializes in small, private theater experiences with fine-dining menus to accompany the films.

Theaters range from four to 20 seats. Bookings start at four hours, and food packages are added to the price. Guests can choose between new releases, special holiday-themed programming, or a specific movie, plus a la carte food.

“Since the dawn of cinema, it has been being tightly packed into a large room with a bunch of strangers,” said League. “So what if we kind of flip that around, and it’s you’re surrounded by friends. And how does that change the experience?”

Pricing for the experience can vary. Example packages on the website list costs starting around $200 per person. When asked about introducing a luxury price point into the theater market, League explains that costs align with the high prices commonplace in the city. “Our meals are $115 for a 13-course meal, which is very much in line with New York pricing.” League added, “We have built a more higher-end, expensive model, but I think what we’re offering is not ridiculous.”

If companies are not expanding the price-point of concessions, the other option is to expand the theatrical viewing experience itself. Sony Pictures Entertainment launched Cosm, a 364-seat immersive theater with an 87-foot curved screen, in 2024. Tickets are roughly $50, with some including themed food options. And massive Las Vegas entertainment complex The Sphere received over $400 million in revenue from sales of its multisensory AI-edited run of “The Wizard of Oz.”

In recent years, audiences have shown growing interest in premium theater presentations. Major studio blockbusters are expected to have exclusive IMAX runs. Films like “Sinners” and “The Odyssey” have driven a rise in interest in IMAX 70mm screenings, letting audiences see movies in the format directors intended.

CJ 4DPlex, the developer of premium screening formats ScreenX and 4DX theaters, reported a 26% increase in revenue in the first half of 2026 compared to 2025. Their technology includes 270-degree panoramic presentations or immersive 4DX theaters with moving seats and water effects. Ticket surcharges can range from $3 to $7 for ScreenX showings and up to $10 for 4DX tickets, compared to a traditional 2D ticket.

But the desire to jump into premium formats is not universal. Laemmle said his theaters have no plans to offer advanced presentations. “We’re not necessarily engaged in the large format with the higher ticket price because we believe that movie-going should be something that’s done regularly…Moviegoing historically was the cheapest form of out-of-home entertainment, and we believe it should stay that way.”

The movie theater industry has always existed on a wire’s edge. Owners and monopolies have come and gone. Projection trends like Cinerama and Vistavision had their moments before becoming obsolete. Television, VHS, DVDs, and streaming have all carried the threat of being the final innovation that would put theatergoing in the past forever.

“The death of our industry has been predicted since the ‘50s with every new turn,” said League. “I just think there’s [now] pressure not to lose sight of the fragility of being an awesome third space.”

2026 is currently on track to have the best box office performance globally since 2019, with the year expected to end with $35.7 billion in global ticket sales.

For Huntsman, the increase is corollary to the output the studios offer: that the box office success of “The Odyssey” and “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is more tied to quality than any other metric. “Anyone that says, ‘Oh, movie theaters are back,” they didn’t go anywhere. There just weren’t any good movies playing.”

At Laemmle Theatres, the biggest draws of the year have been indie success stories, with films like “You Can See Everything,” “NAZA,” and “Filipiñana” bringing the theater some of its largest ticket sales.

Speaking with a variety of theater operators, the common thread in running a successful theater wasn’t what was on the screen. The key was understanding each theater’s audience. For Laemmle Theatres, it’s typically older people who go to the movies often and have a wide variety of tastes. At Metro Cinema, it’s New Yorkers with the funds to splurge on an elevated experience for special occasions. And at Smodcastle, it’s Kevin Smith fans looking for programming only Kevin Smith can provide.

The full scale of how COVID-19 changed culture has yet to be fully realized. But the renewed investment in owning and innovating movie theaters speaks to a broader desire to safeguard community spaces where people can exist between work and home. The theater industry’s revenue streams are more diversified than they’ve been in years. The allure of owning a movie theater isn’t just about making money; public goodwill has added intangible rewards for exhibitors for keeping theaters alive.

Or as Smith said, “It’s good for the heart, good for the soul, good for the optics, good for the brand.”

#3362. The Best Early Black Friday Deals on Smartwatches and Fitness Trackers

Black Friday isn't until Nov. 27, but the early Black Friday sales are in full swing. I've been keeping an eye on all the best fitness trackers and smartwatch deals so that you can snag the best possible price from now until the end of Cyber Monday (Nov. 30). Whether you want a full-featured fitness smartwatch or a more recovery-focused tracker, here are the discounts you can find right now, including on brands like Apple, Oura, Garmin, and more.

The Oura Ring 5 is at its lowest ever price: $299 for black and silver, $399 for all other colors. These are the lowest prices ever for these rings, which usually go for $399 and $499, respectively. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I've tried, although it's worth noting it requires a $5.99/month subscription fee.

For an even cheaper deal, the older Oura Ring 4 is $249—a full $100 off its list price of $349. If you opt for "stealth" (matte black), the price is $279; for gold, it's $286.61, down from $399. While this model has since been replaced by the Oura Ring 5, it's still an accurate and comfortable smart ring—especially if tracking your sleep is your priority.

Whoop may be one of the most expensive smart bands out there, thanks to its subscription-only model. But that price is particularly low right now, since the Peak membership that normally goes for $239 is now $199. Peak is the middle tier, and it's the one I recommend. While you can get Whoop One for $189 in this sale, the $10 you save isn't really worth it given the features you'd be missing. I also wouldn't normally recommend Whoop Life, since its ECG readings and blood pressure estimates aren't really worth the extra $100+. That said, if you do want it, the Life tier is $299 right now instead of $359.

The new Luna band is on sale for $119.20, down from a normal price of $149. The Luna band is made by Indian smartwatch company Noise, the same company behind the Luna Ring that I reviewed last year. The ring is no longer available in the U.S., but the band is. It's a Whoop-style screenless fitness tracker, potentially a worthy competitor to the Fitbit Air and other smart bands.

This is the brand-new Apple Watch model, and it's actually worth the upgrade. One of the biggest reasons is that the Series 12's new processor (called, confusingly, the S11 chip) supports some features older Apple Watches can't, and a good rule of thumb is that whenever there's a break in software compatibility, it makes sense to get the newer model. Right now, I'm seeing it for as low as $329, down from the list price of $399. (And if you're stuck deciding between an Apple Watch and a Fitbit, Beth breaks it all down in her comparison of the two watches.)

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is Nothing's latest smartwatch, and it incorporates AI features powered by ChatGPT; you can currently pick it up at a major discount. Originally $99, you can get the CMF Watch 3 Pro for $55. This is the lowest price this smartwatch has been.

If you're looking specifically for a sporty, outdoors watch, Garmin sets the standard. (You could definitely call me something of a Garmin enthusiast.) Here are the best Black Friday deals on Garmin watches that I've seen so far:

The 44mm Garmin Instinct 3 is 249.99 (down from $449.99). The 1.2-inch color AMOLED display makes the screen more readable in bright daylight conditions, and battery life is best-in-class—a must for those going off-grid.

The Garmin Fēnix 8 in titanium with a gray band is $749.99 (down from $999.99). While this is last year's model, it's a perfectly solid option if you don't specifically need the titanium case or the latest mapping engine in the latest Fenix 9 Pro.

The Garmin Forerunner 265 is $299.99 (down from $449.99). Although it isn't the latest and greatest anymore, this is still a fan favorite among Garmin users. It's a step above entry-level options, with dual-band GPS, power meter compatibility, and advanced analytics (like training status).

These aren't the only sales you'll see on fitness watches and trackers during the big shopping holiday; the following brands have announced they'll be launching more deals on Nov. 19:

Additionally, though the sale has ended, the Google Pixel Watch 5 was recently marked down by $100; I'll be keeping an eye on this device to see if that particular deal comes back once Black Friday officially arrives.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

The best thing you can do is compare the prices with other retailers that have Black Friday sales. If that seems like too much work, you can just follow our Black Friday coverage (we're already doing all the searching and vetting for you). Some other tips are making sure you're not being sold an older or cheaper version and always reading reviews.

For most people, the Apple Watch SE 3 at $199 is a good starting point, covering everyday fitness tracking, notifications, and essential health features without the higher price of the Series 12. If you want more advanced health monitoring and a more premium smartwatch experience, the Series 12 at $329 is worth considering.

Yes, Garmin is one of the best brands when it comes to rugged sports watches and fitness trackers. The Forerunner line especially, is a go-to pick for accurate and reliable GPS tracking for runners.

#3361. The Mosquito Bowl Won’t Let You Forget What It’s Really About

In this ScreenRant Cover Story, director Peter Berg and original author Buzz Bissinger break down the harrowing new war movie coming to Netflix.

On Christmas Eve in 1944, on the Pacific island of Guadalcanal, two regiments of US Marines training for the invasion of Okinawa played a game of football. That game is, ostensibly, the subject of The Mosquito Bowl, the new film from director Peter Berg that will be available to stream on Netflix from November 25, as well as the 2022 nonfiction book by Buzz Bissinger that inspired it. Considering the pairing of Berg and Bissinger once yielded Friday Night Lights, you might feel like you've heard enough to know what you're in for.

I can assure you, you have not. The Mosquito Bowl is in some ways about football – it is certainly about a handful of football players – but it's really a movie about war, and everything war costs. It follows four young men with hopes, dreams, and plenty of talent on the gridiron, who are diverted from whatever paths their lives may have taken and sent into a world of horrific violence and death. A world that is quite shockingly depicted.

"The goal of the movie was to grab the audience by the throat and make them feel something," Berg told ScreenRant's Liam Crowley in an interview alongside Bissinger. "To make something that feels like a participatory experience, not a spectator experience. I've had people see this film, and after it's like, 'Jesus Christ, I need to just go be quiet.'"

For this ScreenRant Cover Story, Berg and Bissinger talked us through what went into The Mosquito Bowl to create such a gripping watch, from its relationship to the true story and the real people that lived it to the quartet of actors and practical filmmaking that brought their experience to life.

Peter Berg and Buzz Bissinger have been looking for more opportunities to collaborate since Friday Night Lights. Creatively, they just clicked. "I don't think Buzz is the only genius writer out there," Berg told us, "but he is a genius writer, and he's my kind of genius writer."

"We knew each other, we knew each other's movements," Bissinger said. Plus, "we are actually legitimate second cousins."

Each time Bissinger embarked on a new writing project, he'd talk to Berg to see if it had big screen potential. But when he started work on what would become The Mosquito Bowl: A Game of Life and Death in World War II, he knew he had something that his cousin would be interested in.

BISSINGER: [In] 2018-2019, when I was beginning to write it, I told him about it. "Pete, this is perfect for you. It involves war, it involves football. You can blow a lot of things up. I think it's great."

Berg, for his part, got the same feeling, even before he had a chance to read the finished book.

BERG: I just could tell he was kind of on one. He was feeling it, he was doing intense research. I was getting the same energy from him that I got when I started reading Friday Night Lights and hearing that he had moved his family to Odessa, Texas, for a year and was living with this football team. I just sensed that. And knowing him as I do, and having read so many of his articles for Vanity Fair when he was just writing these incredible exposés on different aspects of American culture – I find him to be uniquely American in his perspective. I just knew that there was going to be something in the heart and the soul of what he was doing that was going to be very emotional for me and that I'd be able to connect to.

Bissinger's research came with some serious challenges. For one, of the 65 men who participated in the real Mosquito Bowl, "64 were dead by the time I got involved." Speaking to the last surviving player didn't prove all that helpful: "He honestly said, 'I don't remember what I did yesterday, so I definitely don't remember what I did 80 years ago.'"

So, he relied on what so often become the basis for such historical research, and which, he admits, have become "a lost, dying form": letters.

BISSINGER: These guys had a paper trail... The letters were simple, they were beautiful, they were homespun. You could feel their sense of loss; you could feel how much they missed home; you could feel how much they missed their fiancées. And there was a kind of gentle intimacy and beauty to them.

And then, you take the letters, and it's like any reporting: "What can I draw a string on here? How can I enhance it?" You look at a ton of articles, you look at film, you look at everything you possibly can, and interview other people – although there weren't that many, because they were so young when they died. You just interview as many people as you can, and keep drawing that string, and then you make the decision. "All right, I got enough."

Over time, a story took shape that homed in on four of the game's participants: John McLaughry, who was an All-American as a player at Brown University; Dave Schreiner, a future College Football Hall of Famer from Wisconsin; Bob Bauman, Schreiner's Badger teammate; and Tony Butkovich, who led the nation in rushing in his year at Purdue.

Hopefully, if you see this film, you are going to feel like you are in it.

Part of the choice to focus on these four was the drama in their stories – it will come as no surprise, watching the movie, that not all of them make it home from the war. But it was also "a matter of access."

"John McLaughry was a big star at Brown... His family, who I contacted, had kept everything – everything. Every letter, every report card, everything John had done in his life."

BISSINGER: Bauman was very lucky. I didn't get letters from Bauman until the last six months. I had written the book and his family said, "You know what? We have a foot locker from Bob we have never opened." This is his niece. "We've never opened it." It was his uniform, there were hundreds of letters, there were game balls... That's one of the delicious moments of reporting. You don't expect it, you have no idea, and they call and they say, "Well, by the way, you may be interested, we got hundreds of letters." What? Are you kidding me? I'm dying for that!

Both Berg and Bissinger admit it took a little time to crack the dense book's transition to film. But, eventually, Berg latched onto a story about the loss of innocence in war and a beautiful, fleeting moment when that innocence was recaptured.

Berg's vision for The Mosquito Bowl was "to make something that feels immersive... meaning hopefully, if you see this film, you are going to feel like you are in it." One unexpected source of inspiration in defining this approach? Gaspar Noé's Climax.

BERG: I can't recommend that film, but I will recommend that film if you're up for a challenge. It's a very intense movie, but it's experiential. I wanted to hit at that level. And as part of that, let's do it real.

Let's get real sets. Let's use real bombs, real flamethrowers, as safely as we could. Let's shoot 360 degrees, all that sort of stuff. And we were able to make things feel pretty visceral by doing that.

The impact of The Mosquito Bowl's practical, immersive approach to filming is felt from the very first combat sequence, which also happens to be one of the war's most traumatic. Our four protagonists have arrived in the Pacific and are preparing for their first taste of battle on Tarawa Atoll; they wonder to each other whether several hours of bombardment from US ships will have even left them anyone to fight. But as they approach to make their landing, their Higgins boat runs aground on a shallow reef, still a good distance from shore.

They barely have the chance to realize they've become sitting ducks before enemy fire comes raining down on them.

BERG: These guys have not had that much training, but they have been trained. They think they know what's going to happen. They think they're going to make the beach and fight, and they think that the air superiority and the bombardment from the battleships has softened the enemy. And from the moment it starts, they hit the reefs and everything goes to hell. That, for me, was certainly one of the moments that really pierced me when I read the book.

BISSINGER: I've read a lot about Tarawa. I can tell you, that is depicted [in the movie] to a tee. It is totally accurate. They knew the tide might not be high enough, but they let these kids go out anyway in these boats, and they became sitting ducks. They got hung up on the coral. All of a sudden, they're jumping off these boats. They got their rifles over their heads, because they don't want to get [them] wet, and they're being strafed and mortared by Japanese who were dug into the beach. At least 500 men died, and it was one of, maybe the greatest bloodbath and greatest strategic error that the Americans made during World War II.

To give all that visceral violence the emotional anchor it needs requires the right actors to play the four leads, and at least one decision came naturally. "I think it was Bill Skarsgård first," Berg recalled, "just because I really liked him." He plays Bob Bauman as a tough but upbeat man whose transition from football field to war zone feels the most natural of the group. Though he wouldn't seek it out, he is a little more comfortable with killing, something Skarsgård lends a slightly unsettling quality.

Nicholas Galitzine, who plays John McLaughry, and Ray Nicholson, who plays Tony Butkovich, both came through the audition process. "I was seeing so many actors, and I saw Ray, and I saw Nick... and they both kind of popped for me." Galitzine brings a poise that sells McLaughry as an athlete-scholar, and as the one most inclined to see the poetry in the world, his feelings run closer to the surface. Tony Butkovich, meanwhile, flashes that Nicholson family smile, and it tells you all you need to know about how he came to earn the nickname Touchdown Tony.

Before either of them came on board, however, Berg knew he'd found his Dave Schreiner. He just couldn't tell Netflix yet.

BERG: Right around [the time I cast Bill Skarsgård], I went and saw Sunset Boulevard on Broadway, and I saw Tom Francis. And I went back the next night. I saw it twice. He was so good in it. But I couldn't really offer him the role, because nobody knew who he was. I have a bit of say in casting, but if I'm just telling my bosses at Netflix, "It's Tom Francis," and they're like, "Huh? Who?" I had to read him, but I kind of knew he'd be next...

To see this young kid stand up there and command the stage like he did, that kid has real star power. I mean, I think they all do, but Francis, anyone who's seen Sunset Boulevard knows, has got this sequence where he just walks out into Times Square singing – it's mind-blowing. He's a very, very confident man.

Francis' performance balances sturdiness and vulnerability. Bissinger described the real Schreiner as "a natural," saying that "if you wanted to invent an All-American, Dave Schreiner would be it," and this quality comes through on-screen. He has a strong moral center that makes him the kind of character others would naturally follow. But he's also plagued by doubt, which Francis allows to peek through in very affecting ways.

The Mosquito Bowl cast also features a couple of notable cameos. NFL fans may recognize Pat McAfee, the former punter turned sports analyst, as the primary drill instructor yelling at our heroes as they train on Parris Island. He deflates a football with a bayonet, and even gets to recite the Rifleman's Creed.

Right there alongside him, though? Buzz Bissinger.

BISSINGER: Of course, Pete being who he is, I get to the set, and he says, "What are you doing here?" I say, "Pete, well, I wrote the book, and I'm observing, and I think you know that." He says, "No, get to costume, get to wardrobe! What are you doing?" I said, "Pete, why?" He said, "You're playing a marine drill sergeant." I said, "All right, fine."

I get to costume, they cut my hair, they fit me in an outfit. It was very easy for me to do, because all you have to do is tell people to shut the f**k up. That's all I said. And I was so good, I made the cut. That's one of the proudest moments of my life.

BERG: He stole the scene from Pat. We had to tone him down.

BERG: Once Buzz got going, he started barking at a level of intensity that McAfee couldn't keep up with.

Peter Berg also appears much later in the film, as a commanding officer on Guadalcanal who addresses the men in very frank, chilling terms. That small part was intended for Yellowstone franchise boss Taylor Sheridan, who was going to do it until "he realized how far of a flight it was from Texas to the Gold Coast." Berg was his own second choice, but he has no regrets about playing the role. He explained to SR that he believes acting in his films actually makes him a better filmmaker.

BERG: For me, acting in a film, I always try to give myself a little part, and I just like, five, ten years down the road, looking back and seeing, "Oh wow, I remember what I looked like and what I was feeling..." And the other thing, for me as a director, is I started off as an actor, and I haven't really acted in a long time substantially. And a director can forget or not know what the experience of acting is. And it's a uniquely weird job. It's stressful, and it can bring up insecurities, and you don't really feel like you have a lot of agency...

And as a director, sometimes I forget that, and I just might not be paying enough attention to a specific actor if they're struggling, or they want a little extra attention. Playing a part, and going to set as an actor, and going to the little trailer – which is basically a prison cell that you sit in, waiting for them to bring you into hair and makeup – going through that process humbles me, and reminds me of what I'm asking of the actors, because I forget it sometimes. So, I think it actually makes me more empathetic and probably a better director. My actors would maybe disagree with that, but I think it's true.

Not everything that happens in The Mosquito Bowl exactly mirrors history. Take the game itself: In real life, the two teams of Marines played to a scoreless tie. Staying true to that would've been tantamount to cinematic malpractice.

In approaching the adaptation, Berg made the distinction between 'fact' and 'truth.' Some facts were "critical" – where these men died, for example – and it was important that the movie maintain them. "Then I had to bring them together in ways that [were] not necessarily accurate to how they really all came together," he explained. "I had to condense timelines. They were in different battles, and I had to condense it and put them in one, often, certainly with Tarawa." Or, as he put it, "I changed some of the facts, but I kept the truth."

...you will never understand what these kids went through until you see this film.

Throughout, he trusted Bissinger to be his guiding light.

BERG: There's a line of credibility if you're going to say this is based on a true story. And I know that Buzz is going to be my audience, and he's got a real nose for this kind of thing, and he's going to be protective. I would send him pages and I would talk to him about it – and he jokes and says, "Well, if you're the writer of a book, and you agree to a movie, you got to take the money and shut the f**k up."

There's a little truth to that, but there's not, because the truth is also he would tell me if he thought I was crossing a line or doing something that was offensive or fundamentally violating the authenticity of what he's done. He'd tell me. He wouldn't be able to keep his mouth shut.

BISSINGER: I thought what Pete did – and I see this a lot in the film, having seen it now several times – is he took a basis in fact, and then he would have to mold it in a certain direction, because he's got a vision. He's the director. But I think a lot of it was intact. He even put a parrot into it, which I was shocked, because there's a little scene involving a parrot. Watching it was amazing.

Once creative license had its way, the throughline linking every scene was the unique way that football and war intersected for these young men. The movie's ideas emerge from how these two things spark against each other. According to Bissinger, this, too, is a truth extracted from the facts.

BISSINGER: Football played a curious role... The Navy saved college football because the Navy believed in football as the single best source of combat training for officers. What does it teach you? It teaches you the values that we talk about all the time. It teaches you discipline. It teaches you work ethic. It teaches you how to play when you're hurt. It teaches you about teamwork. It teaches you about realizing your dreams. So, it had a place in World War II.

And of course, the Mosquito Bowl was this unbelievable, bizarre, surreal, serendipitous, incredible football game that was really played on the island of Guadalcanal between not just those four guys, but some of the best college players in the country.

Of the 65 who played, 20 were drafted or would be drafted by the pros. There were seven captains. There were three All-Americans. The best receiver in the country was at the Mosquito Bowl. The best sophomore running back was at the Mosquito Bowl. You had talent. They would've beaten, if you put them together, these regiments, NFL teams. And so there was that moment of football.

But this is not a football book. This is a book about kids who play the game, who love the game, who are getting a ton of exposure, and whether they like it or not, they're going to war. This book is about one thing: war. It's sanitized all the time. War is about murder, war is about death, war is about brutality, and you will never understand what these kids went through until you see this film.

Like the book, The Mosquito Bowl is first and foremost about (thoroughly unsanitized) war. The characters are dragged through some of the worst that humanity has to offer, and the audience right along with them. But as much as the movie catches many of Bissinger's observations about how war and football may be complementary, Berg also uses football as shorthand for everything war is not.

The film opens with a quote from Herbert Hoover: "Older men declare war. But it is youth that must fight and die, and it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs." As much as football may prepare someone for the demands of being a soldier, it is also a game that emphasizes the youth of these men on screen. And, paradoxically, it is also inextricably tied to the futures that these talented players could have had. It's both the innocence and the potential that war costs its participants, all wrapped up in one.

For Berg, the Mosquito Bowl itself is the one moment this all shines through. In the historical record, it may be just one blip on the road to the Battle of Okinawa, which serves as this film's heartrending climax. But it's also this story's reason for being.

"It was the heart and soul of the book," Berg said, "even though it was a small moment, it was a powerful moment. It's what made it all kind of click for me, that you introduce trauma, you go deeper, you go deeper, you go deeper, you know you're headed for real trauma, Okinawa, and there's this moment of respite.

"This moment where these kids just get to be happy, as Buzz says, and just be kids and play."

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3360. 8 Perfect Sci-Fi Books With No Bad Characters

Great character writing is not strictly essential to all speculative fiction, but there's a good reason why it's the backbone of most of history's greatest science fiction books. Though worldbuilding, pacing, stakes, and themes are just as crucial for a piece of science fiction to be truly legendary—and, at best, downright perfect—great characters are also important, which is probably why several of the best sci-fi books ever are also among the sci-fi books with the most interesting characters.

There are many things that can make a sci-fi book character great, but the key element is that readers are able to deeply connect with them regardless of whether they're an alien, a cyborg, or a space-faring human. Throughout the years, eight particularly noteworthy sci-fi books that happen to not have a single bad character, on top of being absolutely faultless themselves.

The mere high-concept pitch for Tamsyn Muir's Gideon the Ninth is so deliciously absurd that it makes it instantly clear why this is such an irresistibly fun modern classic: lesbian necromancers exploring a haunted palace in space for just under 450 pages. It's an effortlessly genre-blending gem with elements of space horror, Gothic suspense, and dark fantasy, making it one of the most purely entertaining and original science fantasy novels the world has seen in years.

Another big part of why Gideon the Ninth is one of the best science fantasy books since 1990 is the fact that the whole ensemble of characters is every bit as memorable as the plot. Gideon herself narrates the book with an irreverent voice that feels like a breath of fresh air for this genre. Muir also makes sure to constantly pair characters that may seem disparate on the surface, but this only results in a constant stream of fun moments that make every character come alive perfectly.

Canadian writers' contributions to science fiction sometimes go underappreciated, which should absolutely not happen when praising the brilliance of Emily St. John Mandel's Station Eleven. Before it was turned into one of the most genuinely perfect miniseries of the last couple of decades, it was one of the most perfect post-apocalyptic novels of the 21st century, breaking away from the genre's usual tropes by celebrating the beauty of life and art rather than dwelling on the grimness of its dystopian premise.

Where a lot of post-apocalyptic fiction tends to flatten its characters into cheap stereotypes, Mandel is careful to never do that. Instead, Station Eleven is built on a large ensemble of characters who, though flawed, feel beautifully human and fully realized. No matter how small their role, every character is given a chance to show off their complexity and moral nuances, including a primary antagonist with so many deep layers that he never feels like any kind of villainous caricature.

When it comes to speculative fiction authors, few have ever been as groundbreaking or influential as Ursula K. Le Guin; and when it comes to the sci-fi works of such legends, few have ever been as revolutionary as The Dispossessed. The winner of all three of the Hugo, Nebula, and Locus Awards for Best Novel, this game-changing masterpiece strikes a faultless balance between utopian and dystopian sci-fi, exploring how no sociopolitical system is ever truly finished or beyond any need for change.

It's one of the best soft sci-fi books of all time, written with the utmost intelligence throughout—that intelligence extending to the phenomenal character writing. It would have been abundantly easy for any lesser writer to allow their characters to become mouthpieces for political or philosophical ideologies, but Le Guin never does that. Instead, her characters are vulnerable, psychologically complex, and deeply human. Shevek is one of Le Guin's most enrapturing protagonists, and the rest of the ensemble is just as important in elevating the book's thought-provoking themes.

The 20th century saw the publication of many a great book set on Mars, but remarkably few of them were better than Kim Stanley Robinson's Red Mars. This landmark in modern hard sci-fi writing is a must-read for anyone who loves the genre, setting a new standard for realistic Mars colonization narratives and sociologically complex world-building. It won the Nebula Award and launched the equally successful Mars trilogy; but as great as its sequels are, it's Red Mars that stands out as the best.

On top of the nearly unmatched scientific rigor, the jaw-dropping sense of scale, and the central philosophical question of whether humanity should prioritize terraforming Mars for humanity's benefit or preserving its natural life, you get some of the most human and believable character writing that hard sci-fi literature has ever seen. Every character seems to embody a different attitude toward the core ethical question that fuels the narrative's sense of momentum, but those attitudes feel deeply ingrained into their arcs rather than making them feel like cardboard-cutout archetypes.

Leviathan Wakes and the Expanse series that it sparked were born as a pitch for a massively multiplayer online role-playing game, which then evolved into a tabletop RPG campaign. The journey culminated when Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck, writing under the pen name of James S. A. Corey, finally put pen to paper and turned the concept into Leviathan Wakes, which ended up being one of the greatest space opera books of all time. Grounded, tonally nuanced, and full of geopolitical complexity, it's a perfect masterpiece through and through.

It should come as no surprise that a book which was born out of an RPG campaign has characters with very distinct skills and personalities, clear motivations, and ensemble chemistry that feels remarkably organic. The rest of the Expanse series also has excellent character writing, but Leviathan Wakes perhaps deserves the most credit for being the one to introduce this incredibly memorable cast. As perfect narrative foils for each other, Jim and Joe are the best dual protagonists that a hard sci-fi space opera could possibly ask for.

There are many who would still praise Frank Herbert's Dune as the single greatest and most influential sci-fi novel of the 20th century. Regardless of superlatives, there's practically no denying that as far as space opera books go, it doesn't get much more perfect than this. Thematically layered and narratively momentous, this cautionary tale against the dangers of charismatic leaders and religious fanaticism has only kept getting better with age.

It's one of the most essential sci-fi books to read before kicking the bucket, and that's in no small measure thanks to how timeless and memorable the character writing is. Paul is such a complex and layered protagonist that many people back in the '60s (and today) misunderstood him and saw him as a tragic hero rather than a cautionary figure. Then you get villains like Baron Harkonnen and Feyd-Rautha, and secondary characters like Chani and the Lady Jessica, all amounting to one of the most iconic ensemble casts in the history of sci-fi literature.

If Dan Simmons' Hyperion is one of the most amazing sci-fi books ever written—and it is— it's in no small measure thanks to the character writing. However, by no means is that the only strength that this masterpiece has going for it. Borrowing the structure of Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales, Simmons gave birth to not only the origin of the incredible Hyperion Cantos series, but also to one of the most ambitious and masterfully genre-blending sci-fi novels ever written.

Indeed, Hyperion is an absolute masterclass in virtually every way that matters in sci-fi writing, which inevitably brings the conversation back to its many fascinating characters. Because each pilgrim in this story gets roughly a novella-length backstory dedicated to their psychology and motivations, the characters become the book's entire plot. No one here is a clear-cut hero, which generates friction between characters that likewise results in the book's most engrossing and unforgettable moments of narrative momentum.

Who, if not Ursula K. Le Guin, could possibly be said to be responsible for not only one, but two of the sci-fi books with the most perfect character writing in the genre's history? When it comes to asking what the most perfect sci-fi novel Le Guin ever wrote could be, it's not actually much of a debate at all: Fans tend to agree that it has to be The Left Hand of Darkness. One of the best sci-fi books written since Dune, The Left Hand of Darkness won the Hugo and Nebula Awards thanks to how it completely revolutionized how sci-fi authors wrote first contact stories.

The novel mainly relies on two of the greatest and most fascinating characters that sci-fi literature has ever produced: Genly, a well-meaning but subtly prejudiced Starfleet captain whose journey of learning how to be humble and open-minded is the emotional heart of The Left Hand of Darkness; and Estraven, a disgraced prime minister whose dynamic with Genly is so enrapturing that it's reason enough for any sci-fi fan to immediately pick up this absolutely perfect novel. Add to that an ensemble of great side characters as the cherry on top, and you get one of the best sci-fi books in history.

#3355. GTA 6 PC Port Officially Shut Down By Rockstar

Grand Theft Auto 6 is smashing records in sales, but it's currently doing so without any assistance from the PC market. Despite the juggernaut status of the game's launch, it's only available to those with a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S, leaving plenty of fans anticipating the game to wait until a PC release that is assumed to be on the way.

Some fans who aren't willing to wait, however, have attempted to take things into their own hands first. The biggest project to bring GTA 6 to PC was a recompilation effort called "Leonida," but its development is officially over, in part due to GTA 6 Rockstar Games stepping in.

On X, "Leonida" creator NotRexed announced that they were stepping away from the project thanks to issues that they "can't control." The announcement followed its disappearance from GitHub on the previous day. In a follow-up tweet, they clarified that Rockstar taking down their server was one part of the reason for quitting, but that they already had too much going on as a teenager "without having middle aged men yell and complain to you on discord."

Leonida was intended to provide a framework for running GTA 6 on PC, natively running the code thanks to the similarity of Xbox and PC architecture, reimplementing Xbox system software, and translating graphics computing programs. While it was still in an early stage of development, making it impossible to actually play the game on PC at the moment, it was considered a promising foundation for playability in the future.

Leonida's shutdown likely won't be the last anyone sees of GTA 6 recompilation projects, as the wait for a PC port will leave plenty of fans with time on their hands. Recomps have become increasingly common in recent months thanks to the accessibility of pulling them off with the use of AI "vibe coding," although there have also been recent projects made entirely manually with a higher standard of all-human coding.

For those who are able to play GTA 6 on consoles, it's proven to be a technical masterpiece. The game pushes the PS5 and Xbox Series X to their limits, but it manages to retain visual clarity, using traditional scaling solutions to bump up an internal 1440p resolution to 4K output rather than relying on a sub-HD resolution and a scaling solution like DLSS for blurrier results. Xbox Series S takes a hit, unsurprisingly, but the results are still impressive considering the system's weaknesses.

In terms of performance, the biggest appeal of a PC port would be the potential for 60 FPS performance, which is currently inaccessible even on the PS5 Pro. A port will also open the door to modding, which, in traditional Grand Theft Auto fashion, will doubtless take the game in some wild new directions. Hopefully, Rockstar Games will introduce the world to an official PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6 in 2026, along with the anticipated release of a new online mode.

High Potential was about a slam dunk to earn the coveted lead-in for the network's first Super Bowl in a decade. Enough viewers have fallen in love with Morgan and her unconventional crime-solving ways to make the series a suitably buzzy pick to follow up the biggest sporting event of the year in the U.S.

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

Created by Drew Goddard, High Potential has seen Morgan rise from an LAPD cleaner with an IQ of 160 to a trusted civilian consultant of the Major Crimes Division, using her intellect to solve the crimes that vex the police. Her unique approach makes her the surprisingly perfect partner for the by-the-books detective Karadec (Daniel Sunjata), whose own methods tend to run up against the sleuth's. Season 3 will pick up after a climactic finale that saw Captain Wagner (Steve Howey) left on death's door by a gunshot and Morgan's missing husband, Roman, potentially visit their daughter's art show under the cloak of secrecy. As such, Howey will be sitting out this season, but Javicia Leslie joins Olson and Sunjata among the returning cast, alongside Deniz Akdeniz, Amirah J, Matthew Lamb, and Judy Reyes rounding out the bunch.

#3350. Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.
