#3347. 10 TV Shows Recommended By Oprah

Few figures have shaped the television industry as much as Oprah Winfrey. Throughout her decades-long career, the legendary talk show host has become one of entertainment's most influential voices, using her platform to introduce audiences to compelling stories and talented performers. Although she is best known for The Oprah Winfrey Show, her influence extends far beyond the programs she has hosted herself.

Oprah's recommendations have long carried considerable weight, particularly in literature. Her celebrated book club has introduced millions of readers to new authors and unforgettable stories, demonstrating her ability to influence what audiences consume. However, her appreciation for powerful storytelling isn't limited to the written word.

Television has undergone a remarkable transformation throughout Oprah's career, evolving from traditional sitcoms and procedural dramas into an industry increasingly defined by ambitious narratives and morally complex characters. Her recommendations reflect that evolution, encompassing groundbreaking comedies, acclaimed dramas, and historical series that have helped redefine what television can accomplish.

From beloved classics that challenged societal expectations to modern productions that pushed the boundaries of serialized storytelling, the television shows recommended by Oprah represent some of the medium's most celebrated achievements. While these programs differ considerably in tone and subject matter, each offers something that has resonated with audiences and contributed to television's enduring cultural impact.

Few sitcoms have developed quite the same cult following as Arrested Development. Created by Mitchell Hurwitz, the series follows Michael Bluth (Jason Bateman) as he attempts to hold his dysfunctional family together after his father is arrested for financial crimes. Unfortunately, the Bluth family's selfishness and questionable decision-making continually undermine Michael's attempts to restore some semblance of normalcy.

What distinguishes Arrested Development from traditional sitcoms is its unconventional approach to comedy. Its intricate running jokes, clever callbacks, and layered storytelling reward attentive viewers, with seemingly insignificant moments often becoming important several episodes later.

Although the series struggled to attract a large audience during its original Fox run, its popularity grew considerably afterward, eventually prompting Netflix to revive it. Right from Arrested Development's masterful pilot episode, its distinctive comedic style has helped establish the series as one of television's most influential modern sitcoms.

Created by David Simon, HBO's The Wire offers an uncompromising examination of Baltimore through the interconnected lives of police officers, drug dealers, politicians, and ordinary citizens. Rather than following the familiar structure of a conventional crime procedural, the series explores how deeply entrenched institutional failures affect nearly every aspect of the city.

Each of The Wire's five seasons examines a different institution, gradually expanding its perspective beyond law enforcement to include organized labor, education, politics, and journalism. This ambitious approach allows the series to examine systemic problems without reducing them to individual villains or straightforward solutions.

The best TV shows of all time will be debated forever, but there are clear contenders. These are the very best TV shows of all time, ranked.

The Wire​​​​​​'s morally complex characters and commitment to realism distinguish it from other crime dramas, while its social commentary remains relevant long after its conclusion. Although it never became a major ratings phenomenon, The Wire has earned widespread recognition as one of the greatest television dramas ever made.

Breaking Bad transformed what initially seemed like a straightforward crime drama into one of television's most compelling character studies. Created by Vince Gilligan, the AMC series follows Walter White (Bryan Cranston), a high school chemistry teacher who begins manufacturing methamphetamine after receiving a terminal cancer diagnosis. What starts as an attempt to provide financial security for his family gradually becomes something far more sinister.

Walter White's transformation from an apparently unassuming teacher into the ruthless Heisenberg remains one of television's most memorable character arcs. His increasingly destructive decisions also demonstrate how easily audiences can become invested in morally reprehensible protagonists.

Alongside Aaron Paul's performance as Jesse Pinkman, the show's meticulous storytelling and escalating tension helped redefine expectations for serialized television dramas. Its enduring popularity eventually led to the acclaimed prequel Better Call Saul, further expanding the franchise's legacy.

Adapted from George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire novels, HBO's Game of Thrones became a worldwide phenomenon through its ambitious world-building and willingness to challenge traditional fantasy conventions. Set primarily in the fictional continents of Westeros and Essos, the series follows rival families competing for political power while an ancient supernatural threat emerges beyond the northern border.

Rather than relying on straightforward distinctions between heroes and villains, Game of Thrones develops an expansive ensemble of morally complicated characters whose competing ambitions frequently lead to devastating consequences. The show's shocking character deaths and elaborate political maneuvering helped make the series appointment television, generating widespread discussion between episodes.

Although Game of Thrones' eighth and final season remains controversial, its extraordinary production values, cultural influence, and ability to bring epic fantasy to mainstream television have secured its place in entertainment history.

Larry David built upon his success as the co-creator of Seinfeld with HBO's Curb Your Enthusiasm, a comedy that takes the awkwardness of everyday social interactions to absurd extremes. David stars as a fictionalized version of himself, whose inability to tolerate minor inconveniences or follow unspoken social conventions regularly creates elaborate misunderstandings.

Unlike traditional scripted sitcoms, Curb Your Enthusiasm relies heavily on improvisation, allowing its performers to develop conversations around predetermined story outlines. This approach gives the series a distinctive sense of spontaneity while making its increasingly ridiculous situations feel surprisingly believable.

Throughout Curb Your Enthusiasm's 12 seasons, the comedy also attracted numerous celebrity guest stars, frequently portraying exaggerated versions of themselves. David's willingness to expose the absurdities of social etiquette, even when his character is so often clearly in the wrong, helped establish Curb Your Enthusiasm as a defining achievement in modern television comedy.

Created by Matthew Weiner, AMC's Mad Men transports audiences into the competitive world of advertising during the 1960s. Mad Men primarily follows Don Draper (Jon Hamm), a talented but deeply troubled ad executive whose carefully constructed professional identity conceals a complicated personal history.

Don Draper may have had 3 wives in Mad Men, but that didn't stop Sterling Cooper's creative director from having affairs with 18 women in the series.

Through Don and his colleagues, the show explores the era's changing social expectations and cultural attitudes. Although Mad Men unfolds against the backdrop of a glamorous advertising industry, its greatest strength lies in its examination of deeply flawed characters navigating personal and professional challenges.

The series particularly excels in its portrayal of women confronting workplace discrimination and shifting gender roles, with Peggy Olson and Joan Holloway emerging as two of its most compelling characters. Its meticulous period details and sophisticated writing helped establish Mad Men as a defining example of prestige television.

Few period dramas have achieved the widespread popularity of Downton Abbey. Created by Julian Fellowes, the British series follows the aristocratic Crawley family and their household staff as they navigate the dramatic social changes of early 20th-century England.

Beginning shortly after the sinking of the Titanic, the story explores how historical events gradually transform the lives of those living at the fictional Yorkshire estate. Although the series features the lavish costumes and elaborate settings associated with traditional period dramas, its appeal extends beyond its impressive production design.

By exploring the relationships between the Crawleys and their servants, Downton Abbey examines class divisions alongside the personal struggles shared across social boundaries. Its combination of historical storytelling, family drama, and romance attracted an international audience, eventually inspiring multiple feature films that continued the beloved characters' stories beyond the original series.

Based on Piper Kerman's memoir and created by Jenji Kohan, Netflix's Orange Is the New Black follows Piper Chapman (Taylor Schilling), a privileged woman sentenced to prison for a crime committed years earlier. Initially centered on Piper's adjustment to life behind bars, the series gradually expands its focus to explore the experiences of an exceptionally diverse ensemble of incarcerated women.

Orange Is the New Black distinguishes itself by balancing dark comedy with serious examinations of systemic inequality. Its use of flashbacks provides valuable insight into the women's lives before incarceration, challenging audiences to reconsider their initial perceptions of individual characters.

The series also broke significant ground through its representation of LGBTQ+ characters and its exploration of issues affecting marginalized communities. As one of Netflix's earliest original successes, Orange Is the New Black helped demonstrate the potential of streaming platforms to produce culturally influential television.

HBO's The Sopranos fundamentally changed expectations for television drama when it premiered in 1999. Created by David Chase, the series follows New Jersey mob boss Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini), whose struggles with anxiety lead him to seek psychiatric treatment. Balancing the demands of organized crime with his complicated family relationships, Tony becomes an increasingly fascinating examination of power, masculinity, and moral corruption.

Rather than presenting its central character as a conventional hero, The Sopranos challenges audiences to sympathize with someone capable of extraordinary cruelty. Its psychological complexity and willingness to explore uncomfortable subjects helped popularize the morally ambiguous television antihero.

From The Wire to Breaking Bad to Mare of Easttown, TV audiences have been treated to all kinds of crime drama masterpieces over the years.

The series also demonstrated that television could deliver the same narrative sophistication traditionally associated with acclaimed cinema. Its influence remains evident in countless subsequent dramas, particularly those built around deeply flawed protagonists, making The Sopranos one of the most influential shows in television history.

Long before television became dominated by complicated antiheroes and serialized dramas, The Mary Tyler Moore Show was challenging expectations through its portrayal of an independent career woman. The universally loved sitcom stars Mary Tyler Moore as Mary Richards, a single woman who moves to Minneapolis and begins working as an associate producer at a local television station.

Rather than defining Mary primarily through her romantic relationships, the series emphasizes her professional ambitions, friendships, and personal independence. Premiering during a period of significant cultural change, The Mary Tyler Moore Show offered a groundbreaking depiction of a woman building a fulfilling life outside traditional expectations of marriage and motherhood.

Its talented ensemble and sophisticated humor also helped redefine the workplace sitcom, influencing generations of television comedies. More than five decades after its premiere, the show's progressive storytelling and enduring charm remain essential parts of its extraordinary legacy. Oprah Winfrey has frequently cited The Mary Tyler Moore Show as one of her personal favorites, saying the iconic sitcom is what inspired her to create her own TV show.

#3346. 5 'Tulsa King' Actors Who Also Appeared in 'The Sopranos'

Sylvester Stallone's Dwight “The General” Manfredi may be a fish out of water in Oklahoma, but Taylor Sheridan's popular series Tulsa King is a homecoming for anyone who spent the late ’90s and 2000s in the company of one of HBO's best series, The Sopranos. The key to this show's immense success is, without a doubt, co-creator and showrunner Terence Winter, who was an original writer and executive producer on The Sopranos. In 2010, he went on to create another hit for HBO, Boardwalk Empire, bringing some Soprano alumni along with him.

Similar to Boardwalk Empire, Winter has also brought several stars from The Sopranos into the fold of Tulsa King, including Max Casella, who played Benny Fazio, and Annabella Sciorra, who fans remember for her role as Tony's stunning but troubled gumad, Gloria Trillo. While there's still a chance for more familiar faces to show up in Paramount+'s latest success, this list highlights five stars from Tulsa King (almost no one remembers #5) who also appeared in The Sopranos!

Known for starring alongside Neil Patrick Harris on the hit sitcom Doogie Howser, M.D., Max Casella made his first appearance in the Season 1 premiere of Tulsa King as Armand "Manny" Truisi, an ex-soldier for the Invernizzi crime family who fled New York and settled down to start a quiet life with his wife and kids in Tulsa, where he started working for Margaret Devereaux (Dana Delany) at Fennario Ranch. After squashing the past with Manfredi, Truisi joined his crew, but his broken marriage and financial desperation set him on a course of betrayal and self-destruction that ended with him taking his own life at the end of Season 3.

Before he was the Oklahoma Kid, Casella starred in The Sopranos as Benny Fazio, a loyal soldier who worked his way up in the Soprano/DiMeo crime family. Casella made his first appearance in Season 3, Episode 3, "Fortunate Son," as Fazio, who shows up after being released from county jail and is now working for his friend and recently made man, Christopher Moltisanti (Michael Imperioli). Out of the 20-plus episodes he appeared in, Casella's character is mostly remembered by fans for his hilarious tiff with Artie Bucco (John Ventimiglia) in Season 6, which landed him in hot water with Tony.

In Season 1, Episode 4, "Visitation Place," fans meet Manfredi's younger sister, Joanne Manfredi, played by Annabella Sciorra, who had previously starred alongside Stallone in the 1997 crime thriller Cop Land, which also stars other Soprano alumni including Edie Falco, John Ventimiglia, and Tony Sirico. Throughout the show, Joanne has since become a major player in her brother's extensive operation and is one of the few people who can keep Manfredi in check and level-headed. While Joanne is not a woman to be messed with, she has nothing on Sciorra's character from The Sopranos, Gloria Trillo.

Sciorra made her debut in Season 3, Episode 8, "He Is Risen," as the strong-willed and fiery Gloria Trillo, who meets Tony Soprano (James Gandolfini) in Dr. Melfi's (Lorraine Bracco) office and eventually becomes his gumad, but their passionate affair is short-lived after Tony sees her true, toxic nature. Despite her trauma and baggage, fans remember Gloria and Tony's relationship as one of the most revealing and intense dynamics in the entire series, which also led to Tony having a significant breakthrough about his relationship with his mother, Livia (Nancy Marchand). Even though her time on the show was brief, Sciorra delivered an unforgettable performance, and I know I speak for every fan when I say it's nice to see her back in the spotlight on Tulsa King.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

In Season 3 of Tulsa King, Manfredi has his work cut out for him as he goes head-to-head with a powerful Dixie Mafia leader and boss of a moonshine empire, Jeremiah Dunmire, who is played by the underappreciated Robert Patrick. Widely known for his role as T-1000 in James Cameron's Terminator 2: Judgment Day, Patrick gives an intense and merciless performance in Tulsa King and is easily one of the series' best characters, but before he was setting house fires and terrorizing the people of Tulsa, Patrick appeared on The Sopranos as the degenerate gambler, Davey Scatino.

In Season 2, Episode 6, "The Happy Wanderer," fans meet Scatino, the owner of a local sporting goods store who has known Tony and Artie since they were kids. When word reaches Scatino that Tony is taking over Uncle Junior's (Dominic Chianese) executive card game, he weasels his way into the game (unaware that he was manipulated by Tony), but he makes the grave mistake of thinking that his past with the mobster and the friendship between their kids would get him a pass on the massive debt he accumulated. Even though Dunmire and Scatino couldn't be more different, Patrick executes both roles with incredible ease, which essentially showcases his underrated range and versatility as a performer.

Chris Caldovino stars in Tulsa King as Dennis "Goodie" Carangi, a former high-ranking member of the Invernizzi crime family who joined Manfredi's crew as a consigliere and de facto second-in-command after the General severed ties with the Family. Caldovino delivers a powerhouse performance as Goodie, who is known for his unwavering loyalty, cheeky humor, and quick wit, and has since become a recurring fan favorite. Before he became the General's right-hand man, Caldovino briefly appeared in The Sopranos as Phil Leotardo's (Frank Vincent) younger brother, Billy Leotardo.

In Season 5, Episode 3, "Where's Johnny?," viewers meet Billy Leotardo, who is an associate of the Lupertazzi crime family as well as his older brother's partner in crime. As tensions continue to rise between New York families, Tony's cousin, Tony Blundetto (Steve Buscemi), seeks revenge after his mentor, Angelo Garepe (Joe Santos), is murdered by the Leotardo brothers in retaliation, and ends up killing Billy, essentially dragging Tony and his crew into the chaos. Caldovino appeared in a total of nine episodes of The Sopranos, and even though it would have been nice if he stuck around a little longer, it's great to see him front and center in Tulsa King.

Best known for his breakout role as the charming Charles "Lucky" Luciano in Boardwalk Empire, Vincent Piazza stars in Tulsa King as Vince Antonacci, a former capo turned consigliere in the Invernizzi crime family who initially views Manfredi as a threat to his territory after being released from prison and is a driving force behind sending the General out West. Since establishing himself in Tulsa, Antonacci has landed himself on The General's bad side and has been a constant pain in his ass, operating as the middleman between Manfredi and New York's Quiet Ray Renzetti (James Russo). The majority of people might think Piazza followed Winter from Boardwalk Empire, but only die-hard Sopranos fans know that isn't the case.

Piazza made his debut in Season 6 of The Sopranos as Hernan O'Brien, a wealthy and reckless friend of AJ Soprano's (Robert Iller) who gets the mob boss's son involved in the party scene and plenty of trouble. He made his first appearance in Season 6, Episode 8, "Johnny Cakes," appearing in a total of three episodes, with Season 6, Episode 13, "Soprano Home Movies," being his last. In fairness, Piazza was pretty young when he appeared in The Sopranos, and since he only briefly appeared in several episodes, it's easy to understand how some might forget (or not even recognize) that he was in the groundbreaking series.

#3339. Every Major Movie Releasing Over Thanksgiving Weekend 2026, Including Focker-In-Law

Thanksgiving weekend is one of the busiest of the entire year for movie theaters. Each year, several big movies are released in and around the holiday, all vying for top spot at the worldwide box office. This year is no different, with several titles releasing from Wednesday to Friday. Audiences looking to see a movie over the long weekend will certainly have plenty to choose from, even more so than other years.

Last year, for example, Disney had a huge animated release in the form of Zootopia 2. The sequel, which was in development for nine years before finally debuting in theaters, ended up making a huge amount of money at the box office ($1.8 billion worldwide, to be precise). The fact that it was released around the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States certainly helped a great deal financially, as many are off from work and school.

Disney looks set to continue their trend of releasing an animated movie for Thanksgiving this year. This time, it’s Disney's Hexed, an original film that the studio hopes will gain enough of a following to develop sequels and spinoffs. The movie, which has a star-studded cast that includes Hailee Steinfeld and Walton Goggins, is projected to perform better than other original Disney animated releases from the last few years.

There are a lot more Thanksgiving movies beyond Disney, too. There are comedies, dramas, sequels, and some Christmas movies as well. Not only that, but there are plenty of streaming services debuting new movies this week, too, giving audiences a chance to watch new releases from the comfort of their own home.

One of the sequels being released this Thanksgiving is Focker-in-Law. This is the fourth film in the comedy franchise that began with Meet the Parents in 2000. Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro have starred in every installment, and are set to do so again when Focker-in-Law debuts in theaters. They’re also joined by Owen Wilson, Teri Polo, Skyler Gisondo, and Ariana Grande (the latter two are newcomers to the franchise).

Focker-in-Law follows the next generation of the Fockers, as a new member hopes to join the family. This time, it’s Ariana Grande’s character who is engaged to the son of Ben Stiller's Greg Focker, Skyler Gisonodo's Henry Focker. Mirroring the plot of the first movie in regards to the dynamic between Stiller and DeNiro, Greg has reservations about his son's fiancé.

The aforementioned Disney's Hexed is another movie that will release on November 25. Hexed's star-studded cast includes Steinfeld and Goggins, and also features Rashida Jones, Jodie Foster, Stephen Fry, Tracey Ullman, and Dan Stevens. The story follows a young girl named Billie Doe, played by Steinfeld, who enters the world of Hexe, which is the home of witches.

Another sequel releasing over Thanksgiving is The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. From Netflix, the movie directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino, and is a sequel to the latter’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. Here, it’s Brad Pitt who takes center stage, with Cliff Booth serving as the primary protagonist in the new adventure(s), leaving behind Leonardo diCaprio's character.

The new movie follows Cliff Booth eight years after the events of Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. Rick Dalton has now moved to Australia to shoot a television series, so Booth is operating on his own in the film business. The movie shows his many adventures around Hollywood, including helping a famous television star get out of a bad situation.

From Angel Studios, the biographical film Hershey will also release on the same day as Focker-in-Law, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, and more. Hershey, which stars Finn Wittrock as Milton S. Hershey (the founder of the chocolate empire), tells the story of its title character as he builds the company alongside his wife, Kitty.

Hershey will cap another excellent year for Angel Studios. The studio has experienced some modest successes this year, thanks to releases like Drummer Boy and Young Washington.

Christmas is coming early with the release of Bitter Christmas, which also comes out on November 25. A Spanish language film, this project stars Bárbara Lennie and Leonardo Sbaraglia, and they’re joined by Patrick Criado, Victoria Luengo, Milena Smit, Aitana Sánchez-Gijón, and Quim Gutiérrez.

The story is set in two time periods: 2004 (in Madrid, Spain) and 2026 (also in Madrid). The modern-day portion follows a screenwriter working on a script also called Bitter Christmas, whereas the former focuses on a filmmaker undergoing a personal crisis over the holiday season.

One film releasing in a limited capacity this Thanksgiving is All of a Sudden. From Neon, All of a Sudden is a Japanese French production that tells the story of a quick-forming friendship between a playwright and a nurse. The playwright is suffering from stage four cancer and has only a few weeks to live, which is expected to bring a heartbreaking element to their close relationship.

Another limited theatrical release this Thanksgiving is In Waves. An animated production, In Waves is a romantic drama that tells the story of a teenager named AJ, who develops a relationship with a surfer named Kristen. It chronicles their growing bond, showing them navigating life and all its ups and downs (including a sudden illness for Kristen).

Also releasing on November 27 is the movie 14th. From director Ava DuVernay, 14th is a documentary that highlights the history of the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. The documentary also highlights ongoing battles in Washington related to the amendment, and features interviews with key political figures like Stacey Abrams and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Also debutiing during the week of Thanksgiving is Clashing Through the Snow. A holiday romantic comedy in the same vein as a classic Hallmark Christmas movie, Clashing Through the Snow follows two rival editors who are stranded at an airport during a snowstorm, leading to an unlikely love story.

Fitting in nicely with the upcoming college and NFL football slate for Thanksgiving weekend is The Mosquito Bowl. Directed by Peter Berg, The Mosquito Bowl is an adaptation of the nonfiction book by Buzz Bissinger. The story focuses on four college football players who enlist to join the Marines after the tragedy at Pearl Harbor in 1941. The group go on to play a football game on Christmas Eve before flying to Japan to fight in battle.

#3338. Leonardo DiCaprio’s 120-Minute Classic Is Officially Leaving HBO Max

Leonardo DiCaprio is riding high coming off his acclaimed performance in this year's Best Picture winner, One Battle After Another. While he ultimately lost out on another Oscar to Sinners star Michael B. Jordan, he earned no shortage of praise for his comedic, complex, and heartfelt turn as ex-revolutionary Bob Ferguson, living at the heart of Paul Thomas Anderson's modern classic. The future is now looking busy for him too, with his next Martin Scorsese team-up on the way in the psychological thriller What Happens at Night and the long-awaited Heat 2 set to begin filming in January. It's as good a time as ever to catch up on some of the actor's classics, but one of them won't be sticking around on its current streaming home for much longer.

Romeo + Juliet sticks close to the original story despite the change in setting, though it reimagines the Montagues and Capulets as rival gangs wielding pistols called swords rather than actual blades. Its most memorable aspect, however, is that it keeps the Shakespearean English intact for a unique clash in tone. While crashing a costume ball hosted by the Capulet family, Romeo meets and instantly falls in love with their daughter, Juliet, unaware of who she's related to. Their chance encounter becomes the center of a violent clash between the two families, as they try to defy the stars and be together while their blood tries to rip them apart. Rounding out the starry ensemble are Brian Dennehy, John Leguizamo, Miriam Margolyes, Harold Perrineau, Pete Postlethwaite, Paul Sorvino, and Diane Venora.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

You do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

You do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

While Luhrmann's take on the play initially divided critics, the film overcame those mixed reviews to become a cult classic appreciated for its timeless stylization that blends the Bard's work with modern imagery. It now owns a Certified Fresh 79% score from critics on Rotten Tomatoes, with a similarly solid 77% from audiences. At the time, Romeo + Juliet was also a modest box office hit, grossing $147.6 million globally, just over ten times its reported budget. As a further demonstration of how well it has endured over time, GEA Live recently joined forces with Disney and Luhrmann to prepare Romeo + Juliet in Concert, a special event arriving next year that will see a hybrid ensemble perform the music live alongside a screening of the movie. Tickets are on sale now, with the world tour beginning in Williamsport, Pennsylvania on January 9.

Romeo + Juliet departs HBO Max on November 30. Stay tuned here at Collider for more on all the biggest titles coming to and leaving streaming throughout the year.

#3336. This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.)

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.)

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

But this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.)

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

#3333. Gemini Notebook's New Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

David Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years.

He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.  You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

With a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but says you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection."

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

For something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

#3329. 8 Books That Could Become HBO’s Next Big Series

From The Sopranos to The Wire, Succession, The White Lotus, and more, the television network HBO has cultivated a reputation for hard-hitting drama. A shepherd of what many have dubbed “prestige television,” HBO is known for its complex, character-driven stories, big-budget quality, and novelistic scriptwriting. With that said, watching an HBO series is not too far off from tackling a work of literary fiction; you get all the wordplay of a Pulitzer Prize-winning novel, often with a Nicholas Britell-produced soundtrack and some electric makeup looks thrown in for good measure (looking at you, Doniella "Donni" Davy – the head makeup artist on Euphoria).

While many of the network’s shows feel like a juicy, long book, many novels also feel like prime real estate for an HBO series. It’s not uncommon to hear readers bemoan the news that their favorite book is being adapted into a film; “It won’t do it justice!” they cry. Instead, the royal treatment for any sprawling, dark work of fiction is that sweet, sweet miniseries deal. To get, specifically, an HBO adaptation is the ultimate luxury for book fans – just look at the success of book-to-show adaptations like Big Little Lies, Sharp Objects, or Game of Thrones. So, if any producer for the network is reading this, maybe this shortlist of novels can inspire your next brainstorming sessions.

Of course, Donna Tartt’s The Secret History must be included here. The author’s 1992 debut novel invented a subgenre all its own called dark academia. The vibe is all about indulging in classical literature, the arts, and the moody atmosphere of ancient universities – a prime aesthetic for a television adaptation. On top of its gothic overtones and immersive romantic world, The Secret History follows the crimes and exploits of an unforgettable cast of characters.

Richard Papen is an outsider when he moves from sunny California to snowy Vermont to study at the elite Hampden College. There, he becomes acquainted with his fellow Classics students, a small and eclectic band of Greek mythology obsessives. There’s Henry, the group's leader; Francis, a fiery-haired charmer; Charles and Camilla Macaulay, close-knit twins; and Bunny Corcoran, a brash loose cannon. As Richard becomes increasingly locked into the group, the students become ever fixated on the idea of performing their own Bacchanal – an ancient Greek ritual. Eventually, blood is shed, and lives are changed forever.

The Secret History would make a stellar HBO series because it ticks all the boxes: Dark tone, rich character relationships, and an edge-of-your-seat plot that will have viewers biting their fingernails waiting for the next episode. There have been many stalled or canceled attempts to bring this story to the screen, but HBO might just be the network that’s able to do it justice.

Published in 2026, Sarah Wang’s debut novel would be the perfect novel for HBO to adapt in the current political and cultural moment. New Skin introduces audiences to Linli Feng, a Taiwanese American who has returned home to LA after being away for three years. There’s a dirty surprise waiting for her, though; when Linli arrives home, she realizes that her plastic surgery addicted mother, Fanny, is completely unrecognizable.

After years of undergoing back-alley procedures and under-the-table nips and tucks, Fanny needs help. But she might just be too far gone, as she has another surprise in store: Fanny has just been cast in a reality TV competition titled "America’s Beauty Extreme." There, she will compete against other botched contestants for a chance to win reconstructive surgery. Can Linli pull her mother back from the brink of ultimate exploitation?

New Skin is a sharp critique of modern beauty culture that also serves up a dash of body horror and reality TV twists, not to mention a dark look at the immigrant experience in America. For HBO to take this on, the network would need to be ready to get dark and get real about the effects of plastic surgery on mothers' and daughters’ psyches.

Four women, one K-pop idol, and a kidnapping plot that will have viewers glued to their screens – there’s the elevator pitch for HBO. Korean writer Lee Heejoo’s novel Holy Boy is a psychological thriller that delves deep into the dynamics of fan and celebrity relationships, female loneliness, class dynamics, and more. Translated into English by Joheun Lee, this electric novel follows four women who are brought together by their shared love of Yosep, a 21-year-old K-pop megastar.

There’s Ahna, a wealthy woman in her forties; Nami, a young shaman who feels spiritually connected to the star; Mihee, a young 20-something who doesn’t fit in with other girls her age; and Heeae, a former maid who might just have a real-life biological connection to Yosep. In an echo of Stephen King’s Misery, the four women’s parasocial relationships collide, and they end up stealing Yosep away to a palatial mountain estate in the Gangwon Province – a northern coastal region. Believing he was in a car accident that broke his legs, Yosep trusts these women with his life – but they have more sinister intentions than he could ever imagine. If HBO is interested in some international storytelling, Holy Boy is prime miniseries material, packing a thrilling punch and offering up deliciously creepy female characters.

If HBO producers are looking for a sentimental drama to throw into the mix, then Rebecca Makkai’s 2018 novel The Great Believers will tick the box. Set in alternating time periods – 1980s Chicago and 2015 Paris – this novel primarily looks at the emotional and generational effects of the AIDS epidemic, exploring how grief and loss can leave a mark that lasts for decades.

The main character of The Great Believers is Yale Tishman, a young gay man who is dedicated to his job at a local Chicago art gallery. His climb up the career ladder is interrupted, though, when his friends slowly start to die off, and Yale is rocked by the loss of his dear friend Nico. Fast forward to the 20th century, and Nico’s sister, Fiona, is in Paris, trying to track down her wayward daughter.

While abroad, Fiona stays with a photographer friend who covered the 1980s AIDS epidemic as it was unfolding. Confronted with raw footage of the epidemic that took her brother, Fiona must finally face the toll this loss took on her – all the while, back in the 1980s, Yale and his friends must deal with the AIDS crisis in real time. A finalist for the Pulitzer Prize, The Great Believers is prestige television waiting to happen, and would offer audiences a moving look at one of queer history’s darkest chapters.

Take Lena Dunham’s Girls, throw in a gun and a life at stake, and you’ve got Agnes Lives!. Hallie Elizabeth Newton’s 2026 debut novel follows a bored New York socialite named Agnes Mauruer. As she walks out of a SoulCycle class one morning, a thought occurs to her: She must find someone to kill her before tomorrow’s class.

Unfolding like a twisted take on Mrs. Dalloway, the novel spans the course of a single, wild day, as Agnes traverses the back alleys and posh department stores of New York City, hunting for her murderer.

The daughter of a movie-star father and an emotionally absent mother, Agnes has decided that she has nothing to live for; her boyfriend is cruel, her job is meaningless, and her friends? Who knows if they stick around just for the clout or for Agnes's actual companionship. Set in 2014, Agnes Lives! looks back at a more innocent time in American history, before Donald Trump came into power, before #MeToo rocked the culture, and when millennial optimism reigned. Now that nostalgia for that era has hit its peak, this bizarre, sardonic novel is the perfect story to be brought to television in 2026. Imagine the heat of a film like Uncut Gems told through a Shiv Roy-style sad little rich girl, and you’ve got Agnes Lives!

Longlisted for the 2026 Booker Prize, Djamel White’s debut novel is a raw look at Ireland’s criminal underworld and is practically crying out for the HBO treatment. If any viewer has been missing The Wire, which ended in 2008, then this could be the return of poetic crime entertainment they’ve been waiting for. All Them Dogs takes place in West Dublin and follows Tony Ward, an ex-gangster who has been lying low in England for five years.

However, when he returns to his old stomping grounds, things have changed. Tony's former mentor is dead, and the man he used to call his best friend, Kenny, has left the street life. Eager to ingratiate himself with the new gang leadership, Tony will do anything to hasten his climb up the ladder – even if that means teaming up with the notorious crime enforcer Darren "Flute" Walsh. Gritty, violent, and starring characters that have just as many secrets as they do scars, All Them Dogs could very well be the next Peaky Blinders. HBO would be wise to jump on the hype following the Booker Prize longlist announcement and push this adaptation through to production.

The world knows the story of serial killer Ted Bundy, which has been told multiple times over through documentaries, books, and even a Zac Efron-led Netflix movie. But Jessica Knoll’s 2023 thriller Bright Young Women reimagines his killing spree through the perspective of the women who survived the Bundy tirade. The action begins in 1978 in Tallahassee, Florida, where sorority president Pamela Schumacher awakes one morning to find that her sorority sisters have been murdered in a brutal attack.

On the other side of the country, a woman named Tina Cannon is looking for the man who has kidnapped (and likely murdered) her lover, Ruth. As the Florida case becomes national news, Tina travels down South to link up with Pamela. She believes that the two cases are connected and that, together, the two women can find the man responsible. While these female characters are fictional, and the killer at the center of the story is never actually named as Ted Bundy, the similarities are undeniable.

Knoll uses this recognizable mythology to tell a different story: One that celebrates female perseverance, intelligence, and friendship. If HBO wants to hop on the bandwagon of audiences' true-crime obsession, a television adaptation of Bright Young Things could be a great way to offera new perspective on the genre.

Take all the intrigue and affair-having of The White Lotus, and the atmospheric private school setting of The Secret History, and you’ve got the 2023 novel Mrs. S by K. Patrick. Set in an elite all-girls British boarding school over the course of an especially hot summer, this novel tells the story of an illicit lesbian relationship between an unnamed narrator and the headmaster’s wife. The unnamed narrator is a young Australian woman who comes to the school for a seasonal job as a house mother to the girls staying in the dorms.

Foreign and masculine-presenting, the narrator struggles to find her groove on campus. That is, until she connects with Mrs. S – the regal, feminine wife of the school’s headmaster. Aloof and mysterious, Mrs. S sparks new desires in the narrator. As their relationship begins to heat up, the narrator must decide if this is true love, or if she has the power to let Mrs. S go at the end of the summer. Sparsely written, yet packed with intrigue and queer longing, K. Patrick’s novel would make for a lush HBO miniseries – released in the thick of the summer season, of course.

#3328. 10 Shows Like 'The Body' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other shows dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

When pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

Peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

The new Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

#3322. Former NFL Player Alphonso Smith Jr. Cause of Death Revealed

Ex-NFL cornerback Alphonso Smith Jr. was crying and praying in the moments before he died by suicide ... and a newly released police report reveals he fatally shot himself in front of two women, TMZ has learned.

According to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office report obtained by TMZ ... Smith was at a home in Pahokee, Florida, on September 2 when a woman inside heard him crying, praying aloud and speaking to several people on a conference call.

The woman told investigators she tried comforting Smith and getting him to open up ... but he asked her to go upstairs. Moments later, the mother of Smith's children arrived at the home, and both women witnessed him shoot himself while sitting on a living room couch.

Deputies responding to the scene found Smith suffering from a gunshot wound. He was rushed to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead at 3:19 PM.

Toxicology results also revealed THC, the psychoactive compound found in marijuana, was present in his system.

As TMZ previously reported ... sources with direct knowledge told us Smith died by suicide at a Florida housing community.

A troubling Facebook post published around the time of his death also raised concerns about his emotional state, which seemed to show he was struggling before his passing.

Smith was a standout cornerback and a member of the Hall of Fame at Wake Forest, where he earned All-American honors and set an ACC record with 21 career interceptions.

The Denver Broncos selected him in the second round of the 2009 NFL Draft, and he later played for the Detroit Lions. Smith recorded 8 interceptions, returning a pair for touchdowns over 4 NFL seasons.

#3321. 'Red Dead Redemption' Finally Gets a Massive $100M Live-Action Adaptation Update

Given the success Prime Video has enjoyed with Fallout and HBO with The Last of Us, it's hardly surprising that Hollywood has been looking to get its hands on some of the biggest properties in the video game industry, although arguably the biggest of them all has remained frustratingly out of reach. Rockstar Games has just released Grand Theft Auto VI after a 13-year wait between installments, and given how much money Rockstar makes from its games alone, you can understand why the company hasn't felt a particular need to get involved with Hollywood. However, anyone who's spent the last few years watching Taylor Sheridan's Yellowstone spin-offs will probably be quite interested in which of Rockstar's franchises the company is reportedly more willing to entertain offers for.

According to a new report from Lesley Goldberg at The Ankler, Rockstar Games is reportedly open to bringing Red Dead Redemption to either film or television, despite continuing to reject approaches from Hollywood to adapt Grand Theft Auto. And given the popularity of the Western franchise, which hasn't had a new installment since 2018, getting the rights to adapt the games isn't going to come cheap. An agent who works with writers in the video game industry told Goldberg:

“At one point, they were throwing around a purchase price of more than $100 million minimum for licensing rights.”

That's $100 million just to get the rights, before anybody has even saddled up a horse. For comparison, as Goldberg notes, Amazon spent $250 million acquiring the global television rights to The Lord of the Rings in 2017. We're only speculating when we say the deal to secure the rights is entirely dependent on whether or not Gavin can be located.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

Anyone who's played Red Dead Redemption 2 will know that, for all the time we spent robbing trains and riding around the countryside, it was the relationship between Arthur Morgan (Roger Clark) and Dutch van der Linde (Benjamin Byron Davis) that made the game such a compelling experience. Watching Arthur gradually come to terms with the fact that the man he'd looked up to for much of his life wasn't necessarily the man he thought he was would lend itself particularly well to a long-form television adaptation. And of course, it would naturally lead into a second season following John Marston (Rob Wiethoff), the protagonist of the original Red Dead Redemption.

The success of 1883 and 1923 has also demonstrated that there's an appetite for Westerns on television that extend beyond the modern-day setting of Yellowstone, although there's no indication at this stage that Sheridan, or indeed any particular filmmaker or studio, is involved.

#3320. Report: Apple job listings detail plans for autonomous AI agents

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.
